scholarly_argument_pouderon_free_will_li.description: Pouderon: God created humans, like the angels, free — a 'libre arbitre' (the autexousion, in his transliteration), not a full freedom like God's — so that they can turn toward good or evil. Hence the 'constat paradoxal': evil exists as a consequence of God's goodness, on two counts — he endowed angels and humans with free choice, which presupposed the potentiality of good and evil in the lower world; and the particular providence he delegated to angels turned against humanity, handing it over to the demons.

evidence.quote: Mais Dieu a aussi créé l'homme libre, comme il a créé libres les anges, et l'exercice de cette liberté (il s'agit en fait d'un libre arbitre, to; aujtexouvsion, et non d'une liberté pleine, comme celle de Dieu)
d'autre part parce que l'exercice de la providence sur les hommes, qu'il avait confié aux anges, s'est retourné contre l'humanité, la livrant à la puissance des démons et à la domination du mal

scholarly_argument_pouderon_free_will_li.finding: Quote located verbatim (l. 119-127). Two losses: (1) 'libertarian' is imported; Pouderon writes 'libre arbitre' / 'liberté de choix' and never uses the modern label; (2) the 'constat paradoxal' has two branches — free will AND the delegated providence of the angels turning against humanity — and the node keeps only the first. The list 'Justin, Tatian, Theophilus, Athenagoras' is the node's; Pouderon speaks of 'les Apologistes' (incl. Melito, Ad Diognetum).

scholarly_argument_pouderon_original_hum.description: Pouderon: God did not create man naturally (or entirely) good. Man does have a propensity to good (kinship with God, individual reason), but since God made him free, the original man must be supposed by nature neither good nor bad, able to receive both — a 'double propension' to good and evil willed from the start so that free will can be exercised. Tatian draws the extreme, 'péremptoire' conclusion that the soul is only the receptacle of darkness, a mark of his encratism.

evidence.quote: Dieu n'a donc pas créé l'homme naturellement bon (ou entièrement bon). Certes, l'homme possède en lui une propension au bien
Ainsi, la double propension de l'homme au bien et au mal a été voulue dès l'origine par Dieu pour que l'homme puisse exercer son libre arbitre.
Tatien en conclut un peu péremptoirement que l'âme, loin d'être bonne par nature, n'est que le réceptacle des ténèbres, une position extrême qui est une marque de son encratisme

scholarly_argument_pouderon_original_hum.finding: Quote located verbatim (l. 95-101); Tatian sentence at l. 103-105. But 'morally neutral' flattens Pouderon's construction: he says God did not create man 'naturellement bon', immediately concedes 'Certes, l'homme possède en lui une propension au bien' (kinship with God, reason), and then sums up as a 'double propension de l'homme au bien et au mal' willed so that free will can be exercised.

scholarly_argument_pouderon_stoic_determ.description: Pouderon: whereas the Stoics — 'à en croire leurs adversaires' — implicate God in evil by proclaiming him immanent in changeable, passible matter, and hence in matter that carries evil, the Christian Apologists insist that God is not the author of evil and take care to specify that there is no one beside him to impose evil as he can impose good (texts n°2). The passage concerns divine immanence and the authorship of evil, not determinism.

evidence.quote: Alors que les stoïciens, à en croire leurs adversaires, impliquent Dieu dans le mal, puisqu'ils ils le proclament immanent à la matière changeante et passible, et en conséquence porteuse du mal, les chrétiens insistent au contraire sur le fait que Dieu n'est pas l'auteur du mal

scholarly_argument_pouderon_stoic_determ.finding: Quote located verbatim (l. 40-46) and the body of the description is accurate (it keeps 'à en croire leurs adversaires'). But the heading 'Stoic determinism ... contrasted with Christian free will' adds a topic absent from the passage: Pouderon here contrasts Stoic immanence of God in passible matter (God implicated in evil) with the Christian denial that God is the author of evil. Determinism and free will are not at issue in this passage (they appear only later, l. 293-300, against astrology and gnostic predestination).

scholarly_argument_pouderon_transformati.description: Pouderon: a leitmotiv of the Apologists is that the fault of Adam and Eve profoundly transformed human nature in its very essence. Its main consequence is the intrusion of biological necessities — suffering, illness, bodily desires and needs, death — which are at once the occasions and the motors of the passions and sins that follow (Athenagoras insists on this). But not everything is biological: the primordial fault also brought a 'condition pécheresse' — subjection to Satan or a tendency to evil, tied to the loss of the divine spirit or image, which only baptism heals.

evidence.quote: Ces nécessités biologiques, fruits de la faute initiale, sont donc à la fois les occasions et les moteurs des passions et des péchés qui en résultent, comme le répète à maintes reprises Athénagore
Mais tout n'est pas biologique dans la propension au péché. Car la faute primordiale a aussi entraîné chez l'homme ce qu'il faut bien appeler la condition pécheresse

scholarly_argument_pouderon_transformati.finding: Quote located verbatim (l. 214-224). The node stops before the point of the sentence: the biological necessities are 'à la fois les occasions et les moteurs des passions et des péchés', a leitmotiv of Athenagoras; and it drops the immediate qualification 'Mais tout n'est pas biologique dans la propension au péché' (a 'condition pécheresse', loss of the divine spirit/image, l. 226-235).

scholarly_argument_pouderon_triple_origi.description: Pouderon: in early Christianity, still steeped in Jewish (Enochic) apocalyptic, the original fault is triple: (1) the corruption of the angels, who become demons and, per the Enochic narrative built on Gen 6:1-4, teach humans the practices of sin — this particular etiological narrative is found in Justin and Athenagoras but not in the other Apologists; (2) the disobedience of the 'protoplastes' Adam and Eve, who pass from childlike innocence to adult responsibility and guilt; (3) Cain's fratricide, which introduces murder (texts n°13-14).

evidence.quote: selon le récit hénochien, librement inspiré de Genèse 6, 1-4, les anges déchus vont enseigner aux hommes, avec les arts et les techniques, les mille pratiques du péché : le meurtre, l'impiété, la débauche sexuelle. Ce type de récit étiologique se retrouve à la fois chez Justin et chez Athénagore, mais non chez les autres Apologistes
D'autre part, il y a la désobéissance des hommes, en l'occurrence celle des « protoplastes », Adam et Ève, qui goûtent au fruit défendu

scholarly_argument_pouderon_triple_origi.finding: Quote located verbatim (l. 141-150). Scope error: the sentence 'Ce type de récit étiologique se retrouve ... chez Justin et chez Athénagore, mais non chez les autres Apologistes' concludes the paragraph on the FIRST element only (the Enochic fallen-angel narrative); the node attaches it to the whole triple scheme, as if Adam's disobedience and Cain's fratricide were also absent from the other Apologists — which the text does not say (Theophilus is Pouderon's main witness for Adam/Eve and Cain elsewhere, l. 194-198, 366-372).

scholarly_argument_barclay_2020_grace_cr.description: Barclay (ch. 13), via Luther's Heidelberg Disputation thesis 28: against the dominant philosophical tradition in which love is drawn to a good already present in its object, the love of God 'does not find, but creates what is pleasing to it', confers worth and fashions it out of nothing. On Paul's good news human worth is founded on grace, not on ascribed or achieved 'symbolic capital' — a 'psychology of grace'. Worth resides in the love of God in Christ; Barclay allows (n. 5, Col 1:15-20) that it may reside both in creation and in reconciliation, both 'in Christ'.

evidence.quote: Rather, it *creates* what is pleasing and good, confers it, and fashions it out of nothing.
Thus, the worth of each individual would reside both in their creation and in their reconciliation, and both of these would hold true "in Christ."

scholarly_argument_barclay_2020_grace_cr.finding: Quote located verbatim (l. 1628, ch. 13; anchors page_154-155); 'psychology of grace' and 'symbolic capital' at l. 1626. But 'locates the value of each person not in nature (imago Dei) but in grace' overstates: Barclay's main text grounds worth in 'the love of God in Christ' (l. 1620), and his n. 5 explicitly allows worth to reside 'both in their creation and in their reconciliation', both 'in Christ' (Col 1:15-20). The nature-vs-grace opposition is the node's.

scholarly_argument_barclay_2020_spirit_e.description: Barclay (ch. 8, on Rom 8:9-13): the Spirit does not take the place of the believer, 'as if one agency overrides the other'; Paul instructs believers, who are 'not merely puppets on a string', yet their agency is 'enabled and sourced in the agency of the Spirit'. Believers do not create a new existence but express what has already been created in Christ; the new self is a secondary reality, derived from Christ, which subsists to the extent that it is active. Elsewhere (ch. 12 n. 8) Barclay suggests 'energism' as a 'noncontrastive model' of divine and human agency.

evidence.quote: The Spirit does not *take the place* of the believer, as if one agency overrides the other. Paul can give instructions to believers (here in 8:12--13, and much more in later chapters), who are not merely puppets on a string, controlled by the Spirit. But their agency is enabled and sourced in the agency of the Spirit.
Paul's theology (and his Greek in Phil 2:13) might encourage us to deploy the term "energism," with its noncontrastive model of the relationship between divine and human agency.

scholarly_argument_barclay_2020_spirit_e.finding: The core quote is verbatim (l. 1088, ch. 8 on Rom 8:9-13; anchor page_93), and 'express what has already been created' is in the same paragraph. But the closing gloss puts words in Barclay's mouth: 'non-contrastive' occurs in this book only once, in ch. 12 n. 8 (l. 1554) about the term 'energism' and Phil 2:13, not in the Rom 8 discussion; 'asymmetric' and 'the more God acts, the more the human acts' do not occur anywhere in the file. 'Decisive H1 statement' is thesis framing, not Barclay.

scholarly_argument_belcastro_free_will_l.description: Belcastro hypothesises predestination as the theoretical centre of Origen's thought, in a solution partly irreconcilable with Paul's. Origen's transformation of the idea does not remove the problem: he wants to keep it, interpretable only in his own solution, i.e. the overcoming of the paradox that arises when absolute divine omnipotence and its dispositions are considered together with absolute human freedom of will — which, in Origen's view, would make God's action fall into an insurmountable and blasphemous contradiction. Belcastro treats the definition of free will as dependent on this transformation, not as the centre.

evidence.quote: Il problema della predestinazione è qui ipotizzato come centro teoretico del pensiero origeniano nella diversità, e per certi versi inconciliabilità di soluzione, rispetto a quello paolino

i quali però tendono ad anteporre a quello della ridefinizione della predestinazione i problemi, altrettanto centrali (ma, a mio avviso, dipendenti da questa trasformazione), della definizione della libertà del volere

scholarly_argument_belcastro_free_will_l.finding: Quote located verbatim (l. 66-71, p. 211). But 'making free will central' inverts Belcastro's stance: he hypothesises PREDESTINATION as the 'centro teoretico del pensiero origeniano' and criticises scholars who put the definition of free will first, treating it as 'dipendenti da questa trasformazione' (p. 213). Also the paradox is 'a suo avviso' Origen's perception, and the transformation 'non comporta ... una sua rimozione'. Running header reads ADAMANTIUS 21 (2015), not 22 (2016).

scholarly_argument_belcastro_origen_s_do.description: Belcastro: Origen is the first Christian author to think an organic doctrine of predestination — 'anche se normalizzata e svuotata di qualunque senso paradossale' — and he does so in structural confrontation with gnostic thought, which he reads as a determinist version of the problem, assuming its perspectives and surpassing them synthetically while keeping them dialectically. The debate with the gnostics is too often judged in merely oppositional terms; the gnostics were probably the true initiators of a doctrine of predestination and had already transformed the concept (n. 7-8).

evidence.quote: Origene, in questo senso, è il primo autore cristiano a pensare una dottrina organica della predestinazione (anche se normalizzata e svuotata di qualunque senso paradossale)
Da questo è evidente come anche già gli gnostici abbiano operato prima di Origene una trasformazione semantica (o fusione) del concetto di predestinazione.

scholarly_argument_belcastro_origen_s_do.finding: Quote located verbatim (l. 121-135, p. 212). The node drops the qualification attached to 'primo autore cristiano ... dottrina organica': '(anche se normalizzata e svuotata di qualunque senso paradossale)', and the concession (n. 7-8) that the gnostics were 'probabilmente veri iniziatori' of a doctrine of predestination and had already operated a semantic transformation before Origen. Volume is Adamantius 21 (2015) per running header.

scholarly_argument_belcastro_origen_s_tr.description: Belcastro: Origen's transformation of the Pauline concept expressed by the verb προορίζω passes, in a first sense, from God's predestining action (the verb, and the participial status of the predestined) to 'predestination', a noun expressing a theological doctrine whose history begins with gnostic and Origenian reflection. The transformation does not remove the problem: Origen keeps it, normalised and emptied of any paradoxical sense.

evidence.quote: alla predestinazione, sostantivo che così esprime una dottrina teologica che inizia la sua storia con la riflessione gnostica ed origeniana.
La trasformazione dell'idea di predestinazione in Origene, infatti, non comporta anche una sua rimozione

scholarly_argument_belcastro_origen_s_tr.finding: Quote located verbatim in n. 3 (l. 86-88, p. 211); the Pauline verb is named at l. 61. The node omits that the noun-doctrine 'inizia la sua storia con la riflessione gnostica ed origeniana' — i.e. the transformation is gnostic AND Origenian, not Origen's alone (cf. n. 8). Pages: 211 (n. 3, 'non comporta ... rimozione'), 212 ('normalizzata e svuotata'); nothing on 213 bears on this node.

scholarly_argument_belcastro_predestinat.description: Belcastro (n. 7) agrees only in part with Cipriani: Origen does elaborate a doctrine of predestination first (and radically differently from Augustine's), but in reference to the gnostic thinkers, probably the true initiators of such a doctrine, where Cipriani sees only Origen's opposition. On Cipriani's reading, Belcastro does not accept the substantial flattening of Origen's predestination onto prescience — while granting that prescience remains 'comunque determinante'.

evidence.quote: non concordo con il sostanziale appiattimento di questa sulla (comunque determinante) prescienza.
Concordo solo in parte con N. CIPRIANI

scholarly_argument_belcastro_predestinat.finding: Quote located verbatim in n. 7 (l. 112-151, note begins p. 211, quoted sentence p. 212). The node drops Belcastro's parenthesis conceding that prescience is '(comunque determinante)', and that he agrees 'solo in parte' with Cipriani (he grants Origen a doctrine of predestination before Augustine, but in reference to the gnostics).

scholarly_argument_belcastro_prescience_.description: Belcastro announces (p. 213), to be developed later, Origen's specific reworking of the problem of prescience as 'previsione delle possibilità'. Developed on CRm (p. 220-221): Origen shifts the cause of predestination from prescience-as-cause onto human actions, the content of prescience; God sees merit and can only take note of it, so that predestination is not a cause determining a choice but a prevision confirming the agent's freedom, within a will that remains mutable.

evidence.quote: mi limito ad indicare (lasciando aperta tutta la problematica delle relazioni qui appena tratteggiata), e a sviluppare più oltre, la specifica rielaborazione del problema della prescienza come previsione delle possibilità.
Dunque, la predestinazione non è da considerarsi come causa che determina una scelta, ma come una previsione che conferma la sua libertà.

scholarly_argument_belcastro_prescience_.finding: Quote located verbatim (l. 190-192) but on p. 213, not 212. At this point Belcastro only announces the theme ('mi limito ad indicare ... e a sviluppare più oltre'); 'rather than as determining foreknowledge' is supported later, at p. 221 ('non è da considerarsi come causa che determina una scelta, ma come una previsione'), while 'central to his normalization ... of the charismatic' is the node's splice with n. 11. The verified_reference's 'n. on p. ~205' for Cipriani is wrong: n. 7, pp. 211-212.

scholarly_argument_craig_middle_knowledg.description: Craig (ch. XIII): middle knowledge — God's knowledge of counterfactuals of creaturely freedom — is possible, which suffices to show that God's knowledge of future contingents is not impossible; but as an explanation of prescience it advances little beyond innatism, to which it finally appeals. Its 'real value' is its account of providence and the reconciliation of divine sovereignty with human freedom: so long as middle knowledge is possible, the two are logically consistent. Craig is 'inclined to regard the doctrine as true'.

evidence.quote: it must be admitted t h a t in terms of explaining pre- science, middle knowledge does not make much explanatory advance beyond an innatist view of foreknowledge, since middle knowledge finally appeals to innatism as well.
evidence.citation: [Divine Foreknowledge and human freedom, Craig,1990.md:12404-12407] (Craig 1991, p. 278)

evidence.quote: The real value of the doctrine of middle knowledge comes in the striking account it gives of providence and the reconciliation it effects between divine sovereignty and human freedom.
evidence.citation: [Divine Foreknowledge and human freedom, Craig,1990.md:12407-12410] (Craig 1991, p. 278)

scholarly_argument_craig_middle_knowledg.finding: Quote located (l. 12399-12414, p. 278; OCR letter-spacing aside, verbatim). The node's 'which explains how God can know future contingents' contradicts Craig's own caveat in the quote: for explaining prescience middle knowledge 'does not make much explanatory advance beyond an innatist view'; its 'real value' is the account of providence and the reconciliation of sovereignty and freedom. Craig had already dissolved theological fatalism without middle knowledge (chs. V-X); here he is 'inclined to regard the doctrine as true'.

scholarly_argument_craig_newcomb_s_parad.description: Craig (ch. X): in Nozick's original conditions the predictor does not use precognition, but once the Being is God, whose prediction rests on foreknowledge, a logically demonstrative argument (Plantinga) shows that the only rational choice is the one-box strategy. Craig answers the objections from backward causation and backtracking counterfactuals: our decisions determine God's past beliefs without backward causation or alteration of the past. Foreknowledge entails only that I shall not choose otherwise, not that I cannot; Newcomb's paradox thus vindicates the compatibility of foreknowledge and freedom.

evidence.quote: A parallel argument proves t h a t if one were to choose B2 alone, God would have put $1,000,000 in B2. T h u s , given t h e puzzle conditions, the only rational choice is to choose B 2 alone.
evidence.citation: [Divine Foreknowledge and human freedom, Craig,1990.md:9464-9466] (Craig 1991, p. 211)

evidence.quote: With the justification of the one box strategy, the death of theological fatalism seems ensured.
evidence.citation: [Divine Foreknowledge and human freedom, Craig,1990.md:9930-9932] (Craig 1991, p. 221)

scholarly_argument_craig_newcomb_s_parad.finding: Craig argues the opposite of 'divine foreknowledge does not support the one-box strategy': once the predictor is God with foreknowledge, there is (with Plantinga) 'a logically demonstrative argument for the one box strategy' and 'the only rational choice is to choose B2 alone' (p. 210-211); he defends this against the backward-causation and backtracking-counterfactual objections and concludes that 'with the justification of the one box strategy, the death of theological fatalism seems ensured' (p. 221). The second clause of the node (paradox does not undermine freedom) is correct.

scholarly_argument_craig_temporal_necess.description: Craig (ch. IX), after reviewing Saunders, Pike, Adams, Fischer, Freddoso and Plantinga: 'temporal necessity' is queer and perhaps a misnomer — it concerns counterfactual openness or closedness, not temporality as such. The future is as unalterable as the past, but this logical truth does not threaten freedom. Certain past facts, including God's beliefs about the future, are counterfactually open; only a de facto necessity remains. Intuitions of the past's necessity come from the impossibility of backward causation, which the counterfactual dependence of God's beliefs on future events is not. Temporal necessity is modally weak and no threat to freedom or foreknowledge.

evidence.quote: the notion of temporal necessity is certainly queer and perhaps a misnomer. It really has little to do with temporality per se and everything to do with counterfactual openness or closed- ness.
evidence.citation: [Divine Foreknowledge and human freedom, Craig,1990.md:9150-9152] (Craig 1991, p. 203)

evidence.quote: Oddly enough, then, virtually any past fact is potentially counterfactually open, and the only necessity t h a t remains is purely de facto.
evidence.citation: [Divine Foreknowledge and human freedom, Craig,1990.md:9160-9162] (Craig 1991, p. 203)

scholarly_argument_craig_temporal_necess.finding: Craig does not hold that 'the past is accidentally necessary' with the issue being a 'transfer to future propositions'. His conclusion (pp. 203-204) is that temporal necessity is 'queer and perhaps a misnomer', a matter of counterfactual openness rather than temporality; God's past beliefs are counterfactually open past facts; 'virtually any past fact is potentially counterfactually open, and the only necessity that remains is purely de facto'; the intuition of the past's necessity stems from the impossibility of backward causation.

scholarly_argument_craig_tensed_theory_o.description: Craig favours the A-theory of time over the B-theory, giving only 'a few cursory remarks' (the A-theory captures our intuitions about the sequential nature and transience of time; the B-theory 'spatializes' time) and deferring a fuller defence to a future project on divine eternity. On the A-theory backward causation would be something's being produced by nothing, hence metaphysically impossible (pp. 150-157, 191); this grounds the intuition of the past's necessity without licensing the fatalist's inference.

evidence.quote: I hope t o explore this issue more fully in a future project on the coherence of divine eternity, but a few cursory remarks may here be made. The Α-theory captures more adequately our fundamental intuitions about the sequential nature of time, whereas the B-theory is a distortion guilty of spatializing time.
evidence.citation: [Divine Foreknowledge and human freedom, Craig,1990.md:6989-6994] (Craig 1991, p. 153)

evidence.quote: Given an Α-theory of time, it is metaphysically impossible for a present event to have a future cause.
evidence.citation: [Divine Foreknowledge and human freedom, Craig,1990.md:8615-8616] (Craig 1991, p. 191)

scholarly_argument_craig_tensed_theory_o.finding: Quote located (l. 6987-6994, p. 153, verbatim modulo OCR spacing); A-theory rules out backward causation at pp. 156-157 and 191. But '(tensed, presentist or growing-block theory)' is not Craig's: neither term occurs in the file, and Craig explicitly offers only 'a few cursory remarks', deferring the defence to 'a future project on the coherence of divine eternity'. The node overstates the extent of the defence.

scholarly_argument_crouzel_christ_s_rede.description: Crouzel: Origen's conversion is Platonic in form but Christian in substance because of the stress on Christ's action and grace. 'Ce n'est pas nous qui nous convertissons, mais le Christ qui nous convertit'; man's collaboration is a 'condition sine qua non', yet his will—which itself stems from a certain permanence of the selon-l'image in the sinner—would be ineffective without Christ's Incarnation and Passion. Even the sinner cannot right himself: a 'restriction nécessaire à cette omnipotence du libre arbitre qu'on prête souvent à Origène'. Only Christ, 'notre Isaac', clears the soul's wells and must 'délivrer notre libre arbitre de l'esclavage où le maintenait le péché'.
scholarly_argument_crouzel_christ_s_rede.page_range: 214-215 (folio inferred from running headers; cf. Préface p. 10 for the anti-Pelagian point)

evidence.citation: [05_Origene/(Théologie 34) Henri Crouzel - Théologie de l’image de Dieu chez Origène-Aubier (1956).md:5829]

evidence.quote: omnipotence du libre arbitre qu'on prête souvent à Origène. Seul le
evidence.citation: [05_Origene/(Théologie 34) Henri Crouzel - Théologie de l’image de Dieu chez Origène-Aubier (1956).md:5828]

evidence.quote: inefficace - et cette volonté même provient d'une certaine perma-
evidence.citation: [05_Origene/(Théologie 34) Henri Crouzel - Théologie de l’image de Dieu chez Origène-Aubier (1956).md:5834]

scholarly_argument_crouzel_christ_s_rede.finding: The passage (conversion, voie purgative) is located, but the node inverts one clause: Crouzel writes that the human will itself 'provient d'une certaine permanence du selon-l'image' (the will derives from a persisting image), not that the persistence of the selon-l'image depends on Christ. What depends on Christ is the efficacy of the will and the clearing of the soul's wells; man's collaboration is a 'condition sine qua non'. The anti-Pelagian point is real but stated elsewhere (Préface, p. 10: participation in the image = sanctifying grace). page_range '5828-5831' are md lines, not pages; page_map for this two-column file is unreliable (conf 0.50, gives physical half-page 106). Folio inferred from running headers (l. 5741 = 212/213, l. 5888 = 218/219).

scholarly_argument_frede_alexander_s_shi.description: Frede: Alexander shifts the emphasis so that the moving cause plays the central role, 'thus avoiding a fatal cooperation of all four causes'. Three reasons: (1) an analogy between fate as moving cause in nature and the artist as efficient cause of the statue, ensuring that human decisions and actions are not in fate's domain (167,15); (2) fate becomes an active 'dynamic' ordering force, a rational ordering principle close to natural law that 'echoes the Stoic definition of fate', giving common ground for the critique; (3) limiting fate to the moving cause meets the Stoic restriction of fate to the antecedent cause, the presupposition of their claim that free will, chance and contingency survive.

evidence.quote: plays the central role, thus avoiding a 'fatal' cooperation of all four causes.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Frede - 1982 - The Dramatization of Determinism Alexander of Aphrodisias' De Fato.md:153]

evidence.quote: Third, by limiting fate to the moving cause Alexander also meets the Stoic presupposition of a distinction between their various kinds of causes and the restriction of fate to the role of the antecedent cause, as they define it;
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Frede - 1982 - The Dramatization of Determinism Alexander of Aphrodisias' De Fato.md:172-175]

evidence.quote: comes close to what we would call the concept of a natural law and echoes the Stoic definition of fate.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Frede - 1982 - The Dramatization of Determinism Alexander of Aphrodisias' De Fato.md:164-165]

scholarly_argument_frede_alexander_s_shi.finding: Reasons (1) and (2) are faithful, but the node's reason (3) is not Frede's third reason. 'Avoiding a fatal cooperation of all four causes' is Frede's description of the effect of the shift, stated before the enumeration. Her actual third reason: 'by limiting fate to the moving cause Alexander also meets the Stoic presupposition of a distinction between their various kinds of causes and the restriction of fate to the role of the antecedent cause'. Frede also notes that the definition of nature(=fate) as a rational ordering principle 'echoes the Stoic definition of fate' and creates common ground for the critique. Page is 279, not 278 (page_map conf 0.95).

scholarly_argument_hick_determinism_and_.description: Hick: Calvin's predestination, more consistent than Augustine's in attributing reprobation to God's positive decree, has a genuine religious intention (magnifying free grace) but frustrates it: by stressing sovereign divine freedom in abstraction from the whole Christian conception of God it 'call[s] God's goodness and love seriously into question'; creating beings predetermined to deserve unending punishment is not worthy of worship. Calvin's compatibilist-style definition of freedom (voluntary, not compelled) is the very one Flew turns against the free-will defence. Irenaean thinkers since Schleiermacher see eternal hell as making theodicy impossible (p. 237).
scholarly_argument_hick_determinism_and_.page_range: 121-123 (cf. 237) — body not in the .md; from the FULL pdf

evidence.quote: Calvin so emphasizes the sovereign divine freedom, in abstraction from the total Christian conception of the divine nature, as to call God's goodness and love seriously into question.
It is to be noted that this is precisely the definition of freedom that is used by a contemporary philosopher to create difficulties for the * free-will defence' in theodicy.

scholarly_argument_hick_determinism_and_.finding: The fonds .md (20 pp.) holds only front matter (contents, prefaces, McCord Adams's Foreword); the body was checked in Hick_1966_Evil_and_the_God_of_Love_FULL.pdf (native text, pdftotext, folios read from page footers; no page_map entry). Section 'Predestination versus theodicy' is pp. 121-123. Hick's objection is not that predestination 'makes God the author of sin' (phrase absent) but that Calvin's double decree, by emphasising sovereign freedom 'in abstraction from the total Christian conception of the divine nature', calls 'God's goodness and love seriously into question'; and (p. 237) the doctrine of eternal hell renders 'a Christian theodicy impossible'. The free-will-defence link is only that Calvin's definition of freedom is the one used by a contemporary philosopher (Flew) against the defence (p. 121).

scholarly_argument_hick_fate_necessity_a.description: Hick rejects the Neo-Platonic principle of plenitude, the great chain of being and the aesthetic theme, and both Thomist and Leibnizian answers to 'the best possible world', because they conceive God's relation to creation in impersonal or subpersonal terms and treat the universe's goodness as intrinsic being rather than as fitness for God's purpose; the right question is 'best possible—for what purpose?', answered by the 'vale of soul-making'. He does not deny the necessity of evil: the Irenaean type accepts God's ultimate omni-responsibility for a universe in which evil was inevitable, evil arising through a hazardous adventure in individual freedom.

evidence.quote: Perhaps the most fundamental criticism to be made of the Augustinian type of theodicy concerns a pervasive presup- position within it. This is the impersonal or subpersonal way in which God's relationship to His creation is prevailingly conceived.

The goodness of the universe is not conceived by them in instrumental terms, as its suitability to fulfil some specific divine purpose, but as an intrinsic goodness which is ultimately equivalent simply to existence itself.
sin and natural evil are both inevitable aspects of the creative process.

scholarly_argument_hick_fate_necessity_a.finding: Verified in the FULL pdf. Hick does reject the principle of plenitude and Leibnizian optimism, but not for the reason given. His 'basic criticism' (pp. 193-194) is the 'impersonal or subpersonal way in which God's relationship to His creation is prevailingly conceived'; against Thomism and Leibniz (p. 167) he objects that the goodness of the universe is not conceived instrumentally in relation to God's purpose of soul-making. 'Dysteleological' belongs to ch. XV on suffering, not to this critique. And Hick does not hold that 'evil is not metaphysically necessary': the Irenaean type accepts that God created 'a universe in which evil was inevitable' and that 'sin and natural evil are both inevitable aspects of the creative process' (pp. 236, 238), though within 'a hazardous adventure in individual freedom' (p. 256).

scholarly_argument_hick_free_will_defens.description: Hick presents the free-will defence, common to Augustinian and Irenaean theodicies, in three phases; the first two (limits of omnipotence; personality entails freedom to choose wrongly) are sound and unchallenged. Against Flew and Mackie he argues that God could not make men so that they freely respond to Him in love (hypnosis analogy), which shows theology's need for a stronger conception of liberty as limited creativity and cognitive freedom. Yet the defence cannot save the traditional theodicy: an unfallen creature's fall is either impossible or excusable, so man must be thought of as created at an epistemic distance, 'as a fallen being'.

evidence.quote: To this question the Christian answer, both in the Augustin- ian and in the Irenaean types of theodicy, has always centred upon man's freedom and responsibility as a finite personal being.

But although the Flew-Mackie critique of the free-will defence fails, and reveals at the same time theology's need for this stronger conception of human liberty, yet the latter cannot in the end save the free-will defence.

scholarly_argument_hick_free_will_defens.finding: Verified in the FULL pdf. Three problems: (1) Hick says the free-will answer 'both in the Augustinian and in the Irenaean types of theodicy, has always centred upon man's freedom' (p. 265), so it is not 'part of the Augustinian theodicy' only; (2) 'libertarian' is not Hick's word (no occurrence in the book text); (3) Hick argues that the Flew-Mackie critique 'reveals at the same time theology's need for this stronger conception of human liberty' (freedom as limited creativity, cognitive freedom), so his theodicy does rely on a strong conception of freedom, even though the defence alone cannot carry theodicy because of its internal tensions (virtual inevitability of the fall).

scholarly_argument_hick_moral_responsibi.description: Hick: to be a person one must be 'a morally responsible agent with a real power of moral choice'; goodness built up through histories of moral effort is worth more than innocence or virtue created ready-made, which justifies 'the long travail of the soul-making process'. Yet suffering is often undeserved and excessive; Hick has no rational theory for this and appeals to mystery, suggesting that a world without apparently pointless suffering could not be a scene of compassion and self-giving; the justification is completed only eschatologically by the infinite future good of the Kingdom.

evidence.quote: The problem consists rather in the fact that instead of serving a constructive purpose pain and misery seem to be distributed in random and meaningless ways, with the result that suffer- ing is often undeserved and often falls upon men in amounts exceeding anything that could be rationally intended.
Moreover, I do not now have an alternative theory to offer that would explain in any rational or ethical way why men suffer as they do. The only appeal left is to mystery.
human goodness slowly built up through personal histories of moral effort has a value in the eyes of the Creator which justifies even the long travail of the soul-making process.

scholarly_argument_hick_moral_responsibi.finding: Verified in the FULL pdf. Faithful on personhood and moral responsibility (p. 266) and on the value-judgement behind soul-making (pp. 255-256). But the proviso 'provided that evil is not overwhelming' is not Hick's condition: he concedes that suffering is often 'undeserved and often falls upon men in amounts exceeding anything that could be rationally intended', offers no theory explaining it, and appeals to mystery as itself part of a sphere of soul-making (pp. 333-334), plus eschatological fulfilment (ch. XVI). The node loses the appeal to mystery and the admission of dysteleological excess.

scholarly_argument_hick_the_fall_and_ori.description: Hick adopts the Irenaean 'minority report': man created in the image is 'only the raw material' for a second stage of creation into the likeness, which cannot be effected by fiat but only through free responses; the notions of a lost original righteousness and inherited guilt are rejected. Examining an unfallen creature, he concludes its fall 'is either impossible, or else so very possible as to be excusable', so sin can only arise in creatures set at an epistemic distance from God; man is in effect 'created as a fallen being', emerging from evolution with dim notions of his Creator.

evidence.quote: The creature's fall is either impossible, or else so very possible as to be excusable.
And so man, created as a personal being in the image of God, is only the raw material for a further and more difficult stage of God's creative work.

The accompany- ing notions of an original but lost righteousness of man and perfection of his world, and of inherited sinfulness as a uni- versal consequence of the fall, which jointly render that event so catastrophic and therefore so crucial for the Augustinian theodicy, are both rejected.

scholarly_argument_hick_the_fall_and_ori.finding: Verified in the FULL pdf; the description is faithful to Hick's own position, but pp. 201-234 (chs. IX-X) are his historical exposition of the Hellenistic Fathers and Schleiermacher. Hick's own adoption is in chs. XII-XIII: two-stage creation, man 'emerging out of apedom with only dim and rudimentary notions of his Creator' (p. 281), 'the virtual inevitability of the fall' (pp. 277-280), 'man created as a fallen being' (p. 280); rejection of lost original righteousness at p. 237. Schleiermacher's 'virtually inevitable' sin (p. 226) is reported, not Hick's own statement.

scholarly_argument_crouzel_free_will_lib.description: Crouzel (1962): when philosophy's methods become sovereign in the Church the result is heresy; the gnostics show it, with their aeons, contempt of matter, 'aristocratisme de pneumatiques', 'refus du libre arbitre et de la vraie notion de péché' and 'prédestinatianisme strict d'hérétiques aux natures', judging by Origen's reproaches (p. 154). Origen's conception of free will is dominated by the 'accidentalité essentielle' of rational creatures, who began to be (p. 199). That Origen's insistence on free will is explained by his anti-gnostic polemic is stated in Crouzel 1956, p. 173.

The causal claim 'Origen gives great importance to libre arbitre partly because of anti-gnostic polemic' is Crouzel's, but stated in the 1956 book (p. 173), not here. The 1962 loci cited add other things: p. 20 (what philosophers grant about Providence and free will), p. 32 (Aristotle's goods refuted from Ps. 4,7 via the Philocalia), and p. 199, where what 'domine sa conception du libre arbitre' is the essential contingency ('accidentalité essentielle') of created rational beings. page_range gives md lines.

scholarly_argument_crouzel_hierarchy_of_.description: Crouzel: a Contra Celsum passage gives Origen's order of preference among schools, starting from the worst—the parade of Celsus's 'mauvais médecins': Epicurus and his followers (deniers of Providence, partisans of pleasure); the Peripatetics (also deniers of Providence, suppressing any relation between man and God); the Stoics with their material, corruptible, changing god; finally those who profess 'la stupidité de la métensomatose'—the Pythagoreans, but the Platonists are also hit by that reproach. The doctrines that raise the soul to beatitude near God and teach contempt of the transient, which Scripture calls 'Sagesse de Dieu', are 'surtout le platonisme'.

evidence.quote: Mais les Platoniciens sont aussi atteints, car Origene leur adresse souvent le méme reproche **. Tel est ordre que nous allons suivre.

scholarly_argument_crouzel_hierarchy_of_.finding: quote_verbatim confirmed (p. 27). Crouzel presents the order as Origen's reading of Celsus's 'mauvais médecins' (Contra Celsum): Epicureans (deny Providence, pleasure), Peripatetics (deny Providence, suppress all relation between man and God), Stoics ('dieu matériel, corruptible et changeant'), then those professing 'la stupidité de la métensomatose', the Pythagoreans, 'Mais les Platoniciens sont aussi atteints, car Origène leur adresse souvent le même reproche'. Platonism as the doctrine called 'Sagesse de Dieu' comes from the preceding quotation ('Tel est surtout le platonisme'). 'Closest to truth, especially regarding knowledge of God' is not in this passage; 'vertueux' for the Stoics is only in the chapter title (table of contents, l. 10698). The node drops the caveat on the Platonists. page_range gives md lines.

scholarly_argument_crouzel_origen_s_rela.description: Crouzel (1962, p. 11): against de Faye and Hal Koch, Origen, though possessing a considerable philosophical culture which he constantly uses, 'n'est philosophe ni par son but ni par sa méthode'. A pure philosopher draws his answers from reason, from the deepest experience of being, thinking and acting; for the Christian theologian a Revelation imposes itself, the Word of God in Scripture interpreted by apostolic and ecclesial tradition. The image of philosophy as 'périmée', serving the 'divine philosophie' and fading like stars before the sun, belongs to Crouzel 1956 (Préface, p. 10).

evidence.quote: Cependant il n’est philosophe ni par son but ni par sa méthode.

But the second half of the description and of verified_reference ('n'a jamais voulu être un philosophe', 'périmée', stars fading before the sun) is not in the 1962 book: 'périmée' and 'étoiles' have zero hits in the 1962 file; those words are Crouzel 1956, Préface p. 10. Same author, wrong work.

scholarly_argument_crouzel_platonism_and.description: Crouzel: in Origen's reading (Contra Celsum), the doctrines that raise the soul from things here below to the beatitude awaiting it near God, and that teach contempt of the sensible as transitory so that one hastens toward the invisible, are what Scripture calls 'Sagesse de Dieu'—'Tel est surtout le platonisme' (p. 27). What dominates Origen's conception of free will, according to Crouzel, is a very Origenian idea: the essential contingency ('accidentalité essentielle') of rational creatures, proven by the fact that they began to be (p. 199).

scholarly_argument_crouzel_platonism_and.finding: The opening claim 'Platonism dominates Origen's conception of libre arbitre' is not at l. 903-906 (p. 27) nor anywhere with that subject. The only 'domine sa conception du libre arbitre' in the book (p. 199) has a different subject: the 'accidentalité essentielle' of rational creatures who began to exist. Page 27 says only that the doctrines leading the soul to beatitude near God and teaching contempt of the sensible, which Scripture calls 'Sagesse de Dieu', are 'surtout le platonisme'—and Crouzel is paraphrasing Origen's Contra Celsum. The 'insufficient vs revelation' clause is Crouzel's general thesis but not at this locus.

scholarly_argument_crouzel_synthesis_of_.description: Crouzel: before Origen two contrary currents. Tatian, Hermias, Irenaeus, Tertullian and the author of the Elenchos show a negative attitude, a will to rupture (violent except in the 'pacifique' bishop of Lyons), judging philosophy a danger of heresy incompatible with the transcendence of gospel wisdom. Justin and Clement show real sympathy, refusing to reject philosophy wholesale, seeing it as a school of virtue and truth—Clement even as a third, inferior Testament. 'Origène fait la synthèse de ces deux attitudes et c'est là son originalité': his distrust is great and his critique sharp, more than Clement's, though Clement's is not non-existent.

evidence.quote: Origene fait la synthése de ces deux attitudes et c’est 14 son origina- lité. Sa défiance est grande et sa critique aigué, plus que celle de Clé- ment, qui n’est pas cependant inexistante.
evidence.citation: [05_Origene/Origene et la philosophie -- Henri Crouzel -- 1962 -- 5a6af4185d50873d0876684de1e77087 -- Anna’s Archive.md:7660-7662]

evidence.quote: Chez Tatien et Hermias, Irénée, Tertullien et l’auteur de l’Elenchos une attitude négative, une volonté de rupture, exposée de fagon souvent violente, sauf chez le pacifique évéque de Lyon.
evidence.citation: [05_Origene/Origene et la philosophie -- Henri Crouzel -- 1962 -- 5a6af4185d50873d0876684de1e77087 -- Anna’s Archive.md:7645-7647]

scholarly_argument_crouzel_synthesis_of_.finding: quote_verbatim confirmed (p. 170). The two currents and Origen's synthesis are faithful. But 'his engagement is deeper' is not in the text: Crouzel says 'Sa défiance est grande et sa critique aiguë, plus que celle de Clément, qui n'est pas cependant inexistante', then discusses Molland and Hal Koch who wrongly place Origen with Tatian and Tertullian ('fortement exagéré, mais ne manque pas d'un certain fondement'). The negative camp also includes 'l'auteur de l'Elenchos', with Irenaeus singled out as 'pacifique'; Clement goes so far as to compare philosophy to a third Testament. page_range gives md lines.

scholarly_argument_linjamaa_cosmos_as_sc.description: Linjamaa: the Aeons' 'school of conduct' in the Pleroma and the cosmos as a place of learning show that both heavenly and earthly life follow a pedagogical structure. The social context reflected in TriTrac is 'a dual one': an inner circle of pneumatics—Christian intellectuals gathering in study groups—within a larger community of psychic laypeople; neither is a formal school, and school and church should not be contrasted too rigidly. One cannot advance alone; pneumatics teach psychics as the Savior teaches pneumatics; psychics support and worship with them; oral instruction, probably including pre-baptismal teaching, is delivered by the teachers; moral questions belong to the literate pneumatic level.

evidence.quote: reflecting a group of pneumatics comprising an inner circle within a larger community. We are most likely not dealing with formal school structures in either case.
evidence.citation: [06_Patristique/[Nag Hammadi and Manichaean Studies, 95] Paul Linjamaa - The Ethics of The Tripartite Tractate (NHC I, 5). A Study of Determinism and Early Christian Philosophy of Ethics (2019, Brill) - libgen.li.md:11266-11267]

evidence.quote: I would caution against contrasting the terms school and church too rigidly.
evidence.citation: [06_Patristique/[Nag Hammadi and Manichaean Studies, 95] Paul Linjamaa - The Ethics of The Tripartite Tractate (NHC I, 5). A Study of Determinism and Early Christian Philosophy of Ethics (2019, Brill) - libgen.li.md:10928]

scholarly_argument_linjamaa_cosmos_as_sc.finding: quote_verbatim confirmed (p. 223). But the node misreads the 'dual' structure: for Linjamaa it is 'a group of pneumatics comprising an inner circle within a larger community', and 'We are most likely not dealing with formal school structures in either case'; he explicitly cautions 'against contrasting the terms school and church too rigidly' (p. 216). The church/school dichotomy is what he attributes to Irenaeus and Justin and resists. 'Silent ... instruction' is not in the book (no hit); instruction is oral, 'probably including pre-baptismal instruction'. The Pleroma's 'school of conduct' (71:22-23) is discussed pp. 210-212, but 'imperfectly reflects' is the node's gloss.

scholarly_argument_linjamaa_determinism_.description: Linjamaa: early Christian determinism has been dismissed as 'Gnostic' or written off as a polemical invention (Denzey Lewis, Löhr); TriTrac shows the church fathers did not invent it. Like the Stoics, who held human choice real though limited and free will attainable only by the sage, TriTrac restricts free will—a view Origen and Irenaeus rejected. One chief aim of the study is 'to restore awareness of theories maintaining that human choice was limited' and their importance for early Christian ethics: the rejection of free will and a fixed anthropology did not entail indifference to ethical questions but a pedagogical plan of gradual moral improvement.

evidence.quote: Nevertheless, in light of what we find in TriTrac, we cannot conclude, like Denzey Lewis, Löhr, and others, that the church fathers invented the position of Christian determinism.
evidence.citation: [06_Patristique/[Nag Hammadi and Manichaean Studies, 95] Paul Linjamaa - The Ethics of The Tripartite Tractate (NHC I, 5). A Study of Determinism and Early Christian Philosophy of Ethics (2019, Brill) - libgen.li.md:2474-2476]

evidence.quote: Thus, the rejection of the concept of free will and the fixity of the tripartite anthropology would not have led to an indifference to ethical questions.
evidence.citation: [06_Patristique/[Nag Hammadi and Manichaean Studies, 95] Paul Linjamaa - The Ethics of The Tripartite Tractate (NHC I, 5). A Study of Determinism and Early Christian Philosophy of Ethics (2019, Brill) - libgen.li.md:9297-9299]

scholarly_argument_linjamaa_determinism_.finding: quote_verbatim confirmed (p. 43). The first half (determinism does not undermine ethics; fixed anthropology with room for improvement) is faithful (pp. 184, 264). But Linjamaa never calls the 'bad reputation' 'a modern scholarly construct', nor speaks of 'fate, providence, and moral responsibility ... complexly intertwined'. His claims: early Christian determinism 'has either been presented as Gnostic and then not taken seriously, or ... disregarded as belonging to the inventions of polemics'; against Denzey Lewis and Löhr 'we cannot conclude ... that the church fathers invented the position of Christian determinism'; his aim is 'to restore awareness of theories maintaining that human choice was limited'. The Stoic precedent (choice compatible with a causally determined world, free will only for the sage) is what TriTrac reflects and Origen rejects.

scholarly_argument_linjamaa_free_will_an.description: Linjamaa (§3.6): TriTrac's ethical theory, unlike many early Christian systems, 'did not rest on the doctrine of free will'. As long as passion and false impressions rooted in matter are viable there can be no self-determination; unlike Stoicism, no one in the Logos' cosmic creation possesses complete self-determination. Like the Stoics, TriTrac equates free will with moral perfection—a mind wholly in tune with the Father's will—which is not viable in the cosmos. Cosmic creatures have instead a proairesis, good or bad, more or less prone to assent to the Savior; the three classes correspond to the material, psychic and pneumatic powers, and one's substance becomes known at the Savior's appearance.

evidence.quote: In conclusion, the ethical theory in TriTrac, contrary to many other early Christian systems, did not rest on the doctrine of free will.
evidence.citation: [06_Patristique/[Nag Hammadi and Manichaean Studies, 95] Paul Linjamaa - The Ethics of The Tripartite Tractate (NHC I, 5). A Study of Determinism and Early Christian Philosophy of Ethics (2019, Brill) - libgen.li.md:7420-7421]

evidence.quote: No one in the cosmos is described as being in the possession of a self-determining will, instead the creatures in the cosmic system have a proairesis, which can be good or bad, that is, more or less prone to assent to the Savior.
evidence.citation: [06_Patristique/[Nag Hammadi and Manichaean Studies, 95] Paul Linjamaa - The Ethics of The Tripartite Tractate (NHC I, 5). A Study of Determinism and Early Christian Philosophy of Ethics (2019, Brill) - libgen.li.md:7430-7433]

scholarly_argument_linjamaa_free_will_an.finding: quote_verbatim confirmed (p. 144, §3.6). The node turns Linjamaa's negative thesis into a positive one. His summary: TriTrac's ethics 'did not rest on the doctrine of free will'; while passion and false impressions based in matter persist 'there could be no self-determination'; 'unlike Stoicism, TriTrac presents a moral system where no individuals in the cosmic creation of the Logos possessed complete self-determination'; 'No one in the cosmos is described as being in the possession of a self-determining will', only a proairesis, good or bad, more or less prone to assent to the Savior. Stoic-derived psychology (proairesis, assent, impression) and βούλησις/θέλημα are indeed discussed (ch. 2-3), but the description omits the rejection of free will and adds 'moral accountability', not his term.

scholarly_argument_linjamaa_social_and_p.description: Linjamaa (ch. 6): TriTrac's cosmogony reads as political commentary—material powers, 'love of glory' and 'lust for command' evoke third-century instability—but the oikonomia is not evil: the Logos' system is good in its foundations and set up according to the Father's will. Psychics are driven by the pursuit of honor yet must not be blinded by it; they are to retain positions in society and use them to support the pneumatic leadership, on the model of patron and teacher (Ambrosius and Origen). The ideal for those in the cosmos is metriopatheia, not apatheia. TriTrac fits a context where Christians could attain powerful positions.

evidence.quote: However, the oikonomia is not presented as evil or solely bad. The system the Logos sets up is good in its foundations, established in accordance with the will of the Father.
evidence.citation: [06_Patristique/[Nag Hammadi and Manichaean Studies, 95] Paul Linjamaa - The Ethics of The Tripartite Tractate (NHC I, 5). A Study of Determinism and Early Christian Philosophy of Ethics (2019, Brill) - libgen.li.md:12480-12482]

evidence.quote: A psychic is described as someone who is driven by the pursuit of honor, but who must listen to advice and help pneumatics.
evidence.citation: [06_Patristique/[Nag Hammadi and Manichaean Studies, 95] Paul Linjamaa - The Ethics of The Tripartite Tractate (NHC I, 5). A Study of Determinism and Early Christian Philosophy of Ethics (2019, Brill) - libgen.li.md:9283-9284]

evidence.quote: TriTrac encourages everyday Christians to support the leadership of the community and retain positions in society that enable them to do so.
evidence.citation: [06_Patristique/[Nag Hammadi and Manichaean Studies, 95] Paul Linjamaa - The Ethics of The Tripartite Tractate (NHC I, 5). A Study of Determinism and Early Christian Philosophy of Ethics (2019, Brill) - libgen.li.md:12490-12491]

scholarly_argument_linjamaa_social_and_p.finding: quote_verbatim confirmed (p. 248). Two misreadings. (1) Psychics are not 'expected to ... pursue honor in conventional ways': they are 'described as someone who is driven by the pursuit of honor, but who must listen to advice and help pneumatics' (p. 184); TriTrac calls 'to abandon the blind pursuit of honor', the ideal being metriopatheia (p. 253); pneumatics need support 'from Christians who were not blinded by their involvement in the pursuit of worldly honor'. (2) The oikonomia 'is not presented as evil or solely bad'; the Logos' system 'is good in its foundations', though material powers are linked to instability and 'love of glory'. The node's 'fallen Logos' disordered state' overstates the negative side.

scholarly_argument_linjamaa_stoic_influe.description: Linjamaa (ch. 2 conclusion): reading TriTrac against Stoic and Platonic theories of emotion illuminates its ethics, whose theoretical basis is a theory of cognition; but the text is 'an advanced reception of Aristotelian, Platonic, and Stoic thought, appropriated within a very particular Christian creation myth'. The ideal is freedom from the control of passion, yet apatheia is a divine ideal viable only for the Savior; as in Plutarch and Philo, cosmic life is entangled with emotions, some useful and necessary. Passions function as pedagogical tools and are associated with the heavenly powers; being controlled by them, as the Greeks are, leads to error.

scholarly_argument_o_keefe_swerve_and_co.description: Chapters 5-6 give O'Keefe's own view of the swerve. scholarly_argument_de_monneron_source_in.description: De Monneron distinguishes two incompatibilist conditions: (1) a free act is one the agent could have refrained from (the principle of alternative possibilities), and (2) a free act has no sufficient cause (the 'source incompatibilists' Stump and Widerker keep only 2). His position is 'intermédiaire': he does not accept Stump's and Widerker's arguments against the principle of alternative possibilities, yet prefers to rest his critique of determinism on 2 rather than 1, because he thinks 1 'is explained by' 2 'and therefore reduces to it' — wherever necessity seems to exclude responsibility, it is causal necessity.

Je pense en effet que la première idée s'explique par la deuxième, et donc s'y réduit.

scholarly_argument_sapolsky_determinism_.description: Sapolsky reviews three scientific 'revolutions' — chaos theory, emergent complexity, quantum indeterminacy — in whose 'crevices' 'numerous thinkers believe that you can find free will', and concludes 'they are not where free will dwells'. Chaotic and emergent systems are for him deterministic though unpredictable (unpredictability is not indeterminacy); only quantum effects are indeterministic, and even if they 'bubble up', randomness 'sure isn't a manifestation of free will'. Believers in free will have either missed 'the determinism lurking beneath the surface' or 'erroneously concluded' that the indeterministic aspects of the universe explain character and behavior.

evidence.quote: erroneously concluded that the rarefied aspects of the universe that do work indeterministically can explain your character, morals, and behavior.
evidence.citation: [07_Libre_arbitre_theologie/Robert M. Sapolsky - Determined_ A Science of Life without Free Will (2023).md:149-150]

evidence.quote: This chapter, and the five after it, reviews these three revolutions, and how numerous thinkers believe that you can find free will in their crevices.
evidence.citation: [07_Libre_arbitre_theologie/Robert M. Sapolsky - Determined_ A Science of Life without Free Will (2023).md:3564-3565]

scholarly_argument_sharples_aristotelian.description: According to the extraction's summary of Sharples's Section VI, the question is which divine being exercises providence in Alexander: the Unmoved Mover does not, the heavens do, and providence is connected with the preservation of species through the heavenly motions — a connection Sharples suggests 'may be Alexander's own distinctive contribution' within the Peripatetic tradition (pp. 122-123). No claim that Alexander thereby steers between Stoic determinism and Epicurean indifference is recorded.

scholarly_argument_tolan_moral_responsib.description: Tolan (I.3.3 'Theodicy: Corruptibility as the Basis for Possessing the Good as One's Own') reads De Principiis II.9.2 as an account of evil as privatio boni that 'introduces, in terms of theodicy, a "free will defence"': diversity, or evil, is 'something we introduce to creation through our own free will, ergo God is not the cause of evil', and a corruptible creation is better than an incorruptible one because 'through our free motions we are able to make goodness our own'. I.3.4 then treats satiety in the Good and the cooling of the intellects (Harl, Chadwick, Bostock, Philo).

scholarly_argument_tolan_what_depends_on.description: Tolan: 'Origen follows Epictetus by dividing' what is up to us from what is not, adding why things are up to us ('we have the logos as a judge and examiner of phantasiai') and placing the division within his categories of motion. scholarly_argument_currado_divine_electi.description: Summarising what he takes to be the shared position of Chrysostom and Origen on Romans 9, Currado lists: election 'is based on foreseen qualities' and 'is not arbitrary'; 'called according to purpose' (no possessive pronoun in the Greek, he notes) can mean God's decision to call those he foreknew would respond; the 'gift and potential of faith' is universal, so everyone can yield to or resist God. Currado endorses this consensus as his own reading.

evidence.quote: Nevertheless, they both have a clear consensus in the following matters:

God’s Election is based on foreseen qualities – God “will render to every man according to His deeds” (Romans 2:6) – those who yield to Him in humility (while not deserving His grace) He grants fellowship with Himself; those who resist Him, He condemns. Election is not arbitrary.
The gift and potential of faith toward God is universal – everyone can submit to the grace and goodness of God or can resist Him.

scholarly_argument_currado_hippolytus_on.description: Currado reproduces, without comment, the ANF translation of Hippolytus, Refutatio X (his 'Chapter 28-29'): man was created 'endued with a capacity of self-determination' though 'a slave to his passions'; evil arises 'from the fact of his possessing a capacity of self-determination' and had no existence from the beginning; because man 'has free will' God gave a law for his guidance, the Word 'summoning him to liberty through a choice involving spontaneity', not 'by force of necessity'. scholarly_argument_currado_romans_interp.description: Currado attributes to Chrysostom and Origen a shared reading (p. 3): Paul confronts a 'hostile inquisitor' relying on Jewish heritage, deliberately confuses and silences him in 9:15-23, and gives the 'clearest answer' in 9:30-10:4; God is the Potter, but people become vessels of wrath through their own choice to flee from God. His Summary (p. 15) concludes that the Fathers read Romans 9 not as rejecting 'libertarian free will' but as rejecting 'legalistic works-salvation and ethnocentric entitlement'.

scholarly_argument_dettwiler_free_will_a.description: Dettwiler reads Peter's request ('Seigneur, si c'est toi...') as a faith-filled response, not an initiative: his walk 'ne saurait résulter d'une initiative propre à Pierre' and is made possible 'exclusivement' by Jesus' word (p. 336). Faith is 'une réponse', 'pas un acte humain fondé en lui-même', not its own beginning (p. 344); it is not an act of which man is master but a renunciation of walking by oneself and of all securities (p. 345); in the cry-prayer Peter can no longer draw on his own capacities (p. 347). No language of free will or cooperation.

evidence.citation: [La conception matthéenne de la foi (Mt 14,22-33).md:223-225] (Dettwiler 1998, p. 336)

scholarly_argument_dettwiler_moral_respo.description: Peter's failure is 'oligopistia', a key Matthean concept distinct from apistia (unbelief, reserved for the crowd): not a smaller faith but 'l'incrédulité au sein de la foi', born of the tension between Jesus' word and the evidence of the world. Dettwiler stresses that Matthew does not demand 'de façon moraliste' a faith untouched by doubt — the failing Peter is precisely the one saved — yet doubt is neither idealised nor glorified: faith ultimately 'vise à surmonter le doute'. Peter recreates the distance 'de façon coupable' (p. 336).

evidence.quote: Le manque de foi (oligopistia), ensuite, n'est pas à comprendre comme une foi petite à laquelle s'opposerait une foi plus grande (cf Mt 17119-20 !). L' oligopistia doit plutôt être comprise comme l'expression. de l'incrédulité au sein de la foi

scholarly_argument_dettwiler_moral_respo.finding: Dettwiler does say Peter recreated the distance 'de façon coupable' (p. 336) and that Jesus saves him, but the node loses his central qualifications: oligopistia is not apistia (the crowd is unbelieving, not the disciples), it is not a 'small' faith but 'l'incrédulité au sein de la foi'; the text does not demand 'de façon moraliste' a pure faith; doubt is neither idealised nor glorified, and faith 'vise à surmonter le doute' (p. 346). scholarly_argument_dettwiler_hellenistic.description: Because Paul's Judaism, like any minority culture of the time, is influenced by Hellenistic culture, Pauline literature is also 'imprégnée' by specifically Greco-Roman anthropological elements: Paul's extensive use of typically Greek concepts (body, mind/reason, moral conscience) without direct Hebrew equivalent 'plaide dans ce sens'. Dettwiler then reports, in the conditional and on Bultmann's authority (BULTMANN 1984, 202-203), that some passages (2 Co 5,1ss; 12,2-4; 1 Co 7,1-7) would attest a more direct Hellenistic influence tending to devalue corporeality along Platonic body-soul dualism.

evidence.quote: Déjà le fait que Paul utilise de manière extensive des concepts typiquement grecs comme σῶµα (« corps »), νοῦς (« pensée, raison, entendement ») ou συνείδησις (« conscience morale ») qui n’ont pas d’équivalent direct en hébreu plaide dans ce sens.
De plus, selon Rudolf Bultmann, plusieurs passages (2 Co 5,1ss ; 2 Co 12,2-4 ; mais aussi 1 Co 7,1-7) témoigneraient d’une influence plus directe de la pensée hellénistique

scholarly_argument_dettwiler_hellenistic.finding: Quote verbatim, p. 3. But the second claim (2 Co 5,1ss; 12,2-4; 1 Co 7,1-7 showing a more direct Hellenistic influence devaluing corporeality) is reported in the conditional and attributed to Bultmann ('selon Rudolf Bultmann, plusieurs passages ... témoigneraient'), not asserted by Dettwiler; the node states it flat. The three Greek terms are in the file as σῶµα, νοῦς, συνείδησις.

If retained, reword as a curator note: the phrase 'free will' does not occur in Dunn's Theology of Paul the Apostle; his discussion of human agency runs through faith as 'utter dependence' (§14.7), the divided 'I' under the eschatological tension (§18.3) and the Spirit as 'enabling power' (§16, §23).

Searched the full 847-page extraction (rg -i 'free.?will|freedom of (the )?will|determinis|libertarian'): zero hits, so the phrase 'free will' never occurs in the book — which corroborates the silence, but a knowledge-graph 'scholarly_argument' cannot rest on absence. 'Libertarian' is imported vocabulary. §18 'The eschatological tension' (node's page range) is about flesh/Spirit and the divided I, not about free will as a philosophical problem.

scholarly_argument_dunn_grace_and_human_.description: Justification by faith alone is, for Dunn, 'a relation of utter dependence, of unconditional trust': dependence on grace must be unqualified, which is why Paul opposed works of the law as an accompaniment or addition to faith (p. 379). Dunn denies that Paul was polemicising against 'self-achieved righteousness'; the issue is Israel's works of the law and Gentile acceptability (§14.6, p. 370). Gal 5.6, 'faith operating effectively through love', is a single concept, 'love-energized-faith', that does not make faith a 'work' nor compromise the sola fide (§23.3, pp. 637-638).

evidence.quote: It was a profound conception of the relation between God and humankind — a relation of utter dependence, of unconditional trust. Human dependence on divine grace had to be unqualified or else it was not Abraham's faith
In all these cases, therefore, it is difficult to sustain the claim that Paul was polemicizing against "self-achieved righteousness."
This is not to imply (to use the terminology of later centuries) that Paul turned faith into a "work" or compromised the sola fide.

scholarly_argument_dunn_grace_and_human_.finding: Quote verbatim, but on printed p. 379 (end of §14.7; page_map says 377 — the map for this file is 2-3 pages low against the PDF folios and the file is AUDIT-FAIL). The appended gloss misframes Dunn: he does not say works of the law are excluded 'but human effort is not'; in §14.6 (p. 370) he argues it is 'difficult to sustain the claim that Paul was polemicizing against "self-achieved righteousness"' — the issue is Israel's works of the law vis-à-vis Gentile acceptability. Gal 5.6 is treated in §23.3 (pp. 637-638), where Dunn insists 'faith working through love' does not turn faith into a 'work' nor compromise the sola fide.

scholarly_argument_dunn_predestination_a.description: On Rom 9.14-23 Dunn grants that Paul portrays God 'in quite arbitrary terms' and goes 'a little way down' the predestinarian road, but reads the passage in three facets: Paul stresses God's sovereign initiative to undercut Israel's claim to define the limits of mercy; he criticises the operative 'dogma of predestination' (Israel sole beneficiary, Esau/Pharaoh its foil) rather than mounting one; and the 'strongest note is that of mercy', with a role reversal making Israel the 'vessels of wrath'. Predestination is thus 'caught within the eschatological tension' (pp. 511-513).

evidence.quote: Paul was quite clear that he was thereby portraying God in quite arbitrary terms.
Second, it follows that Paul was attempting not so much to mount a theology of predestination as to criticize the theory which was presently in operation.

Paul's theology of predestination is itself caught within the eschatological tension — the bright side of predestination as a function of the already, the dark side of predestination as a function of the not yet of God's ultimate purpose of mercy.

scholarly_argument_dunn_predestination_a.finding: Quote verbatim (printed p. 513; map says 510). 'Double predestination' is not Dunn's term (0 hits). His argument in §19.3 is more specific than the node: Paul 'was quite clear that he was thereby portraying God in quite arbitrary terms' and 'presses a little way down that road' of predestinarianism; but Paul's aim is 'not so much to mount a theology of predestination as to criticize the theory which was presently in operation' (Israel as sole beneficiary of election); the strongest note is mercy; and there is a role reversal in which Israel itself becomes 'vessels of wrath' / hardened Pharaoh (11.7, 25). Rom 11.25-26 is §19.6, not checked here.

scholarly_argument_dunn_the_spirit_and_h.description: Dunn presents three mutually supportive images of the beginning of salvation: justification (restored status), being in Christ (participation), and the gift of the Spirit, which 'provided the motivating and enabling power by which they were to live'; together they combine 'intellectual appeal, embracing experience, and motivated ethic' (p. 414). He does not frame this against 'human autonomy'.

evidence.quote: In turn, the gift of the Spirit provided the motivating and enabling power by which they were to live. The three images — restored status, participation in Christ, and divine enabling — together made for an integrated and mutually supportive matrix

scholarly_argument_dunn_the_spirit_and_h.finding: Quote verbatim, printed p. 414 (PDF folio; map 412), in the introduction to §16 — within the node's 413-440 range. The quote supports 'divine enabling' and 'participation in Christ' as Dunn's 'three images'; 'not human autonomy' and 'moral responsibility is real but Spirit-enabled, not self-achieved' are the node's extrapolations, not Dunn's phrasing on this page ('autonomy' occurs only for Adam's 'moral autonomy' in Genesis and for local churches). The 552-561 reference to 1 Cor 12-14 was not verified.

scholarly_argument_eskola_double_predest.description: Eskola's 'problem of double predestination' (§9.3) is a problem of exegesis: Calvin's deterministic doctrine has coloured readings of both Second Temple Judaism and Paul. His own conclusion is that Second Temple predestination was synergistic, not deterministic, and that double predestination (election of only part of humankind) 'is not compatible with the teaching of Paul', whose radicalized predestination is Christocentric: God has imprisoned all in disobedience (Gal 3:22; Rom 11:32) 'so that he may be merciful to all' — 'divine coercion' whose ultimate purpose is 'Christocentric universalism' (pp. 180-183, 296, 302-303).

evidence.quote: This kind of double predestination is inevitably deterministic. In the beginning God elected those individuals who would be saved.
evidence.citation: [Timo Eskola - Theodicy and Predestination in Pauline Soteriology (Wissenschaftliche Untersuchengen Zum Neuen Testament_ 2. Reihe)-Wipf and Stock.md:8538-8539] (Eskola 1998, p. 180)

evidence.quote: The concept of double predestination maintains that God has elected only part of humankind to salvation. Such an idea is not compatible with the teaching of Paul. Paul was convinced that the atonement relates to the whole world.
evidence.citation: [Timo Eskola - Theodicy and Predestination in Pauline Soteriology (Wissenschaftliche Untersuchengen Zum Neuen Testament_ 2. Reihe)-Wipf and Stock.md:8609-8611] (Eskola 1998, p. 182)

evidence.quote: God has imprisoned all humankind in disobedience so that he may be merciful to all. The purpose of these contrast formulas is Christocentric. This reveals that the ultimate purpose of Paul's predestinarian theology is Christocentric universalism.
evidence.citation: [Timo Eskola - Theodicy and Predestination in Pauline Soteriology (Wissenschaftliche Untersuchengen Zum Neuen Testament_ 2. Reihe)-Wipf and Stock.md:13893-13896] (Eskola 1998, p. 303)

scholarly_argument_eskola_double_predest.finding: §9.3 'The problem of double predestination' (pp. 180-183) is about a hermeneutical problem in scholarship (Calvin's deterministic doctrine projected on Judaism and Paul), and Eskola's verdict is the reverse of the node: double predestination 'is not compatible with the teaching of Paul', who 'was convinced that the atonement relates to the whole world' (p. 182); Paul's 'radicalized concept of predestination' is Christocentric and 'not deterministic' (p. 296). 'Particularist in mechanism' is not Eskola's. §15.3 gives 'divine coercion' = imprisoning all in disobedience so as to be merciful to all, with 'Christocentric universalism' as its purpose. Pages from the PDF folios (page_map for this file is 4 pages low, AUDIT-FAIL).

scholarly_argument_eskola_human_moral_ag.description: Paul's anthropology rests on 'universal sinfulness': since Adam all humankind lives under the power of sin ('total domination of sin', §7.1), which produces a 'paradoxical polarization' — no difference between Jew and Greek, the basic opposition being God versus sinful humankind. Paul ends with the 'predestination of judgment': God has imprisoned all in sin and disobedience, so soteriology can no longer rest on 'sapiential synergism'; 'one cannot solve the problem of sin by increasing the responsibility of man'. This imprisonment is the 'divine coercion' whose purpose is mercy to all (pp. 125-129, 187, 303).

evidence.quote: God has imprisoned all men in sin and disobedience. This is why soteriology can no longer be based on traditional sapiential synergism. One cannot solve the problem of sin by increasing the responsibility of man.
evidence.citation: [Timo Eskola - Theodicy and Predestination in Pauline Soteriology (Wissenschaftliche Untersuchengen Zum Neuen Testament_ 2. Reihe)-Wipf and Stock.md:8843-8845] (Eskola 1998, p. 187)

evidence.quote: Paul's radical soteriology is based on the idea of divine coercion. In his interpretation the history of salvation becomes a story about predestination. Predestination is God's coercive act where the whole of humankind is imprisoned in disobedience.
evidence.citation: [Timo Eskola - Theodicy and Predestination in Pauline Soteriology (Wissenschaftliche Untersuchengen Zum Neuen Testament_ 2. Reihe)-Wipf and Stock.md:13888-13891] (Eskola 1998, p. 303)

scholarly_argument_eskola_human_moral_ag.finding: Quote verbatim, in the Summary of Chapter II, printed p. 187 (map says 183). §7.1 'The total domination of sin' is pp. 125-129. But 'requires divine coercion for salvation' misreads Eskola's 'divine coercion' (§15.3, p. 303): it is God's act of imprisoning the whole of humankind in disobedience (Gal 3:22; Rom 11:32) so as to be merciful to all — a premise of the theodicy, not a coercion of individuals unto salvation. 'Works of the law futile' belongs to Ch. III (pp. 190ff., 208ff.).

scholarly_argument_eskola_law_and_justif.description: Predestinarian theology explains the law's 'paradoxical function': God's good law kills instead of giving life (§10, p. 190). The 'works of the law' are the Avodat Israel, Jewish service to God — in Judaism a positive term for a life of obedience, in Paul's soteriology 'utterly negative in respect of salvation' (§10.3, p. 208). Eskola rejects the 'identity markers' reading as 'too narrow': the denial of works of law concerns God's law and human conduct, not ethnocentric markers (pp. 233, 310). Justification comes through the righteousness of Christ, apart from synergistic nomism.

evidence.quote: predestinarian theology helps us to understand why Paul gives God's good law of love a rather paradoxical function in soteriology. He does say that the law is good in itself.
evidence.citation: [Timo Eskola - Theodicy and Predestination in Pauline Soteriology (Wissenschaftliche Untersuchengen Zum Neuen Testament_ 2. Reihe)-Wipf and Stock.md:8926-8928] (Eskola 1998, p. 190)

evidence.quote: As regards Jewish tradition, we are dealing with a positive term denoting a life of obedience in accordance with the will of God. In the theology of Paul, however, this term becomes utterly negative in respect of salvation.
evidence.citation: [Timo Eskola - Theodicy and Predestination in Pauline Soteriology (Wissenschaftliche Untersuchengen Zum Neuen Testament_ 2. Reihe)-Wipf and Stock.md:9764-9766] (Eskola 1998, p. 208)
