evidence.citation: [Timo Eskola - Theodicy and Predestination in Pauline Soteriology (Wissenschaftliche Untersuchengen Zum Neuen Testament_ 2. Reihe)-Wipf and Stock.md:14170-14172] (Eskola 1998, p. 310)

scholarly_argument_eskola_law_and_justif.finding: 'Paradoxical function' is Eskola's (§10, p. 190: God's good law kills instead of giving life). But 'markers of ethnic identity that Paul abandons' is the Dunn/Sanders reading that Eskola explicitly rejects as 'too narrow' (pp. 233, 310): the works of the law are the Avodat Israel, 'a positive term denoting a life of obedience in accordance with the will of God', which in Paul's soteriology 'becomes utterly negative in respect of salvation' (p. 208); 'the denial of works of law is not directed against ethnocentric "markers"' (p. 310). Section headings are on pp. 190 and 208 (map says 204).

scholarly_argument_eskola_predestination.description: Against both the view that Paul criticises a deterministic Jewish predestination and the view that he accepted covenantal nomism, Eskola holds that Paul opposes the 'synergistic nomism' taught by nearly all Second Temple groups: he 'radicalizes soteriological polarization and teaches full predestination'. This concept 'is not deterministic, however', but grounds his Christological interpretation of the revelation of God's saving righteousness: every sinner is consigned to judgment, all die in Adam, and hope comes only from the righteousness of God (pp. 296-297).

scholarly_argument_gill_later_ancient_re.description: Gill summarises Frede's claim ('According to Frede') that the Stoic complex of ideas powerfully influenced later thought: it stimulated Alexander of Aphrodisias to a competing Aristotelian-style, 'indeterminist' conception of will; was adopted 'wholesale' by Plotinus so far as his metaphysics allowed; and shaped Christian thinkers, who modified it either by holding that all humans have a free will, not merely the capacity to develop one (Origen), or that this capacity is limited by 'original sin' and needs 'divine grace' (Augustine). Gill then judges the study 'highly controversial'.

evidence.quote: According to Frede, this complex of ideas exercised a powerful inﬂuence on later ancient thought, both Greco-Roman and Christian.
evidence.citation: [CR de GILL A Free Will  Origins of the Notion in Ancient Thought.md:152-155] (Gill 2014, p. 797)

evidence.quote: they modiﬁed the Stoic view either by maintaining that all humans have a free will, not simply the capacity to develop one (Origen), or by claiming that this capacity has been limited by an “original sin,” hence requiring the intervention of “divine grace” to allow it to be realised fully (Augustine).
evidence.citation: [CR de GILL A Free Will  Origins of the Notion in Ancient Thought.md:174-180] (Gill 2014, p. 798)

scholarly_argument_gill_later_ancient_re.finding: The paragraph opens 'According to Frede, this complex of ideas exercised a powerful influence on later ancient thought' — Gill is reporting Frede's thesis (which he goes on to call 'highly controversial'), not arguing it. The node turns Gill's report into Gill's position. Content otherwise accurate (Alexander's 'competing Aristotelian-style ("indeterminist") conception'; Plotinus 'wholesale... as far as his metaphysical framework allowed'; Origen: all humans have a free will; Augustine: capacity limited by original sin, needing divine grace). Pages 797-798 correct (Gill, European Legacy 19.6, 2014).

scholarly_argument_gill_methodological_c.description: Gill judges Frede's study 'bold and original, arresting in its claims and powerful in argumentation', yet 'also highly controversial and open to challenge, for instance' in its stress on the pervasive influence of Stoicism, or in the move — 'which some would see as a retrojection' — of analysing Stoic theory in the later ancient terminology of will and free will. He nonetheless finds it 'outstandingly clear' and 'indispensable'.

evidence.quote: Frede’s study is bold and original, arresting in its claims and powerful in argumentation. It is also highly controversial and open to challenge, for instance, in its stress on the pervasive inﬂuence of Stoicism
evidence.citation: [CR de GILL A Free Will  Origins of the Notion in Ancient Thought.md:181-191] (Gill 2014, p. 798)

evidence.quote: For anyone interested in the emergence of the idea of free will in early European thought this short but powerfully stated study is indispensable.
evidence.citation: [CR de GILL A Free Will  Origins of the Notion in Ancient Thought.md:199-202] (Gill 2014, p. 798)

scholarly_argument_gill_methodological_c.finding: Quote verbatim, p. 798. But Gill's sentence is one half of a balanced verdict: the study is 'bold and original, arresting in its claims and powerful in argumentation', 'outstandingly clear', and 'indispensable' for anyone interested in the emergence of free will; 'for instance' (not 'particularly') introduces the two points of challenge, and the retrojection charge is what 'some would see', not Gill's own. The node keeps only the critical clause.

scholarly_argument_gill_stoic_compatibil.description: In Gill's summary of Frede's account, Stoic psychological and ethical notions were linked to a 'metaphysical or cosmic perspective': although events were shaped by 'all-embracing providential determinism', this 'allowed room for human agency (or will) as one of the types of causal factors shaping events', so that the capacity to make the choices needed for a good life is 'ineluctably, part of human nature' — 'in that sense we all have will and the ability to develop free will'. Gill does not use the term 'compatibilism'.

evidence.quote: Although events were seen as shaped by all-embracing providential determinism, this allowed room for human agency (or will) as one of the types of causal factors shaping events.
evidence.citation: [CR de GILL A Free Will  Origins of the Notion in Ancient Thought.md:141-145] (Gill 2014, p. 797)

evidence.quote: Hence, according to Frede, Stoicism provided the core conceptual content of the notion of free will even though this was subsequently translated into Christian terms.
evidence.citation: [CR de GILL A Free Will  Origins of the Notion in Ancient Thought.md:104-113] (Gill 2014, p. 797)

scholarly_argument_gill_stoic_compatibil.finding: Quote verbatim, p. 797. Two losses: (1) the topic label 'Stoic compatibilism' is not Gill's word — 'compatibilism' does not occur in the review; (2) the passage is Gill's exposition of the 'conceptual content' that, 'according to Frede', Stoicism supplied, not a position Gill defends in his own name (he calls the stress on Stoicism 'controversial').

scholarly_argument_gill_stoic_conception.description: Expounding Frede's account, Gill explains that the will is 'our ability to make choices or decisions which make us act in the way we do' (Frede, p. 8), expressed in Stoic terms, especially by Epictetus, as prohairesis, with motivation depending on 'assent' to a 'rational impression'. Gill adds that this conception is 'thus more rational than the "voluntarist" or "volitional" idea presupposed by Dihle'; all adult humans are constitutively capable of exercising will and of developing 'freedom' of the will by liberating themselves from 'self-enslavement' to false ethical beliefs.

evidence.quote: The Stoic conception of will is thus more rational than the “voluntarist” or “volitional” idea presupposed by Dihle. Stoics presented all (adult) human beings as constitutively capable of exercising will, in this sense
evidence.citation: [CR de GILL A Free Will  Origins of the Notion in Ancient Thought.md:128-132] (Gill 2014, p. 797)

evidence.quote: This freedom depends on liberating oneself from the “self-enslavement” that consists in subjecting oneself to false and misguided ethical beliefs.
evidence.citation: [CR de GILL A Free Will  Origins of the Notion in Ancient Thought.md:135-138] (Gill 2014, p. 797)

scholarly_argument_gill_stoic_conception.finding: Quote verbatim, p. 797 (the '(8)' is Gill citing Frede's p. 8). The comparison with Dihle's 'voluntarist' idea is Gill's own gloss, but the whole paragraph answers 'What is that conceptual content?' — i.e. it expounds Frede's reconstruction of the Stoic/Epictetan notion (prohairesis, assent to a rational impression, freedom as liberation from 'self-enslavement'). The node presents it as Gill's independent position on Stoic will.

scholarly_argument_guillon_compatibilism.description: To sort the contemporary 'mosaïque de positions', Guillon finds it convenient ('commode') to use the traditional opposition between 'conceptions compatibilistes' and 'conceptions incompatibilistes'. Compatibilist conceptions, inherited mainly from Hobbes, Locke and Hume, hold that free will, when properly conceived, is compatible with causal determinism, so that a scientific proof of determinism need cause no worry. Incompatibilist conceptions, in the large majority (perhaps alone represented) before the 17th century and enjoying a 'retour en force' for some forty years, defend by various arguments the intuition that determinism would deprive us of free will.

evidence.quote: Pour y voir plus clair dans cette variété de positions, il est commode de recourir à l'opposition traditionnelle entre « conceptions compatibilistes » du libre arbitre et « conceptions incompatibilistes ».

Les conceptions incompatibilistes au contraire (qui étaient largement majoritaires - peut-être seules représentées - avant le XVIIème siècle, et qui font l'objet d'un retour en force depuis une quarantaine d'années) défendent par divers arguments l'intuition selon laquelle le déterminisme nous priverait du libre arbitre.

scholarly_argument_guillon_compatibilism.finding: Guillon presents the compatibilist/incompatibilist opposition as a convenient sorting device ('il est commode de recourir à l'opposition traditionnelle'), not as the way the debate 'is best understood'. The node drops his two qualifications: compatibilism holds free will 'lorsqu'il est bien conçu' compatible with determinism 'de telle sorte qu'il n'y a nullement à s'inquiéter d'une éventuelle preuve du déterminisme par la science', and incompatibilist conceptions were 'largement majoritaires - peut-être seules représentées - avant le XVIIème siècle'. Page: p. 6 of the Avant-propos (§5), also in the résumé p. 1; not 'pp. 1-5'.

scholarly_argument_list_determinism_fate.description: List argues that the two Platonic doctrines Justin rejects in Dial. 4 (the soul's vision of God; transmigration) 'happen to be foundational' to the anthropologies of Carpocrates, Basilides and Simon/Helen, teachers probably refuted in the lost Syntagma. Their use of transmigration was tied to christology, 'divine judgement' (Basilides' martyrs suffering for sins of a previous embodiment) and cosmology. Justin's rejection was therefore 'religious competition', undermining rivals and defining Christianity on his own terms. List says nothing about fate, determinism or moral responsibility.

evidence.quote: The Platonic anthropology rejected by Justin happens to be foundational to the theological systems of his Christian demiurgical opponents: Simon and Helen, Basilides, and Carpocrates

the appropriation of Platonic anthropology by Christian Demiurgists was integrally tied to a host of broader theological concerns, whether it be christology (Carpocrates' Jesus as remembering the forms), divine judgement (Basilides' martyrs suffering for sins in a previous embodiment), or cosmology

scholarly_argument_list_determinism_fate.finding: The first half is List's thesis (abstract p. 1; §2 pp. 9-16; conclusion p. 21). The node's title ('determinism, fate, and moral responsibility') and its closing clause ('the transmigration doctrine has implications for moral responsibility') are not in List: the article contains no occurrence of 'fate', 'determinism', 'free will' or 'responsibility' (rg over the whole file). What List does discuss is judgement: for Basilides, martyrs 'suffering for sins in a previous embodiment'; for Justin, animals 'benefit in no way ... from such punishment' (Dial. 4.7). '§§3-4' in the reference are section numbers, not pages.

scholarly_argument_list_epistemological_.description: For List, anthropology was 'foundational' to Justin's Platonism, so conceding that the rational soul cannot perceive God 'meant a complete overhaul of his epistemological system'. If Justin remained a Platonist ('and I think he did'), it was a Platonism 'completely revolutionised by this new epistemological foundation (Spirit-inspired biblical prophecy)', not one 'completed' or 'corrected' by Christianity (against Thorsteinsson). At root, the issue with the Christian demiurgists 'was one of epistemology': Justin could not square Spirit-inspired prophecy with their Platonic epistemology. No anti-fatalist theology is discussed.

evidence.quote: If Justin remained a Platonist (and I think he did), it was not a Platonism "completed" or "corrected" by Christianity (which Thorsteinsson calls "a secondary phenomenon in Justin's life"),35 but a Platonism completely revolutionised by this new epistemological foundation (Spirit-inspired biblical prophecy).
rather, at root, the issue was one of epistemology. Justin could not square his understanding of Spirit-inspired prophecy with the Platonic epistemology adopted by the Christian demiurgists.

scholarly_argument_list_epistemological_.finding: The quote is verbatim (p. 9) and List's conclusion confirms the epistemological point ('at root, the issue was one of epistemology'). But the node adds an 'anti-fatalist theology' that List never mentions (no 'fate'/'fatal' in the file), and the 'proof from prophecy' appears only as a theme shared by the Apologies and the Dialogue (p. 5, l. 182), not as something the epistemological shift 'is the context for'. List's contrast is 'Spirit-inspired biblical prophecy' versus the Platonic epistemology of the demiurgists, i.e. the soul's vision of God, not 'of the Forms'.

scholarly_argument_list_justin_martyr_s_.description: Returning to den Dulk's insights, List locates the answer to why Justin rejected the soul's vision of God and transmigration, but not Platonism in toto, in 'Justin's anti-heresiological programme'. His critique of the Christian Demiurgists (Carpocrates, Basilides, Simon) was 'multi-faceted, extending beyond theology into the areas of anthropology and epistemology'. Nothing in the article bears on free will or determinism.

evidence.quote: But while demiurgism may loom large in Justin's critique of his opponents, I wish to show that Justin's critique of Christian Demiurgists was multi-faceted, extending beyond theology into the areas of anthropology and epistemology.

scholarly_argument_list_justin_martyr_s_.finding: Quote verbatim (p. 9) and the first sentence is faithful. The second sentence ('undergirds his broader theological positions relevant to free will and determinism') is invented: List's article contains no discussion of free will or determinism. List's own extension of the point is to 'anthropology and epistemology', not to free will. The auxiliary references (Contra Celsum 5.62, Edwards 1991) are not needed to support the node.

scholarly_argument_matteoli_free_will_li.description: Matteoli reads the Expositiones on Rm 1,24 and 11,8 (God 'abandons' sinners to safeguard free will), 7,14-21 and 9,16-24 as Pelagius's defence of 'libero arbitrio' against a 'lettura in senso deterministico' of Paul, before the controversy with Augustine. Her conclusion, however, is that here Pelagius 'nella sostanza non innova': the defence of human freedom is common to practically all his sources (Origen above all), he keeps to his predecessors' explanations of Rm 9, and it is Augustine, from the Ad Simplicianum, who introduces a different perspective.

evidence.quote: Del resto, la difesa della libertà dell'uomo è tema comune praticamente a tutte le fonti di Pelagio : per quanto concerne quella che diverrà una delle tematiche fondamentali del pelagianesimo nei suoi sviluppi successivi, non si riscontra nelle Expositiones una presa di posizione innovativa o estremista che rompa con la tradizione precedente.

Senza dubbio Pelagio avverte più dei suoi predecessori il problema della difesa del libero arbitrio, ma nella sostanza non innova, inserendosi al contrario in una tradizione di pensiero ben consolidata.

scholarly_argument_matteoli_free_will_li.finding: Quote verbatim (p. 118) and the passages listed are indeed ch. 4 §1 (pp. 118-135). 'Deterministic readings' is Matteoli's own vocabulary ('visione deterministica', 'lettura in senso deterministico'). But the node loses her central conclusion: on free will Pelagius 'nella sostanza non innova' — the defence of human freedom is 'tema comune praticamente a tutte le fonti di Pelagio', he follows his predecessors on Rm 9, and it is rather Augustine from the Ad Simplicianum on who introduces a new perspective. 'Already central' is the node's phrasing, not hers.

scholarly_argument_matteoli_grace_gratia.description: Matteoli finds that gratia in the Expositiones has several meanings: the prevailing exemplum Christi, but also forgiveness of sins and reconciliation with God, and adiutorium (Rm 8,26, the Spirit helping our weak capacities). The 'apparent contradiction' between gratuitous grace and merits, faith alone and works, 'si risolve solo distinguendo due momenti' of justification: sola fide at conversion, works necessary afterwards (Rm 4,5; Gal 3,10) — a scheme already in Ambrosiaster and Origen. She reads this as an embryonic, not yet dogmatic, phase of Pelagius's theology.

evidence.quote: si risolve solo distinguendo due momenti diversi nel processo di giustificazione.
anche se a prevalere è il principio dell'exemplum Christi, non mancano riferimenti alla grazia come perdono dei peccati e riconciliazione con Dio, e alla grazia come adiutorium.

scholarly_argument_matteoli_grace_gratia.finding: Quote verbatim (p. 169; ch. 5 §3 = pp. 166-170, §2 = pp. 162-166). The node keeps 'tension' but drops Matteoli's resolution: the contradiction is 'apparente' and 'si risolve solo distinguendo due momenti diversi nel processo di giustificazione' (sola fide at conversion, works thereafter, cf. Rm 4,5 and Gal 3,10). Her conclusion is that, against expectation, gratia in the Expositiones has several meanings (exemplum Christi prevailing; forgiveness and reconciliation; adiutorium, e.g. Rm 8,26), that the two-phase scheme is attested in Ambrosiaster and Origen, and that this is an 'embryonic' phase of his thought. 'Salvation by works alone' is the node's phrase, not hers.

scholarly_argument_matteoli_impeccantia_.description: Matteoli starts from Jerome's term impeccantia (the principle that man, if he wills, can be without sin), contested by Jerome (Ep. 133, Dialogus adversus Pelagianos, In Hieremiam) and Augustine. Her examination of the Expositiones finds that passages genuinely attributable to this doctrine 'sono ben pochi' — only 1Tim 1,5, Rm 6,7 and Rm 8,3 — and are 'espressa comunque con estrema cautela'; most are generic exhortations to a holy life like Ambrosiaster's. The concept has not yet found its full formulation at this stage.

evidence.quote: Il principio secondo cui l'uomo può, se vuole, essere senza peccato, è espresso da Gerolamo con il termine impeccantia, che ancora oggi è spesso impiegato per indicare la dottrina dei pelagiani.
Solo nel commento di Pelagio a 1Tim 1, 5, Rm 6, 7 e Rm 8, 3 si possono ravvisare effettivi riferimenti alla dottrina dell'impeccantia, espressa comunque con estrema cautela.

scholarly_argument_matteoli_impeccantia_.finding: Quote verbatim (p. 175), but it reports Jerome's term for the later Pelagian doctrine. Matteoli's own finding for the Expositiones is the opposite of the node's flat attribution: passages actually attributable to impeccantia 'sono ben pochi' (only 1Tim 1,5; Rm 6,7; Rm 8,3), 'espressa comunque con estrema cautela', in a phase where the concept 'non ha ancora trovato' its formulation; elsewhere only generic calls to a holy life such as Ambrosiaster also makes. The node turns her cautious, embryonic reading into a settled belief of Pelagius.

scholarly_argument_matteoli_original_sin.description: For Matteoli, Pelagius's 'vera novità' is on Adam's sin: the term mortalitas is absent from his Romans commentary; the death introduced by Adam is exclusively spiritual death, acquired through individual sins 'per imitazione' of the first man, so the contradiction his sources faced (universal sinfulness vs. personal responsibility) is eliminated. On the lex naturae, Pelagius gives each of the three ages (nature, law, faith) an autonomous value: natural law and Mosaic law could guarantee salvation only while in force, before Christ, each later rendered insufficient by the 'consuetudo peccatorum'.

evidence.quote: si tratta esclusivamente della morte spirituale, acquisita tramite i peccati individuali per imitazione della trasgressione del primo uomo.

egli attribuisce ad ogni epoca un valore autonomo, ritenendo sia la legge di natura sia la legge mosaica capaci di garantire la salvezza limitatamente al tempo in cui furono in vigore, quindi prima dell'avvento di Cristo.

scholarly_argument_matteoli_original_sin.finding: Quote verbatim (p. 110; ch. 3 = pp. 55-116). Faithful on Adam: spiritual death 'acquisita tramite i peccati individuali per imitazione', which Matteoli calls Pelagius's 'vera novità'. But 'the lex naturae provides sufficient moral guidance' flattens her ch. 2 thesis: natural law and Mosaic law can guarantee salvation only 'limitatamente al tempo in cui furono in vigore', and each became insufficient because of the 'consuetudo peccatorum' (p. 49). 'Born with the capacity for sinlessness' is not stated in ch. 3.

scholarly_argument_moore_josephus_s_phil.description: Moore holds that Heimarmene in its Stoic definition had no Hebrew equivalent and 'was a conception alien to all Jewish thinking'; Jewish determinism 'was theological, not philosophical'. How Josephus came to classify the sects by attitude to Fate 'is a matter of guess-work'. Either his Greek literary assistants supplied the word (Josephus hardly aware of its incompatibility), or — Moore's preferred guess — the classification came 'from a foreign source', Nicolaus of Damascus, whose brief account of Jewish sects 'in terms of current Greek philosophical controversies' passed into the War and Ant. xviii with Stoic-sounding explanations.

evidence.quote: How Josephus came, in the three passages quoted above, to classify the Jewish "philosophies" of his time by their attitude severally toward Fate is a matter of guess-work, and what I have to submit are guesses
evidence.citation: [02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/Fate and Free Will in the Jewish Philosophies according to Josephus, George Foot Moore.md:583-586] (Moore 1929, p. 382)

evidence.quote: On the whole, however, I am more inclined to a different guess, namely that the classification of the Jewish 'philosophies' by their attitude toward Fate came originally from a foreign source.
evidence.citation: [02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/Fate and Free Will in the Jewish Philosophies according to Josephus, George Foot Moore.md:623-626] (Moore 1929, p. 383)

evidence.quote: All these things would be explicable enough in a general historian in Herod's time, who was trying to give his readers a brief account of Jewish sects in terms of current Greek philosophical controversies.
evidence.citation: [02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/Fate and Free Will in the Jewish Philosophies according to Josephus, George Foot Moore.md:644-647] (Moore 1929, p. 384)

scholarly_argument_moore_josephus_s_phil.finding: Moore never says Josephus 'deliberately' cast the sects in Greek philosophical categories. He calls the origin of the fate-classification 'a matter of guess-work'. His guesses: (a) Josephus's Greek literary assistants chose Heimarmene, Josephus's acquaintance with philosophy being 'hardly ... sufficient to make him aware how incompatible it was with Jewish religious thought', or Josephus used the word meaning 'divine determinism'; (b) his preferred guess: the classification 'came originally from a foreign source', Nicolaus of Damascus, a historian describing Jewish sects 'in terms of current Greek philosophical controversies'. Pages 382-384, not 371-375.

scholarly_argument_moore_pharisee_doctri.description: Moore sets three Josephan accounts side by side: Ant. xiii.5.9 (some things the work of fate, some 'in men's own power'); War ii.8.14 (the Pharisees 'attribute everything to fate and to God', doing right or wrong 'lies chiefly in men's power, but fate is auxiliary'); Ant. xviii.1.3, where Josephus 'is apparently endeavoring to make plainer' the War statement, though his explanations 'do not make the attitude of the Pharisees any plainer to us'. He finds the Pharisee exposition 'especially strange', asks whether the phrasing (auxiliary causes, impulse, assent) is specifically Chrysippean, and treats the whole classification as guess-work, probably from Nicolaus of Damascus.

evidence.quote: attribute everything to fate and to God. To do right or the contrary lies chiefly in men's power, but fate is auxiliary in each particular case.
evidence.citation: [02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/Fate and Free Will in the Jewish Philosophies according to Josephus, George Foot Moore.md:199-200] (Moore 1929, p. 374)

evidence.quote: Coining then to their attitude toward Fate, he is apparently endeavoring to make plainer what he had said on this subject in the War twenty years or more earlier:
evidence.citation: [02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/Fate and Free Will in the Jewish Philosophies according to Josephus, George Foot Moore.md:232-235] (Moore 1929, p. 375)

evidence.quote: The striking thing in these passages is that the Jewish sects (as we are in the habit of calling them) should be primarily characterized by their attitude toward fate, and especially strange is the exposition of the doctrine of the Pharisees on this point.
evidence.citation: [02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/Fate and Free Will in the Jewish Philosophies according to Josephus, George Foot Moore.md:242-246] (Moore 1929, p. 375)

scholarly_argument_moore_pharisee_doctri.finding: Several misreadings. (1) In the War the Pharisees 'attribute everything to fate and to God', doing right or wrong 'lies chiefly in men's power, but fate is auxiliary' — it is fate, not God, that is auxiliary. (2) Moore does not rank the War as 'the more deterministic-sounding': Ant. xviii.1.3 also says 'all things are brought about by Fate' while preserving 'the volitional faculty'. (3) Moore says Josephus in Ant. xviii 'is apparently endeavoring to make plainer' the War statement, with explanations that 'do not make the attitude of the Pharisees any plainer to us' — not that he 'distorted the original teaching'. (4) 'c. 75 CE' is not Moore's; he says the War was written twenty years earlier, 'in the first years of his residence in Rome'. Pages 371, 374-375, 383-384.

scholarly_argument_moore_the_fourth_phil.description: Moore introduces Judas the Galilean's 'fourth philosophy' only because its rise (census of Quirinius, 6 AD) is 'the occasion for the introduction of the three older schools' in War ii.8 and Ant. xviii.1. Following Josephus, he reports that the party 'made a religious principle of their political theory' (God sole ruler; tribute a recognition of mortal sovereigns), endured torture, assured partisans that 'the Deity would help only those who did their best to help themselves', were 'a party of action', and — Judas having associated the Pharisee Sadducus — agreed with the Pharisees in all but political intransigence. Moore draws no free-will doctrine from this.

evidence.quote: The occasion for the introduction of the three older schools in Bell. Jud. ii. 8, 2-14 and in Ant. xviii. 1,1 ff. is the rise of a new party which Josephus calls "the fourth philosophy."
evidence.citation: [02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/Fate and Free Will in the Jewish Philosophies according to Josephus, George Foot Moore.md:110-112] (Moore 1929, p. 372)

evidence.quote: Judas associated with himself a certain Sadducus, a Pharisee, and his party are said in all respects except their political intransigeance to have agreed with the Pharisees.
evidence.citation: [02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/Fate and Free Will in the Jewish Philosophies according to Josephus, George Foot Moore.md:146-148] (Moore 1929, p. 373)

scholarly_argument_moore_the_fourth_phil.finding: Quote verbatim (p. 373) and the Sadducus/Pharisee point is Moore's. But 'emphasized human agency' is a free-will reading Moore does not make: he reports Josephus's account of Judas's party (God sole sovereign, refusal of tribute, 'a party of action') only because its rise is 'the occasion for the introduction of the three older schools' in War ii.8 and Ant. xviii.1. Moore attaches no doctrine of fate or free will to the Fourth Philosophy; his subject is the three older sects.

scholarly_argument_oviedo_rahner_s_theol.description: Oviedo reads Rahner's 1965 'Theology of freedom', framed by 'transcendental neo-Kantian anthropology', as the most updated Catholic attempt for its time, asking 'which points require some updating, complement or even deep revision'. Rahner radicalises freedom in Christian terms: real freedom of choice, 'rather a demand and a task than freedom', is fully seen only in Christianity, becoming 'freedom from God and towards God' under the highest responsibility before God's love. Oviedo locates Rahner's 'big paradox' elsewhere: God founds freedom, yet freedom can culpably deny its own ground. He asks 'how much dated is that view'.

evidence.quote: The revelation in Christ assumes a funding character for human freedom, which becomes exalted to the highest imaginable level, as far as it becomes freedom from God and towards God.

The mentioned article reports about a big paradox at the centre of Rahner's transcendental treatment of that human trait: God is at the same time the foundation or condition of possibility of human freedom, but, nevertheless, humans can use that faculty to deny their own source or foundation

scholarly_argument_oviedo_rahner_s_theol.finding: Two problems. (1) 'Paradoxically' is misplaced: 'rather a demand and a task than freedom' is Rahner's own wording quoted by Oviedo under 'Christian Radicalization of the Concept of Free Will' (p. 69) with no paradox attached; Oviedo's 'big paradox' is elsewhere (section c, p. 71): God is the condition of possibility of freedom, yet freedom can 'culpably deny the very condition of its own possibility'. (2) Pages: the framework label is on p. 68, but 'demand and a task', 'highest responsibility' and 'freedom from God and towards God' are on p. 69; 'how much dated is that view' on p. 71. 'Valuable but dated ... needs updating' fairly renders pp. 68-70.

scholarly_argument_oviedo_sin_grace_and_.description: Oviedo lists three principles of theological anthropology in which free will is involved: the Imago Dei, with freedom as a postulate of similarity to God; sinfulness, 'viewed in terms of freedom trimming or limited'; and grace, including 'with some nuances' a 'restored full capacity for freedom, liberation from sin's bondage'. Confessional positions long debated the extent of free will under sin, but 'in some way' those discussions 'seem to be overcome' by new awareness; in ecumenical dialogue 'the reached consensus seems quite peaceful'. He nonetheless holds that the question 'still needs to be assumed and tackled'.

evidence.quote: However, in some way, old confessional discussions seem to be overcome by new awareness and the revision of early held positions concerning the corrupting effect of sin and the re-generating consequence of grace.
Even in ecumenical dialogue apparently free will does not play a great role, since the reached consensus seems quite peaceful and agreement dominates over discussion.

scholarly_argument_oviedo_sin_grace_and_.finding: Quote verbatim (p. 67). The node hardens Oviedo's hedges: 'in some way, old confessional discussions seem to be overcome by new awareness' becomes 'are now largely overcome'; 'the reached consensus seems quite peaceful' (abstract, on ecumenical dialogue) becomes 'consensus replacing controversy'. It also omits his own verdict that the question 'still needs to be assumed and tackled' (p. 68).

scholarly_argument_runia_philo_and_free_.description: Runia's book is a survey of Philo's reception in Christian literature, not a study of Philo's own positions. Chapter 2 §2 lists 'those themes in Philo's writings and thought which are of importance for his reception', including, under religious themes, '(f) Free will and ethics': man 'is unique in that he can choose to follow the course of good or the course of evil'; liberation from the passions is required, total absence of passion being reached only by the exemplum Moses, a reasonable moderation by others. Fate and determinism are not treated as such.
scholarly_argument_runia_philo_and_free_.page_range: 37-43 (paragraph (f) on p. 41, folio read from running header; page map unavailable)

evidence.quote: (f) Free will and ethics. Man is unique in that he can choose to follow the
evidence.citation: [02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/Runia - 1993 - Jewish Traditions in Early Christian Literature, Volume 3 Philo in Early Christian Literature A sur.md:1439]

evidence.quote: for purposes of orientation it may be of some value briefly to list those themes in Philo's writings and thought which are of importance for his reception in the patristic period.
evidence.citation: [02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/Runia - 1993 - Jewish Traditions in Early Christian Literature, Volume 3 Philo in Early Christian Literature A sur.md:1304-1306]

scholarly_argument_runia_philo_and_free_.finding: Correct that the book is a reception survey, but the node overlooks that Runia's 'Main themes in Philo' (ch. 2 §2) contains an explicit paragraph '(f) Free will and ethics': man 'is unique in that he can choose to follow the course of good or the course of evil', liberation from passion required, apatheia only for Moses, metriopatheia for others. agentic_search cannot project pages for this file (map_conf 0.00, 'p.?'), so citations are by line; the running header 'PRELIMINARIES 41' on the same extracted page gives printed p. 41 for the paragraph, with ch. 2 §2 = pp. 37-43 per the table of contents.

scholarly_argument_runia_philo_s_influen.description: Runia's conclusions distinguish three streams of Philonic reception: before Clement a broader 'Philonism' (Barnabas, Justin, Theophilus), whose direct dependence on Philo cannot be proved; a 'direct tradition' running through the Alexandrian school (Clement, who first names him, Origen, Didymus) and its sympathisers (Eusebius, Gregory of Nyssa, Ambrose, Augustine); and, after Origen and Eusebius, an 'indirect tradition' in which Philonic themes are taken over at second hand. Most Patristic use 'is not advertised by the mention of his name': Ambrose names Philo only once, Jerome more often.
scholarly_argument_runia_philo_s_influen.page_range: 335-343 (ch. 16; folios from running headers, page map unavailable)

evidence.quote: Philo is not explicitly named in Christian sources until the end of the 2nd century, when he is extensively used by Clement of Alexandria.
evidence.citation: [02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/Runia - 1993 - Jewish Traditions in Early Christian Literature, Volume 3 Philo in Early Christian Literature A sur.md:8931-8933]

evidence.quote: His copious usage, predominantly in the area of allegorical interpretation, is somewhat camouflaged by the translation into Latin and the fact that he only once refers to his source by name.
evidence.citation: [02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/Runia - 1993 - Jewish Traditions in Early Christian Literature, Volume 3 Philo in Early Christian Literature A sur.md:8975-8977]

evidence.quote: after Origen and Eusebius the reception of Philo splits up into a direct and an indirect tradition.
evidence.citation: [02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/Runia - 1993 - Jewish Traditions in Early Christian Literature, Volume 3 Philo in Early Christian Literature A sur.md:9040-9041]

scholarly_argument_runia_philo_s_influen.finding: Runia's conclusions (ch. 16) are more articulated than the node. He distinguishes three streams: a 'direct tradition' of reception mediated through the Alexandrian school (Clement, Origen, Didymus, then Eusebius, Gregory of Nyssa, Ambrose, Augustine), a broader pre-Clementine 'Philonism' (Barnabas, Justin, Theophilus, 'if they did not read Philo directly'), and an 'indirect tradition' after Origen and Eusebius. Naming is a separate matter: Philo 'is not explicitly named' before Clement; Ambrose uses him copiously but 'only once refers to his source by name', Jerome names him more often; most Patristic usage 'is not advertised by the mention of his name'. So 'direct citation rare except Clement, Origen, and Ambrose' conflates direct use with citation by name. Page map unavailable; folios inferred from running headers (ch. 16 = pp. 335-347).

scholarly_argument_runia_philo_s_status_.description: Runia traces the 'gradual development' of Philo's Christian status through testimonia: Eusebius, the first to connect Philo with the Christians (De vita contemplativa as witness to the first Christians in Egypt; meeting with Peter), does 'not explicitly' present him as a Christian; Jerome and Epiphanius bring him near conversion, Ps.Prochorus and Photius record it, and Byzantine Catenae head extracts 'Philo the Bishop'. The loss of this status begins with Fabricius's 1693 dissertation showing Philo's thought was Platonist; thereafter he is studied as a Greco-Roman author, and acceptance into the Jewish heritage comes only in the 19th century.
scholarly_argument_runia_philo_s_status_.page_range: 3-6, 31-33 (folios from running headers, page map unavailable)

evidence.quote: The first recorded witness to make an explicit connection between Philo and the Christians was Eusebius in his celebrated Ecclesiastical History
evidence.citation: [02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/Runia - 1993 - Jewish Traditions in Early Christian Literature, Volume 3 Philo in Early Christian Literature A sur.md:402-404]

evidence.quote: In Eusebius (l-5) Philo is not explicitly presented as a Christian, but he stands so close to the early Christians that his evidence is invaluable.
evidence.citation: [02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/Runia - 1993 - Jewish Traditions in Early Christian Literature, Volume 3 Philo in Early Christian Literature A sur.md:474-475]

evidence.quote: From this time onwards Philo gradually loses his status as a honorary Church father and theological authority, and comes to be studied primarily as a rather unusual author from the Greco-Roman world
evidence.citation: [02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/Runia - 1993 - Jewish Traditions in Early Christian Literature, Volume 3 Philo in Early Christian Literature A sur.md:1172-1174]

scholarly_argument_runia_philo_s_status_.finding: Runia describes a 'gradual development' of the legend, not a status conferred by Eusebius: Eusebius is 'the first recorded witness to make an explicit connection' (Therapeutae as first Christians in Egypt; meeting Peter), but 'in Eusebius (1-5) Philo is not explicitly presented as a Christian'; conversion appears only in Ps.Prochorus and Photius, and the Catena lemma 'Philo the Bishop' is Byzantine. The loss of status is dated by Runia to Fabricius's dissertation of 1693 establishing Philo's Platonism, after which Philo is 'studied primarily as a rather unusual author from the Greco-Roman world'; real Jewish acceptance comes only in the 19th century. 'Jewish identity reasserted' is not his explanation. Page map unavailable; folios from running headers (ch. 1 §1 pp. 3-6, §5 pp. 31-33).

scholarly_argument_frankfurt_concept_of_.description: Frankfurt rejects Strawson's and Ayer's use of 'person' for any entity bearing both psychological and corporeal predicates, since that misappropriates a valuable philosophical term. He locates 'one essential difference between persons and other creatures' in 'the structure of a person's will': persons can form second-order desires. He then specifies (p. 10) that what is essential to being a person is having second-order volitions (wanting a desire to be one's will), 'and not having second-order desires generally'.

evidence.quote: It is my view that one essential difference between persons and other creatures is to be found in the structure of a person's will.
Now it is having second-order volitions, and not having second-order desires generally, that I regard as essential to being a person.
evidence.citation: [Frankfurt-FreedomConceptPerson-1971.md:326-327] (p. 10; page_map conf 0.85, folio confirmed by running head at line 293)

scholarly_argument_frankfurt_concept_of_.finding: Quote located verbatim at lines 64-72 (p. 5). The Strawson/Ayer contrast is faithful. But (a) Frankfurt states 'one essential difference between persons and other creatures', not a definition of the person; and (b) the criterion he regards as essential is not the capacity for second-order desires generally but for second-order volitions (p. 10: 'it is having second-order volitions, and not having second-order desires generally, that I regard as essential to being a person'). The node collapses this distinction.

scholarly_argument_frankfurt_free_will_a.description: Frankfurt holds that 'one essential difference between persons and other creatures' lies in 'the structure of a person's will': besides first-order desires, which many animals share, it 'seems to be peculiarly characteristic of humans' that they form 'second-order desires'. He stresses that person-attributes are not necessarily species-specific (nonhuman persons are conceptually possible) and later narrows the essential criterion to second-order volitions (p. 10).

evidence.quote: It is conceptually possible that members of novel or even of fa- miliar nonhuman species should be persons; and it is also con- ceptually possible that some members of the human species are not persons.
It seems to be peculiarly characteristic of humans, however, that they are able to form what I shall call "second-order desires" or "desires of the second order."

scholarly_argument_frankfurt_free_will_a.finding: Quote located verbatim at lines 122-126 (p. 6). Two qualifications are lost: Frankfurt writes that the capacity 'appears' peculiar to humans and explicitly holds that 'It is conceptually possible that members of novel or even of familiar nonhuman species should be persons' (p. 6) — so 'uniquely human' is a presumption, not his thesis; and the essential feature is second-order volitions, not second-order desires as such (p. 10). The node's title 'free will' is also not the topic of this passage (persons).

scholarly_argument_blackson_early_stoics.description: Blackson argues that Epictetus believed E (adults choose to exercise their ability to use impressions), not D (adults choose to assent to impulsive impressions); since E is the minimum belief a Stoic must have for a notion of a will, Frede is right that Epictetus had one, but because the early Stoics 'probably believed E too', Frede is 'very likely wrong' that the first notion of a will belongs to late Stoicism. What is new in Epictetus is how he talked about standard Stoic doctrine.

evidence.quote: Because, however, the early Stoics probably believed E too, Frede is very likely wrong that "the first time we have any notion of a will" (p. 46) is in the time of late Stoicism.
evidence.citation: [Blackson - Epictetus, the Early Stoics, and Frede's Argument for the First Notion of a Will.md:852-854] (p. 99)

evidence.quote: The early Stoics probability had a notion of a will too.
evidence.citation: [Blackson - Epictetus, the Early Stoics, and Frede's Argument for the First Notion of a Will.md:150] (p. 84)

Blackson' (line 866) — printed p. 99, not p. 84 (page_map gives p. 98 at conf 0.80; the running heads are decisive). The same claim is stated on p. 84 (line 150).

scholarly_argument_faure_cyclical_vs_lin.description: Faure and Valli (Introduction): the view that Greeks conceived time as cyclical, popularised since Nietzsche's eternal return, has been challenged in two respects. First, following Aristotle (Ph. 223b28-224a2) and Sorabji, cyclicity is 'not necessarily an intrinsic feature of time' but of the elements by which time is witnessed; seasons and rituals are paradigmatic rather than cyclical. Second, linearity 'is not absent' from Greek culture — Fränkel held that the Greeks adopted linear time after the archaic period — but this 'somewhat teleological' stance has its weaknesses (Darbo-Peschanski): Greek conceptions of time were multiple.

evidence.quote: First, cyclicity is not necessarily an intrinsic feature of time, but rather of the elements that help people witness time elapse, as Aristotle has it:
According to Fränkel (1931), the Greek world gradually left cyclicity and adopted a linear temporal conception after the archa- ic period.
shows, this novel (somewhat teleological) stance contained its own weaknesses, because it allowed for the possibility that Greek conceptions of time were not single or double, but multiple

scholarly_argument_faure_cyclical_vs_lin.finding: The Introduction is co-authored by Richard Faure and Simon-Pierre Valli (not Faure alone). Quote located verbatim at lines 135-141, p. 2 (pdftotext folio: PDF page 8 = printed 2; the md's page headers are emitted at the end of each page; page_map for this file is AUDIT-FAIL). The first challenge is faithful. The second is misreported: the text says linearity 'is not absent from Ancient Greek culture', and reports Fränkel's view that the Greek world 'adopted a linear temporal conception after the archaic period' — not 'from the archaic period onward' — then, with Darbo-Peschanski, calls that stance 'somewhat teleological' and weak, concluding that Greek conceptions were 'multiple' (p. 4).

scholarly_argument_faure_g_del_s_relativ.description: Faure and Valli (Introduction): whereas Sorabji finds no Greek 'radical thesis' that time itself is cyclical, and cyclical stances are extremely rare (Winand), Gödel's rationale based on Einstein's relativity 'may lead to a "radical thesis"': if simultaneity is relative, succession becomes illusory and only observer-dependent 'nows' remain, leading Gödel to an idealistic conclusion. Though 'cyclical' is not suitable for his conception, he entertains the possibility of 'round trips' in time, so that instances may be lived more than once.

evidence.quote: In contrast, Gödel's (19703 [19491]) rationale, based on Einstein's relativity theory, may lead to a "radical thesis."

Although he does not use the word cyclical, which is not suitable for his conception, since cyclicity still rests on the view that time elapses, he entertains the idea that "round trips" in time are possible

scholarly_argument_faure_g_del_s_relativ.finding: Co-authored by Faure and Valli. Quote located verbatim at lines 170-182, p. 3 (pdftotext folio). evidence.quote: Hence the ultimate contrasts in Paul are eschatological: life "according to the flesh," lived according to the present age that has been condemned through the cross and is passing away, or life "according to the Spirit," lived in keeping with the values and norms of the coming age
