scholarly_argument_fischer_response_to_m.description: Replying to Pereboom's four-case argument, Fischer holds that Professor Plum meets the minimal conditions for guidance control, and so for moral responsibility, in all four cases; he does not distinguish the cases with respect to responsibility. Moral responsibility is only the 'gateway' to praise and blame: Plum is not blameworthy in cases one and two because of the provenance of his motivational states. Responsibility and blameworthiness require different histories.

evidence.quote: I have contended that Plum meets the minimal conditions for guidance control and moral responsibility in all four cases; thus, I do not seek to distinguish the cases with respect to moral responsibility. But clearly Plum is not blameworthy in cases one and two, given the provenance of the motivational states that lead to his behavior.

moral responsibility is the "gateway" to such notions as praiseworthiness and blameworthiness; an individual is morally responsible to the extent that he is an apt candidate for the reactive attitudes and moral praise and blame, but further conditions have to be met

scholarly_argument_fischer_response_to_m.finding: Fischer's 'Response to Pereboom' (pp. 185-186, lines 8010-8060) says the opposite of the node: Plum 'meets the minimal conditions for guidance control and moral responsibility in all four cases; thus, I do not seek to distinguish the cases with respect to moral responsibility'. What differs across the cases is blameworthiness, which depends on 'the provenance of the motivational states'. The node's claim that the cases 'differ in whether the mechanism is the agent's own' is not Fischer's reply.

scholarly_argument_fischer_sourcehood_an.description: Fischer's account of guidance control has two chief elements: the mechanism issuing in action must be the agent's own, and it must be appropriately reasons-responsive; 'mechanism' means only the process or way things go, and the locus of control remains the agent. He treats 'sourcehood' as the incompatibilist's worry (section 6) and argues that a notion of sourcehood compatible with causal determination is available, so that source incompatibilism is at best inconclusive.

evidence.quote: On my approach to guidance control, there are two chief elements: the mechanism that issues in action must be the "agent's own," and it must be appropriately "reasons-responsive."

Here I wish to explore some of the reasons why philosophers have contended that causal determinism rules out sourcehood in the sense required by moral responsibility, and I wish to offer some plausibility-arguments against this contention.

scholarly_argument_fischer_sourcehood_an.finding: Quote verbatim located at lines 3517-3519, p. 78. But Fischer does not call the control relevant to responsibility 'sourcehood': 'sourcehood' is his name for the source-incompatibilist requirement examined in section 6 (pp. 66-70), where he argues a compatibilist notion of sourcehood is available and the incompatibilist versions are inconclusive. His own positive notion is 'guidance control', whose two elements are the mechanism being the agent's own and 'appropriately' reasons-responsive. 'Moderately reasons-responsive' and the 'some different reasons, not all' gloss are not in this text.

scholarly_argument_gorday_augustine_s_de.description: Gorday finds Augustine, like his Greek predecessors, concerned to locate free will in Rom 9:10-13, though by different routes. In the Ad Simplicianum 1,2 Augustine rejected the argument from foreseen merits as a way of vindicating free will in salvation, a rejection following from his 'radical insistence on the utter gratuity of grace, apart from any act of human deserving, faith included'; the example of Jacob and Esau is thereby 'turned on its head'. De libero arbitrio III is cited for the bondage of the will as a penal condition.

evidence.quote: In the De Diversis Quaestionibus ad Simplicianum, 1,2, however, he rejected the argument from foreseen merits as a way of vindicating free will in salvation. This rejection followed from Augustine's radical insistence on the utter gratuity of grace, apart from any act of human deserving, faith included.

In the De Libero Arbitrio, particularly in portions of Book III composed about the year 395, Augustine was concerned with this same issue of the bondage of the will, specifically with the point that bondage is a penal condition

scholarly_argument_gorday_augustine_s_de.finding: Quote verbatim located at lines 14276-14290 (ch. V, Augustine; page map p. 166, conf 0.80, AUDIT-FAIL; folio garbled in extraction). Gorday's turning point is the Ad Simplicianum rejection of 'the argument from foreseen merits', flowing from 'the utter gratuity of grace'. The node's claim that Gorday notes 'earlier more Origen-like positions in De libero arbitrio' is not supported: Gorday's De libero arbitrio reference (line 15002) concerns the bondage of the will as a penal condition (Book III, c. 395), not an Origen-like reading. 'Deterministic' is not Gorday's word for Augustine; 'rigid predestinarianism' appears only as the reception's charge (line 22541).

scholarly_argument_gorday_origen_s_view_.description: Gorday reads Origen's Romans commentary as holding that a real human response is necessary to realize the divine intention, which cannot be accused of injustice. Those whom God has predestined and foreknown obtain their inheritance, but only through the long and arduous exercise of free will amid hardship; foreknowledge does not preclude free will because it applies to those who will freely allow themselves to be conformed to Christ, and the potter molds the vessels 'in accordance with his own foreknowledge of merit'. Gorday does not use the word 'compatibilist'.

evidence.quote: The will of God indeed is that those whom he has predestined and foreknown shall have that inheritance that is theirs, but only by the long and arduous process of exercising free will amidst all manner of hardship and opposition.
God's foreknowledge in this process may be said not to preclude free will, since foreknowledge may be said to apply only to those who will freely allow themselves to be conformed to Christ.

scholarly_argument_gorday_origen_s_view_.finding: Quote verbatim located at lines 4774-4787 (ch. III, Origen; page map p. 45, conf 0.80, AUDIT-FAIL). 'Compatibilist' is not Gorday's word. The node's 'God foreknows but does not predetermine' drops Gorday's point that for Origen predestination stands but is conditioned on foreknown merit: 'those whom he has predestined and foreknown shall have that inheritance ... but only by the long and arduous process of exercising free will'; 'foreknowledge may be said to apply only to those who will freely allow themselves to be conformed to Christ'; molding 'in accordance with his own foreknowledge of merit'. The page_range 'Preface, throughout' is wrong (ch. III).

scholarly_argument_gorday_patristic_exeg.description: In his preface Gorday presents the book as an attempt to get behind the Reformation-era reading of Paul in which 'justification' is the center of gravity, hoping that a fresh evaluation of patristic exegesis may aid Catholic-Protestant rapprochement. Repristination would be a mistake, but the early centuries can help in 'rethinking the modern task'; the key is reading the patristic texts for 'the subtleties and structures by which Scripture is a unity for the fathers'. The free-will/determinism framing is not Gorday's here.

evidence.quote: As a study in the patristic exegesis of Romans this work represents an attempt to get back behind the Reformation-era interpretation of Paul wherein "justification" becomes the center of gravity in explaining every aspect of the Apostle's thought.

He then argued that the Augustinian perspective, focusing initially on the determinism/ indeterminism issue, must be banned from these chapters: in fact they deal with Jews and Gentiles as peoples in the divine plan, not with individuals

scholarly_argument_gorday_patristic_exeg.finding: Quote verbatim located at lines 235-252 in the Author's Preface (folio 'vii' at line 170, 'ix' at 292: pp. vii-viii). Gorday's preface is about getting 'behind the Reformation-era interpretation of Paul wherein justification becomes the center of gravity' and 'Catholic-Protestant rapprochement'; it says nothing about free will versus determinism or a 'determinism/libertarian dichotomy'. The node's 'preserves both divine sovereignty and human responsibility without systematic resolution' is not in the preface; the only related remark (Conclusions, lines 20012-20015) reports Beyschlag's view that 'the Augustinian perspective, focusing initially on the determinism/indeterminism issue, must be banned from these chapters'.

scholarly_argument_graeser_epictetus_inf.description: Graeser's short chapter on Plotinus and Epictetus (pp. 82-84) registers nine verbal and thematic parallels: the soul's return to its native country, the sage's disregard of misfortunes, courage and caution not mutually exclusive, fears likened to children's, the outside world as 'sport', souls 'entirely free to achieve happiness' against Gnostic objections to theodicy, no evil for the good man, wicked men punished as wolves. He notes Plotinus is 'indebted to' or 'approximates' Epictetus; he does not discuss the eph' hemin distinction in this chapter.

evidence.quote: It seems that Plotinus is indebted to Epictetus. The Stoic philosopher likes to speak of man as
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Plotinus and the Stoics- A Preliminary Study -- Andreas Graeser -- Philosophia Antiqua 22, 1972 -- Brill Archive -- 10.1163-9789004320437 -- 40e2ba2071c19c7f4c4ab4b045ddfb83 -- Anna’s Archive.md:4008-4009] (Graeser 1972, p. 82)

evidence.quote: When arguing against the Gnostic objections to theodicy (III 2 [47J 5,3 [T6nOLJ), Plotinus is apparently "stoicizing", in that he asserts that souls are entirely free to achieve happiness.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Plotinus and the Stoics- A Preliminary Study -- Andreas Graeser -- Philosophia Antiqua 22, 1972 -- Brill Archive -- 10.1163-9789004320437 -- 40e2ba2071c19c7f4c4ab4b045ddfb83 -- Anna’s Archive.md:4085-4087] (Graeser 1972, p. 83)

scholarly_argument_graeser_epictetus_inf.finding: Work confirmed in the fonds (MANIFEST line 83). Chapter III 'Plotinus and Epictetus' (TOC: pp. 82-84; lines 4001-4100) is a list of nine loci (#87-95): the soul's journey home, the sage's disregard of misfortunes, courage and caution, fearful men like children, the outside world as sport, souls free to achieve happiness against Gnostic objections to theodicy, no evil for the good man, wicked men turned into wolves. No discussion of the eph' hemin / not-in-our-power distinction, and no thesis of transformation into 'freedom from bodily determination'. Plotinus' notion of what depends on us is treated in ch. VI in relation to Chrysippus' causes, not Epictetus.

scholarly_argument_graeser_plotinus_crit.description: Graeser holds that, as regards empirical responsibility, Plotinus is a determinist in the Stoic sense, though he would have objected to the comparison; neither Plotinus nor the Stoics take the empirical self to be the 'ultimate principle' of action. In criticizing fate (Enn. III 1) Plotinus misrepresents the Stoics' 'rigid necessity' and declines to engage Chrysippus' distinction of causes. Plotinus' real aim is to make the non-empirical, metaphysical self an independent principle prior to the events necessitated by fate; the problem of free will thus runs 'on two levels'.

evidence.quote: Yet from what follows one cannot but receive the impression that Plotinus does not want to enter into the discussion of the distinction drawn by Chrysippus.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Plotinus and the Stoics- A Preliminary Study -- Andreas Graeser -- Philosophia Antiqua 22, 1972 -- Brill Archive -- 10.1163-9789004320437 -- 40e2ba2071c19c7f4c4ab4b045ddfb83 -- Anna’s Archive.md:2657-2660] (Graeser 1972, ca. p. 49)

evidence.quote: As far as the question of empirical responsibility 1 is concerned, the answer to this must be on the affirmative,2 although Plotinus would have objected strongly to any assessment of his views which might bring them too close to the position held by the Stoic school.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Plotinus and the Stoics- A Preliminary Study -- Andreas Graeser -- Philosophia Antiqua 22, 1972 -- Brill Archive -- 10.1163-9789004320437 -- 40e2ba2071c19c7f4c4ab4b045ddfb83 -- Anna’s Archive.md:5184-5187] (Graeser 1972, p. 112)

evidence.quote: What he was really aiming at is not difficult to see: the human soul, in order to function as the independent principle that it is supposed to be, must be prior to all the preceding events necessitated by
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Plotinus and the Stoics- A Preliminary Study -- Andreas Graeser -- Philosophia Antiqua 22, 1972 -- Brill Archive -- 10.1163-9789004320437 -- 40e2ba2071c19c7f4c4ab4b045ddfb83 -- Anna’s Archive.md:5704-5707] (Graeser 1972, p. 123)

scholarly_argument_graeser_plotinus_crit.finding: Quote verbatim located at lines 5701-5707, ch. VI, under running header 'PLOTINUS ON MAN'S FREE WILL I23' (line 5676): printed p. 123 (page map p.118, conf 0.80, is off by the front-matter shift). Graeser does not say Plotinus rejects Chrysippus' distinction of causes: on Enn. III 1 he says Plotinus 'does not want to enter into the discussion of the distinction drawn by Chrysippus', misrepresents the Stoics' 'rigid necessity', and argues from a standpoint close to Chrysippus' universal causation (#54-55, lines 2660-2703). In ch. VI he calls Plotinus a determinist 'as far as the question of empirical responsibility is concerned' and finds Plotinus and the Stoics 'basically in agreement'; the independence claim concerns the metaphysical, non-empirical self.

scholarly_argument_graeser_plotinus_enga.description: Graeser's starting point is Porphyry's remark that Plotinus' writings are 'full of hidden Stoic doctrines': Plotinus makes use of Stoic ideas, especially in theodicy and cosmology, while openly attacking Stoic ontology, theology, psychology and physics, so that his work shows 'strong repudiation of Stoic doctrines, as well as tacit acceptance of some of them'. On free will, Graeser judges that with respect to empirical responsibility Plotinus is a determinist in the Stoic sense, the difference lying in the metaphysical self as an independent principle.

evidence.quote: Thus, one is confronted with the rather surprising fact that the writings of Plotinus apparently contain strong repudiation of Stoic doctrines, as well as tacit acceptance of some of them.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Plotinus and the Stoics- A Preliminary Study -- Andreas Graeser -- Philosophia Antiqua 22, 1972 -- Brill Archive -- 10.1163-9789004320437 -- 40e2ba2071c19c7f4c4ab4b045ddfb83 -- Anna’s Archive.md:363-365] (Graeser 1972, p. xi)

evidence.quote: Has Plotinus to be considered a determinist in the sense of the word which is applicable to the Stoics's idea of universal causation? As far as the question of empirical responsibility 1 is concerned, the answer to this must be on the affirmative
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Plotinus and the Stoics- A Preliminary Study -- Andreas Graeser -- Philosophia Antiqua 22, 1972 -- Brill Archive -- 10.1163-9789004320437 -- 40e2ba2071c19c7f4c4ab4b045ddfb83 -- Anna’s Archive.md:5182-5185] (Graeser 1972, p. 112)

scholarly_argument_graeser_plotinus_enga.finding: The second half is Graeser's preface (p. xi, lines 355-365): Plotinus 'makes use of Stoic ideas, especially in the context of Theodicy and Cosmology' alongside 'strong repudiation of Stoic doctrines, as well as tacit acceptance of some of them'. The first half ('develops his own theory of free will in conscious opposition to Stoic determinism, particularly Chrysippus' compatibilist account') is not Graeser's: ch. VI opens by answering affirmatively that Plotinus is a determinist as far as empirical responsibility goes, and 'compatibilist' is not his word. Graeser's own phrasing for the free-will topic is that the problem 'must be viewed on two levels'.

scholarly_argument_grant_origen_s_self_c.description: Grant reads Eusebius' account of Origen as a 'life of St. Origen' from which Eusebius or Pamphilus 'have vigorously expunged nearly every human trait': the boy wonder, the sleeping beauty, the ascetic who rejects Greek literature, goes shoeless, abstains from wine and most foods, sleeps on the floor and castrates himself. He asks whether there is 'a real Origen here at all' and warns that it is 'extremely precarious for a historian to make any use of these stories'. He does not characterize them as voluntary choices.

evidence.quote: When he does not become a martyr, he rejects Greek literature, stops wearing shoes, abstains from wine and most foods, sleeps on the floor, castrates himself. Is there a real Origen here at all?
In any event, it is extremely precarious for a historian to make any use of these stories, and he must not be seduced by Euse-

scholarly_argument_grant_origen_s_self_c.finding: Quote verbatim located at lines 106-110, p. 134 (folio '134' at line 65 opens the page). Grant does not treat these practices as 'deliberate voluntary choices that Origen made'; he lists them as items of a hagiographic 'life of St. Origen' from which 'nearly every human trait' has been expunged, asks whether there is 'a real Origen here at all', and concludes it is 'extremely precarious for a historian to make any use of these stories'. The 'voluntary choice' framing is imported.

scholarly_argument_grant_origen_s_volunt.description: Against Eusebius' portrait, Grant says Origen's own works show 'a rather vain man, self-righteous, humorless', who attacks Demetrius and other bishops yet blames Ambrose before the bishop of Rome. In the same vein he notes, 'whether by chance or not', that Origen seems to be absent from Egypt at the 14-year intervals when poll-tax registration would have required an oath. Grant leaves the motive open and does not describe it as a principled choice.

evidence.quote: Origen's own works provide a somewhat different picture of him. He turns out to be a rather vain man, self-righteous, humorless.
Whether by chance or not, he seems to be absent from Egypt just at the 14-year intervals when poll-tax registration would make taking an oath necessary.

scholarly_argument_grant_origen_s_volunt.finding: Quote verbatim located at lines 137-143. The page is 135, not 134: the running header 'EARLY ALEXANDRIAN CHRISTIANITY' at line 122 opens p. 135 (agentic_search p.135, conf 0.95). The cautious 'Whether by chance or not' is preserved, but the gloss 'a strategic choice to avoid compromising his principles' loses Grant's framing: the remark sits in a list of unflattering traits drawn from Origen's own works ('vain, self-righteous, humorless', blaming Ambrose), i.e. as possible evasion of the census oath, not as principled stand.

scholarly_argument_grant_origen_s_volunt.description: Grant identifies 'Origen himself was ever eager for martyrdom' as one of the leading apologetic themes of Eusebius' biography, a 'life of St. Origen' that begins 'in the realm of folklore' and presents Origen as the Wunderkind and 'divine man'. He summarizes the boyhood episode ironically ('the boy wonder who urges his father to die but cannot be a martyr himself without his clothes') and judges it 'extremely precarious' for a historian to use such stories. He offers no analysis of the eagerness as a personal choice.

evidence.quote: His life was "philosophical" in the sense that it was rigorously ascetic. Origen himself was ever eager for martyrdom. His teaching, never secret, was always encouraged by episcopal authority. In short, Eusebius was using, and further developing, a life of St. Origen.
He is the boy wonder who urges his father to die but cannot be a martyr himself without his clothes.

scholarly_argument_grant_origen_s_volunt.finding: Quote verbatim located at lines 99-105, p. 134. Grant lists 'Origen himself was ever eager for martyrdom' among the 'leading themes' of Eusebius' purposefully apologetic narrative, which he treats as folklore about a 'divine man'; the 'boy wonder ... cannot be a martyr himself without his clothes' is his ironic summary. Grant does not treat the eagerness 'as a chosen orientation', does not mention the mother, and says nothing about 'later ... various circumstances'; his point is that the historian must not use these stories.

scholarly_argument_grant_irenaeus_agains.description: Grant's introductory chapters summarize the Valentinian system Irenaeus refutes, including the three kinds of entities (material, psychic, spiritual) and the 'three races of men' read out of the Gospels, and note that psychics have 'free will but not stability'. Grant does not, in his own analysis, present Irenaeus as a defender of universal free choice against Gnostic determinism; that claim would have to be sourced elsewhere.

evidence.quote: There are also three classes of human beings: material (incapable of salvation); psychic
evidence.citation: [06_Patristique/Robert M. Grant - Irenaeus of Lyons (The Early Church Fathers)  -Routledge (1996).md:817] (Grant 1996, ch. 2-3)

evidence.quote: Since he is psychic, with free will but not stability, he chose not to follow.
evidence.citation: [06_Patristique/Robert M. Grant - Irenaeus of Lyons (The Early Church Fathers)  -Routledge (1996).md:852-853] (Grant 1996, ch. 3, reporting Valentinian exegesis)

scholarly_argument_grant_irenaeus_agains.finding: Searched Grant's own chapters (lines 158-1900: 'The Life of Irenaeus', 'Gnostic Origins', 'Against the Valentinians', 'Christian Books and Traditions', 'Greek Education', 'Rhetoric in Theology') for free will / free choice / self-determin / determin / fixed nature / unity of humanity / capacity for all. Grant describes the Valentinian 'three classes of human beings' and 'three races of men' (pp. 8-20; translation of Heresies I.5-7), but nowhere in his own voice says Irenaeus opposed these as determinism or 'defended the unity of humanity and the capacity for all to choose salvation through free response to God's grace'. The node's thesis is not in the book.

scholarly_argument_grant_irenaeus_on_fre.description: In Grant's translation, Irenaeus (Heresies IV.15.2) says that God 'has always preserved both human free will and his own exhortation, so that those who disobey may be justly judged for having disobeyed, and those who obey and believe will be crowned with imperishability'. This is Irenaeus' own statement; Grant offers no analysis of Irenaean free will in his introductory chapters, and AH IV.37-39 is not among the passages he translates.

evidence.quote: and that God has always preserved both human free will and his own exhortation, so that those who disobey may be justly judged for having disobeyed, and those who obey and believe will be crowned with imperishability.
evidence.citation: [06_Patristique/Robert M. Grant - Irenaeus of Lyons (The Early Church Fathers)  -Routledge (1996).md:4946-4948] (Irenaeus, Heresies IV.15.2, trans. Grant 1996, Book IV pp. 109-122)

scholarly_argument_grant_irenaeus_on_fre.finding: No analysis of Irenaeus' doctrine of free will in Grant's own prose (same search as the previous node). The only statement of the kind in the volume is Irenaeus' own, in Grant's translation of Heresies IV.15.2 (line 4946), not Grant's scholarly position. The verified_reference cites AH IV.37-39, which Grant's selection does not translate (Book IV chapters included: 1-4, 6, 11, 13-15, 20, 22-27, 29-30, 33, 35). The translation pages carry no folios in the extraction (Book IV runs pp. 109-122 per the contents).

scholarly_argument_grant_irenaeus_synthe.description: Grant calls Irenaeus 'the most important Christian controversialist and theologian between the apostles and ... Origen', who combined the traditions of Asia Minor, Syria and Rome to refute the Gnostics. His theology 'resembled a French Gothic cathedral', supported by columns of biblical faith and tradition, illuminated by exegetical and logical argument, and upheld by flying buttresses of rhetorical and philosophical considerations from outside. Grant draws no conclusion here about human moral agency.

evidence.quote: He built up a body of Christian theology that resembled a French Gothic cathedral, strongly supported by columns of biblical faith and tradition, illuminated by vast expanses of exegetical and logical argument, and upheld by flying buttresses of rhetorical and philosophical considerations from the outside.
evidence.citation: [06_Patristique/Robert M. Grant - Irenaeus of Lyons (The Early Church Fathers)  -Routledge (1996).md:163-166] (Grant 1996, p. 1)

scholarly_argument_grant_irenaeus_synthe.finding: Quote verbatim located at lines 160-166, ch. 1, printed p. 1 (folio '1' at line 158; page map has no entry for this file). The cathedral image is faithfully reported, but the added claim that 'this synthesis supported a coherent account of human moral agency against Gnostic fragmentation of human nature' is not in Grant: the passage concerns Irenaeus' combination of traditions from Asia Minor, Syria and Rome to refute the Gnostics, with no reference to moral agency.

scholarly_argument_grant_tradition_and_m.description: Grant notes that Irenaeus tells of his early life in Heresies and in two letters preserved by Eusebius; writing to Florinus to dissuade him from heresy, he recalls his youth in Smyrna with Polycarp and 'insists that early memories are best', presumably because critics were questioning his claims about traditions. Grant makes no contrast with philosophical speculation and no link between this appeal to memory and human accountability.

evidence.quote: He insists that early memories are best, for presumably critics were questioning his claims about traditions.
evidence.citation: [06_Patristique/Robert M. Grant - Irenaeus of Lyons (The Early Church Fathers)  -Routledge (1996).md:185-186] (Grant 1996, p. 1)

evidence.quote: upheld by flying buttresses of rhetorical and philosophical considerations from the outside.
evidence.citation: [06_Patristique/Robert M. Grant - Irenaeus of Lyons (The Early Church Fathers)  -Routledge (1996).md:165-166] (Grant 1996, p. 1)

scholarly_argument_grant_tradition_and_m.finding: Quote verbatim located at lines 179-185, p. 1. Grant reports that Irenaeus 'insists that early memories are best, for presumably critics were questioning his claims about traditions'. The node's 'rather than in philosophical speculation' contradicts Grant's own image three sentences earlier (theology 'upheld by flying buttresses of rhetorical and philosophical considerations'), and 'this epistemological choice reinforced human accountability' is nowhere in Grant. The page_range '43-44' points to the translation's preface, which is unrelated.

scholarly_argument_kowalski_epictetus_on.description: Epictetus, per Kowalski, speaks of freedom 'in an inner, psychological and attitudinal sense' and explains it through proairesis, translatable as 'volition', which 'constitutes our true self, a rational particle of divinity within us'; thanks to it we make free moral choices 'which Zeus himself does not interfere with'. Epictetus's 'God-directed world' (Long) is 'a deterministically constructed space' that nonetheless leaves room for free will and autonomous acts; proairesis needs constant care to stay unimpeded by desires, emotions and externals.

evidence.quote: He explains it with the notion of proairesis, which can be translated as “volition,” and which constitutes our true self, a rational particle of divinity within us. Thanks to it, we are capable of making free moral choices which Zeus himself does not interfere with.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Kowalski - 2022 - Divine and Human Spirit in Rom 816. Paul and Epictetus on Free Will.md:1130-1133] (Kowalski 2022, p. 536)

evidence.quote: structed space where everything depends on the Creator, but at the same time leaves us room which is “exclusively and wonderfully ours” for free will and autonomous human acts.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Kowalski - 2022 - Divine and Human Spirit in Rom 816. Paul and Epictetus on Free Will.md:374-375] (Kowalski 2022, p. 520)

scholarly_argument_kowalski_epictetus_on.finding: Content faithful, but the quote_verbatim sits in the conclusion at lines 1128-1133 = printed p. 536, not pp. 513-514 (only the abstract sentence on proairesis as 'true self' is on p. 513). The 'deterministically ordered universe' element comes from section 3.1, p. 520. Kowalski's own gloss of proairesis is 'volition' / 'true self', not 'faculty of choice'.

scholarly_argument_kowalski_free_will_in.description: Kowalski: Pauline freedom is 'a divine gift, closely related to the Christ event and the work of the Spirit'; it means new life in Christ, freedom from sin, orientation to God's righteousness, sanctification and eternal life (Rom 6:22). Outside Christ, mind and volition cannot free themselves from sin (Rom 3:1-20; 7:7-25); in Christ, freedom 'comes as a gift from God which transcends human mind and volition'. The indicative is interwoven with the imperative: the new life is 'a joint effort of the Christian and the Spirit'.

evidence.quote: In Pauline vision, Christian freedom is a divine gift, closely related to the Christ event and the work of the Spirit; it means the new life in Christ, being free from sin, and directed towards God’s righteousness, sanctification
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Kowalski - 2022 - Divine and Human Spirit in Rom 816. Paul and Epictetus on Free Will.md:51-53] (Kowalski 2022, p. 513)

evidence.quote: the believers are freed from the slavery of sin and death; their freedom comes as a gift from God which transcends human mind and volition (Rom 3:21–26; 7:24b; 8:1–4; 10:9).
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Kowalski - 2022 - Divine and Human Spirit in Rom 816. Paul and Epictetus on Free Will.md:750-751] (Kowalski 2022, p. 528)

scholarly_argument_kowalski_free_will_in.finding: Description faithful: first sentence mirrors the introduction (lines 51-53, p. 513; Rom 6:22 at line 63, p. 514), 'joint effort' at line 137 (p. 515). But the quote_verbatim ('their freedom comes as a gift from God which transcends human mind and volition') is at lines 749-751 = printed p. 528, outside the stated 513-515.

scholarly_argument_martin_determinism_an.description: Martin quotes Josephus's report that the Pharisees posit a 'fusion' in which the will of man 'with his virtue and vice' is 'admitted to the council-chamber of fate' (Ant. XVIII,13), and relays Wächter's conclusion that determinism and free will were 'paradoxical' for the Pharisees. His own reading: Josephus, 'not a philosophical thinker', uses heimarmene casually, in its popular negative sense, as 'a semantic ploy' contrasting life under Torah (pronoia, freedom, responsibility) with life apart from it (universal determinism).

evidence.quote: These latter events depend upon human actions, but under God in obedience to Torah.
evidence.citation: [02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/Josephus' Use of Heimarmene in the Jewish Antiquities Xiii, 171-3.md:127-129] (Martin 1981, p. 129)

evidence.quote: but, as Josephus concludes of the Pharisees, in the paradoxical attribution of everything to Fate and God.
evidence.citation: [02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/Josephus' Use of Heimarmene in the Jewish Antiquities Xiii, 171-3.md:153-155] (Martin 1981, p. 130)

evidence.quote: His use of the term can be understood as a semantic ploy which sets up an apologetic contrast: life under and life apart from Torah.
evidence.citation: [02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/Josephus' Use of Heimarmene in the Jewish Antiquities Xiii, 171-3.md:333-335] (Martin 1981, p. 134)

scholarly_argument_martin_determinism_an.finding: Martin never uses 'compatibilist' (grep: no hit; 'cooperates' occurs only inside the Bell. II quotation). 'Fusion' and 'council-chamber of fate' are Josephus's words (Ant. XVIII,13, Thackeray) quoted on p. 127; 'paradoxical' is Wächter's conclusion which Martin reports (p. 129) and echoes (p. 130). Martin's own thesis runs the other way: Josephus's heimarmene is a non-technical, popular term and 'a semantic ploy' opposing life under Torah (pronoia, freedom, responsibility) to life apart from it (universal determinism), pp. 132-136. The node turns a heresiographic report plus Wächter's view into a theory of Fate/free-will cooperation attributed to Martin.

scholarly_argument_martin_josephus_use_o.description: Martin notes heimarmene occurs in only four passages of the Antiquities and that in XIII,171-3 (with XVIII,12-22 and Bell. II,162-6) Josephus makes attitude to heimarmene 'the single issue which distinguishes the three philosophies': Pharisees (some events by Fate, others up to us), Essenes ('Fate is mistress of all things' — perhaps Josephus's own perception of their community discipline), Sadducees (do away with Fate). He concludes Josephus really distinguishes the parties by their attitude to the law, presented through 'the more comprehensible terminology of heimarmene'.

evidence.quote: Josephus presents the attitude towards heimarmene as the single issue which distinguishes the three philosophies:
evidence.citation: [02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/Josephus' Use of Heimarmene in the Jewish Antiquities Xiii, 171-3.md:55-57] (Martin 1981, p. 128)

evidence.quote: and as declaring that "Fate is the mistress of all things" (Ant. XIII, 172), perhaps Josephus' perception of their strict adherence to community rule.
evidence.citation: [02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/Josephus' Use of Heimarmene in the Jewish Antiquities Xiii, 171-3.md:149-151] (Martin 1981, p. 130)

scholarly_argument_martin_josephus_use_o.finding: Quote verbatim at lines 18-25 (p. 127); 'single issue which distinguishes the three philosophies' at p. 128. But 'the Essenes embracing complete fatalism' flattens Martin's caution that 'Fate is mistress of all things' may be 'Josephus' perception of their strict adherence to community rule' (p. 130), and omits his conclusion that the real criterion is attitude to the law, rendered for Hellenistic readers in heimarmene terminology (p. 136).

scholarly_argument_martin_stoic_influenc.description: Martin grants that Stoic borrowing is 'an accepted tenet of much Josephus scholarship' and that, from the Stoic side, Wächter's identification of heimarmene with God or pronoia is 'fully justified'. He objects that Agrippa's speech (Ant. XIX,347) identifies God's will with pepromene, not heimarmene, and that Josephus, 'not a philosophical thinker', used such borrowings 'in an extremely casual manner'; the operative sense is therefore the popular, astrological one of heimarmene as a negative designation of existence.

evidence.quote: And even if we do, this text identifies the will of God with pepromene and not with heimarmene which is associated in this passage with Agrippa's mortality.
evidence.citation: [02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/Josephus' Use of Heimarmene in the Jewish Antiquities Xiii, 171-3.md:163-165] (Martin 1981, p. 130)

evidence.quote: we must conclude that if Josephus was influenced by Stoicism in his use of heimarmene, he did not use his philosophical borrowings technically, but in an extreme-
evidence.citation: [02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/Josephus' Use of Heimarmene in the Jewish Antiquities Xiii, 171-3.md:228-231] (Martin 1981, p. 132)

scholarly_argument_martin_stoic_influenc.finding: Quote verbatim at lines 161-165 (p. 130). The node stops at the doubt and drops Martin's actual conclusion: even granting Stoic influence, Josephus 'did not use his philosophical borrowings technically, but in an extremely casual manner', so the relevant sense is the popular astrological one (pp. 132-133). It also omits that Martin calls Wächter's Stoic identification 'fully justified' from the Stoic side (p. 132).

scholarly_argument_maso_fate_and_chance_.description: Masi and Maso (Introduzione) state the volume's third question: how far chance and fortune are justified within ancient ontological and causal theories, and in particular their relation to another causal principle admitted by common sense and many schools, fate. The aim was 'to establish whether fate and chance are mutually exclusive causal principles or, instead, compatible and integrable into more complex causal models' — a question set for the contributors, not a thesis asserted in the introduction.

evidence.quote: Ci si è proposti, più specificamente, di stabilire se destino e caso siano principi causali mutuamente esclusivi o se, invece, siano compatibili e integrabili in modelli causali più complessi.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Maso - 2013 - Fate, Chance, and Fortune in Ancient Thought.md:426-429] (Masi and Maso 2013, p. 12)

scholarly_argument_maso_fate_and_chance_.finding: The Introduzione poses this as the question the volume set itself ('stabilire se destino e caso siano principi causali mutuamente esclusivi o se, invece, siano compatibili'); the node converts the question into an assertion held by 'Maso'. Also co-authored (Masi–Maso) and on p. 12, not 12-13.

scholarly_argument_maso_human_agency_and.description: Masi and Maso (Introduzione), fourth question: how and to what extent fate and chance 'interfere with deliberative processes', since admitting them raises a compatibility problem with the capacity of the 'human agent' to determine the course of its actions autonomously and effectively. They add that the volume's aim is not so much to justify the agent's capacity for self-determination of moral progress as to clarify how far the success of action can be facilitated or impeded by such factors.

evidence.quote: È noto, infatti, che l’ammissione dell’esistenza del destino e del caso pone un problema di compatibilità tra questi stessi fattori, da un lato, e la capacità dell’«essere umano agente» di determinare autonomamente il corso delle proprie azioni e di essere efficace, dall’altro.

scholarly_argument_nagasawa_foreknowledg.description: Nagasawa presents, as quotations from Justin Martyr, the statement that 'God's foreknowledge is intuitive, not active, and is caused by man's choices' (unreferenced) together with 1 Apology 43: rewards and punishments follow merit; if all things happened by fate nothing would be in our power and neither praise nor blame would be deserved. Later Justin excerpts add that those 'foreknown to be unrighteous' are not made wicked by God's fault.

Otherwise, if all things happen by fate, then nothing is in our own power.

scholarly_argument_nagasawa_foreknowledg.finding: The 'intuitive, not active' sentence is given by Nagasawa as a Justin quotation (no edition reference) followed by 1 Apol. 43 (lines 144-149); the file attributes the 'intuitive' formulation to Justin only, not to 'other early fathers'. The anti-fate argument matches. Source is an unpaginated web essay ('Last modified: August 5, 2013'), page_map conf 0.50: cite by md line, no printed pages.

scholarly_argument_nagasawa_free_will_an.description: Nagasawa argues, against Calvin (Inst. 2.2.4), that the early theologians were 'very clear' and reached 'a consensus among them about human free will'. He supports this with Schaff (Greek fathers' 'undeveloped synergism' of will and grace versus Augustinian monergism; earlier Latins stressed hereditary sin and God's grace without denying freedom) and Kelly (grace and free will co-operate; the initiative rests with man's will, grace perfects what the will freely determined, 'yet our will is only ours by God's mercy').

evidence.quote: They were not ‘confused, vacillating, and contradictory.’ In fact, on this subject, they were very clear, and there is a consensus among them about human free will.
The part of grace, it would seem, is to perfect that which the will has freely determined; yet our will is only ours by God’s mercy.’

scholarly_argument_nagasawa_free_will_an.finding: Quote verbatim at lines 23-25. 'Initiative rests with man's free will' and 'grace perfects what the will has freely determined' are J.N.D. Kelly's words quoted by Nagasawa, with Kelly's qualifier 'yet our will is only ours by God's mercy' dropped; Schaff (also quoted) reserves 'synergism' for the Greek church and says the Latin church under Augustine 'advanced to' monergism, earlier Latins stressing hereditary sin and sovereignty of grace 'without, however, denying freedom'. Unpaginated web essay.

scholarly_argument_nagasawa_semi_pelagia.description: Nagasawa quotes Schaff's judgement that after Augustine's death 'the intermediate system of Semi-Pelagianism, akin to the Greek synergism, became prevalent in the West'. In his own voice he claims the early-church consensus on free will grounded John Cassian's disagreement with the later Augustine on monergism, that Augustine 'was known to have broken with the theological consensus of church tradition', and that the same consensus underlies the Eastern Orthodox doctrine of synergism as opposed to Augustine's monergism.

evidence.quote: After Augustine’s death, however the intermediate system of Semi-Pelagianism, akin to the Greek synergism, became prevalent in the West.’
This consensus also laid the foundation for the Eastern Orthodox to articulate the doctrine called synergism, in contrast to Augustine’s monergism.

scholarly_argument_nagasawa_semi_pelagia.finding: 'Akin to the Greek synergism' is Schaff's phrase quoted by Nagasawa (lines 36-37); 'not a novel deviation' appears nowhere in the file. The second sentence (Eastern Orthodox synergism continues the consensus Augustine broke with) is Nagasawa's own, lines 82-87 (quote verbatim). Unpaginated web essay.

He does not argue for this account in the paper ('nor does this paper's success rest on accepting it'); he states 'for the record' that he believes Epicurus is a reductionist but not a compatibilist.

scholarly_argument_pouderon_determinism_.description: Pouderon (§7, pp. 177-179): the affirmation of free will is, oddly, clearer in the Supplique (men choose freely between vice and virtue, L. XXIV,4) than in the Traité, where 'la liberté humaine se tire de la notion de responsabilité' (D.R. XVIII,4). Free will is 'le juste équilibre' between a set of determinations — divine Providence, natural laws, corporeal nature; demons and the Prince of matter — and the judgment of reason. The providential doctrine of L. XXIV-XXV is 'imprégnée des conceptions stoïciennes', evil being the fruit of the demons' malignity. Heimarmene is not discussed.

XVIII,4). Free will is 'indispensable à la notion de vertu'.

scholarly_argument_rousseau_irenaeus_s_o.description: SC 264 edits Book I, Irenaeus's exposition of the Valentinian, Marcosian and other systems; it contains no statement of Irenaeus's own doctrine of free will, which belongs to Book IV (IV,37-39) and to the refutation of Book II. Within Book I the only free-will language is Irenaeus's report of the Valentinian claim that the psychic element is 'suae potestatis' (I,6,1). Any inference about Irenaeus's own position must be drawn from those later books, not from this volume.

scholarly_argument_sorabji_aristotle_tra.description: Sorabji (Preface): the commentators' most significant importance is their profound influence on subsequent Islamic and European philosophy, due partly to their preserving anti-Aristotelian material that helped inspire medieval and Renaissance science, and still more to their presenting an Aristotle transformed 'in ways which happened to make him acceptable to the Christian Church'. It is this transformed Aristotle, embedded in the commentators' philosophy, not Aristotle himself, that lies behind later thinkers' views.

scholarly_argument_vicens_responses_to_t.description: Vicens sets out three types of response to the puzzle of sin and free will — a libertarian stance (Section 2), a soft determinist one (Section 3), and free will skepticism (Section 4) — intending to show that none is without costs for natural interpretation of biblical passages, theological doctrine and common sense; she then proposes what she takes to be the least costly resolution, 'somewhere between free will skepticism and compatibilism about free will and determinism' (p. 5).

evidence.quote: In the fourth and ﬁnal section I propose what I take to be the least costly resolution to the problem, which might be located somewhere between free will skepti- cism and compatibilism about free will and determinism.
evidence.citation: [Christianity and the Problem of Free Will-Cambridge University Press (2023).md:361-364]

scholarly_argument_vicens_responses_to_t.finding: Quote verbatim at lines 351-360, p. 5 (conf 0.98). The description stops at 'weighing the costs and benefits' and omits the sentence that immediately follows, where Vicens announces her own positive proposal: the least costly resolution, located between free will skepticism and compatibilism.

scholarly_argument_vicens_augustinian_or.description: Vicens: Augustine's two central ideas, original guilt and constitutional fault, are prima facie incompatible with libertarianism — the former posits responsibility for Adam's sin itself, the latter determination to sin by something outside one's control. Some libertarians ('Augustinian realists') hold we participated in Adam's sin: Crisp favors one persisting entity of which Adam and his heirs are parts; Rea considers a fission theory but judges its costs 'too high a price'. How one evaluates such views depends on one's starting point; the difficulty Crisp addresses is generated largely by a starting assumption of libertarianism (p. 14).

evidence.quote: Michael Rea, in contrast, considers a theory according to which Adam and his posterity are distinct individuals who shared a common temporal state and who underwent ﬁssion at the time of Adam’s ﬁrst sin
evidence.citation: [Christianity and the Problem of Free Will-Cambridge University Press (2023).md:796-799]

evidence.quote: Rea suggests that the metaphysical commitments of ﬁssion theory come at “too high a price” (2007, 345), but Crisp
evidence.citation: [Christianity and the Problem of Free Will-Cambridge University Press (2023).md:801-802]

evidence.quote: But it should be noted that the difﬁculty Crisp is attempting to overcome is generated in large part by a starting assumption of libertarianism.
evidence.citation: [Christianity and the Problem of Free Will-Cambridge University Press (2023).md:815-816]

scholarly_argument_vicens_augustinian_or.finding: Quote verbatim at lines 779-788, p. 14 (conf 0.98). Two misreadings: (1) Vicens does not present Rea as an Augustinian realist who 'attempts to restore control'; Rea 'considers a theory' of fission and 'suggests that the metaphysical commitments of ﬁssion theory come at "too high a price"' — Crisp is the one who 'favors' the one-entity view. scholarly_argument_wang_divine_determini.description: Wang (Abstract): the primary principle Paul underscores in Romans 9 is that the cross is 'the supreme expression of God's purpose of election'. The cross 'not only is a statement about God's determination in election, but it also has an existential purpose in its ways and works'. The cruciform reading of predestination presents 'the eternal decision of God, vested in the immanent Trinity', in which Christ is elected to accomplish salvation through the cross; the ultimate goal is that this purpose be revealed existentially in the elect community.

evidence.quote: The cross of Christ not only is a statement about God’s determination in election, but it also has an existential purpose in its ways and works.

the cruciform reading of predestination presents the eternal decision of God, vested in the immanent Trinity, in which Christ is elected to accomplish human salvation through the atonement of the cross.

scholarly_argument_wang_divine_determini.finding: Quote verbatim in the Abstract, lines 66-70, printed p. ii (roman folio at line 82; page map returns p.?). Wang's sentence is 'not only ... but also': the cross 'not only is a statement about God's determination in election, but it also has an existential purpose'. The description turns this into 'Election is not about deterministic divine decree but about ... love', which Wang's own abstract contradicts: cruciform election 'presents the eternal decision of God, vested in the immanent Trinity'.

scholarly_argument_wang_moral_responsibi.description: Wang: Paul encourages the elect in Christ to serve as Christ did, 'poor, yet making many rich' (2 Cor 6:10) — 'the paradox in the election of self-giving service and self-sacrificing life'; Christ beckons the elect to take up their cross (p. 266). The theology of the cross shifts the Reformed paradigm of election 'from individual privilege to community wellbeing'. The purpose of election has four scriptural and practical foci: self-giving service, embracing the offender with mercy and hope, bringing light and healing to the world's darkness, and conforming to Christ's image (p. 291).

evidence.quote: He thus beckons the elect to take up their cross and follow Him. Furthermore, the theology of the cross transforms the paradigm of the Reformed doctrine of election from individual privilege to community wellbeing, from personal destiny

a) the election to self-giving service and self-sacrificing life; b) the election to embracing the offender with mercy and hope; c) the election to bringing light and healing to the darkness of the world; and d) the election to conforming to the image of Christ as a showcase of His grace.

scholarly_argument_wang_moral_responsibi.finding: Quote verbatim at lines 14764-14772, printed p. 266 (conf 0.95); the four foci (self-giving service, embracing the offender with mercy, bringing light and healing, conforming to Christ's image) are at lines 16111-16115, p. 291 (conf 0.95). The closing gloss 'suggesting active human participation rather than passive determinism' is not Wang's: in the passage his contrast is a shift of paradigm 'from individual privilege to community wellbeing', not participation versus determinism.

scholarly_argument_wang_predestination_a.description: Wang reassesses (rethinks) the Reformed doctrine of predestination through Paul's theology of the cross and his Jewish background, proposing to put 'cruciform election' foremost in our understanding of predestination. On the ground of theologia crucis the predisposition to hold the traditional doctrine of double predestination 'can be cautiously avoided' (p. 16). Cruciform election still 'presents the eternal decision of God, vested in the immanent Trinity, in which Christ is elected to accomplish human salvation through the atonement of the cross' (p. iii).

evidence.quote: this dissertation reassesses the Reformed doctrine of predestination

On the ground of theologia crucis, the predisposition of holding the traditional doctrine of double predestination, wherein a strict dichotomy dictates humanity either to eternal salvation or to damnation, can be cautiously avoided.
my proposition is to put “cruciform election” foremost in our understanding of predestination.

scholarly_argument_wang_predestination_a.finding: No quote supplied. Abstract (p. ii-iii, lines 52-92) and p. 16 (lines 1173-1175) checked. evidence.quote: when Paul discusses election, he engages a specifically Trinitarian articulation of God, who works out His election of grace in a definite yet surprising manner.

scholarly_argument_karamanolis_free_will.description: Karamanolis (ch. 4, pp. 130-165): free will, responsibility and providence concerned early Christian philosophers as deeply as their Hellenic contemporaries. Christians (Irenaeus, Tertullian, Clement, Origen, Basil, Gregory) sought to refute astral determinism and the Valentinian view that free will belongs to only one class of humans, and had to articulate a positive theory of agency addressing theodicy. Scripture lacks the terminology; to eph' hemin, prohairesis and autexousion are of Stoic provenance, and the Christians took up the Stoic notion of free will because they shared Stoic theological assumptions (pp. 132-133, 139).

evidence.quote: Early Christian thinkers were concerned with refuting both views, those of the astral determinists and those of Valentinian Gnostics
evidence.citation: [[Ancient Philosophies] George E. Karamanolis - The Philosophy of Early Christianity (2021, Routledge_Acumen) - libgen.li.md:6573-6574]

evidence.quote: All three terms are of Stoic provenance.
evidence.citation: [[Ancient Philosophies] George E. Karamanolis - The Philosophy of Early Christianity (2021, Routledge_Acumen) - libgen.li.md:6593]

evidence.quote: This is the notion of free will that the Christians take up from the Stoics.
evidence.citation: [[Ancient Philosophies] George E. Karamanolis - The Philosophy of Early Christianity (2021, Routledge_Acumen) - libgen.li.md:6876]

scholarly_argument_karamanolis_free_will.finding: Ch. 4 = pp. 130-165 (ch. 5 begins p. 166). Its framing is the reverse of the node: the Christians' opponents are the 'astral determinists' and the Valentinian/Basilidean Gnostics (p. 132), while the three key terms (to eph' hemin, prohairesis, autexousion) 'are of Stoic provenance' (p. 133) and 'This is the notion of free will that the Christians take up from the Stoics' (p. 139). 'Often against Stoic determinism and Platonist fate' is not Karamanolis's claim. The 'school of thought' thesis is a book-level claim (pp. ix, 21), not made in ch. 4.

scholarly_argument_karamanolis_methodolo.description: Karamanolis's method (Introduction, pp. 20-22): focus on how selected early Christian philosophers engage key philosophical issues (first principles/cosmogony, knowledge, free will, soul-body, happiness), outlining the relevant ancient debate first; read them within their dialogue with each other and against the parallel debates of Platonists, Peripatetics, Sceptics and Stoics; show that Christian views resulted from reflection and disagreement, not Scripture alone, and constitute a distinct school of thought. He rejects the 'Christian Fathers' rubric that studies them as theologians and students of Scripture (p. 22).

evidence.quote: early Christian philosophers were in dialogue not only with past and contemporary philosophers but also with each other, and their views cannot be fully understood unless they are considered within the framework of this dialogue and set against the parallel debates among Platonists, Peripatetics, Sceptics, and Stoics.
evidence.citation: [[Ancient Philosophies] George E. Karamanolis - The Philosophy of Early Christianity (2021, Routledge_Acumen) - libgen.li.md:1354-1358]

evidence.quote: sheds light on the distinct ways they conceptualized traditional philosophical issues and made some intriguing contributions.
evidence.citation: [[Ancient Philosophies] George E. Karamanolis - The Philosophy of Early Christianity (2021, Routledge_Acumen) - libgen.li.md:26-27]

scholarly_argument_karamanolis_methodolo.finding: Pages 27-54 are ch. 1, 'The Christian conception of philosophy and Christian philosophical methodology' — the Christians' own methodology, not Karamanolis's method of studying them. His own method is set out in the Introduction section 'The method, scope and limits of this study' (pp. 20-22, lines 1340-1425) and echoed in the back-cover blurb (lines 22-29) and Preface p. ix. The description's generic content ('distinct ways ... conceptualized traditional philosophical issues', 'original contributions') matches the blurb; 'careful engagement with primary texts' is not his phrasing — he stresses outlining the ancient debate first and reading Christians within their dialogue with each other and with the schools.

scholarly_argument_still_paul_as_apologi.description: Still (Afterword, pp. 291-292) returns to Wilhite's question whether Paul may be considered an apologist. Paul offers no general defence of Christians against outsiders' accusations as later apologists did; but 1 Thess 2:1-12 is best read as an apologia, Paul mounts defences in the Corinthian letters and is shackled for 'the apologia of the gospel' (Phil 1:16). Conclusion: not an apologist in the same way as the later writers, yet 'clearly an apologist for the gospel' — while not best or primarily regarded as an apologist (n. 1).

evidence.quote: If Paul was not an apologist in one and the same way as those whose works treated herein were, he was clearly an apologist for the gospel that he unashamedly declared and disseminated “from Jerusalem all the way around to Illyricum” (Rom 15:19).

To pursue the question of whether Paul might be construed as an apologist is not meant, of course, to suggest that Paul may be best perceived or primarily, much less exclusively, regarded as an apologist.

scholarly_argument_still_paul_as_apologi.finding: Afterword 'Was Paul an Apologist?' by Todd D. Still, pp. 291-292 (lines 16266-16352). Still does not leave the question open as a matter for debate: he argues that 1 Thess 2:1-12 is an apologia, cites Phil 1:16, and concludes that Paul 'was clearly an apologist for the gospel', with the qualification (n. 1) that Paul is not best or primarily regarded as an apologist and (p. 292) that he was not an apologist 'in one and the same way' as the later writers.

scholarly_argument_still_paul_s_role_as_.description: The Apologists and Paul (eds Still & Wilhite, 2024). Wilhite's Introduction (pp. 1-20) treats 'apologist' as an unstable, pragmatic, catch-all category, and asks whether Paul himself might be considered an apologist — if so, 'the oldest extant Christian apologist' — noting that Paul's apologiae are self-defences of his authority rather than general defences of Christians (p. 11). Still's Afterword (pp. 291-292) takes up Wilhite's question and concludes Paul was 'clearly an apologist for the gospel', though not in the same way as the later apologists.

For my part, in this afterword, I would like to return to a question posed by my coeditor and colleague, David E. Wilhite, in his introduction, namely, if and in what sense might Paul himself be considered an apologist.

scholarly_argument_still_pauline_recepti.description: Edited volume (Still & Wilhite, 2024; 15 contributors) on Paul's reception among writers grouped, pragmatically, as apologists: Aristides, Justin, Tatian, Athenagoras and Pseudo-Athenagoras, Melito, Aristo of Pella and Hegesippus, Theophilus, Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, Minucius Felix, Hippolytus, Novatian, Dionysius of Alexandria, Cyprian, Arnobius and Lactantius, Methodius. scholarly_argument_barclay_divine_and_hu.description: Barclay (Introduction, pp. 1-2): Paul's statements on the relation of divine to human agency 'strike us as paradoxical, if not downright incoherent' (e.g. Phil 2:12-13, where the human imperative is grounded on the divine indicative); their reception has spawned violent debates. Rather than accept 'a constellation of deep and irresolvable conundra', the book claims that agency issues are 'neither stale nor uninteresting' and that fresh light can be shed by 'a well-tuned comparative approach' with Paul's cultural environment.

evidence.quote: some of Paul’s statements on the relation of divine to human agency strike us as paradoxical, if not downright incoherent.
Should the study of Pauline theology simply accept that there is here a constellation of deep and irresolvable conundra and move on to other terrain?
and that fresh light can be shed on this central issue in Pauline theology by adopting a well-tuned comparative approach.

scholarly_argument_barclay_divine_and_hu.finding: Introduction by John M. G. Barclay alone (header line 159-161), pp. 1-2 (running header '2 Divine and Human Agency in Paul' at line 200; 'BARCLAY Introduction 3' at line 245). Barclay says the statements 'strike us as paradoxical, if not downright incoherent', and asks whether to accept 'a constellation of deep and irresolvable conundra'; his claim is that agency issues are 'neither stale nor uninteresting' and that comparison sheds fresh light. He does not assert that they are 'not incoherent'; that is the graph's inference.

scholarly_argument_blackwell_deification.description: Blackwell's subject is deification (christosis) in Pauline soteriology read through Irenaeus and Cyril, not free will as such. Yet in the Irenaeus chapter he states explicitly that rationality and free will play a central role in Irenaeus's anthropology (p. 40), that for Irenaeus 'human destiny is determined by free will and not by nature' (p. 50), and that Irenaeus notes self-determination (potestas) as a likeness to God — an emphasis 'explicit where it is found only implicitly, if at all, in Paul' (p. 52 n. 69).

scholarly_argument_blackwell_deification.finding: Page map is AUDIT-FAIL; printed pages read from the running headers embedded in the file (e.g. '40' at line 2106, '50' at 2583, '52' at 2676). scholarly_argument_blackwell_irenaeus_on.description: Blackwell on Irenaeus: humans, like Adam, are created in infancy with only the capacity for perfection if they grow into it (p. 40); Irenaeus explains that human destiny is determined by free will, not by nature, God having designed humans for growth and progress towards him, with judgment for those who turn away (pp. 50-54). Progression from infancy to maturity, moral as well as relational, is central: as believers exercise free will according to rationality they become like God and grow to maturity, and growth continues even after the resurrection (p. 64).

evidence.quote: Central to Irenaeus’ anthropology is also the concept of progression from infancy to maturity, which culminates in, among other things, incorruption.
evidence.citation: [[Wissenschaftliche Untersuchungen Zum Neuen Testament  314] Ben C Blackwell - Christosis_ Pauline Soteriology in Light of Deification in Irenaeus and Cyril of Alexandria (2011, Mohr Siebeck).md:3230-3231]

evidence.citation: [[Wissenschaftliche Untersuchungen Zum Neuen Testament  314] Ben C Blackwell - Christosis_ Pauline Soteriology in Light of Deification in Irenaeus and Cyril of Alexandria (2011, Mohr Siebeck).md:3249-3250]
