scholarly_argument_blackwell_irenaeus_on.finding: Content on growth is faithful: Adam 'created in a state of infancy and childlike understanding' (p. 40); §3.1.4 ''Gods' but Not Perfect From the Beginning' (pp. 50-54); §3.4.2 'Progress' (p. 64, line 3229 after header '64' at line 3224): 'progression from infancy to maturity'. But the hedge 'Blackwell does not explicitly frame this in terms of free will' is wrong: he frames it with 'free will' and 'self-determination' (pp. 40, 50, 52, 64 — 'As believers express free will according to rationality, they become like God and grow to maturity'). He does not use 'determinism'.

scholarly_argument_blackwell_methodology.description: Blackwell (pp. 14-24): two equally valid, even compatible, routes exist for assessing deification in Paul — history of religions and history of interpretation; he takes the second, reading Paul in light of patristic interpreters (Irenaeus, Cyril) because their proximity and a tradition not shaped by deification give 'fresh eyes' to view Paul. The aim is comparison of Paul's thought in his context with later theological constructions, not a search for origins; the project is deliberately not theological interpretation, and patristic comments are kept out of the reading of the Pauline texts themselves.

evidence.quote: the focus will not be a search for origins of Paul’s thought but rather a comparison of Paul’s thought within his context with theological constructions, albeit later, that wrestle with similar topics within their own contexts.
evidence.citation: [[Wissenschaftliche Untersuchungen Zum Neuen Testament  314] Ben C Blackwell - Christosis_ Pauline Soteriology in Light of Deification in Irenaeus and Cyril of Alexandria (2011, Mohr Siebeck).md:1418-1421]

evidence.quote: We have the option to choose one of two equally valid (and even compatible) paths: history of religions or history of interpretation.
evidence.citation: [[Wissenschaftliche Untersuchungen Zum Neuen Testament  314] Ben C Blackwell - Christosis_ Pauline Soteriology in Light of Deification in Irenaeus and Cyril of Alexandria (2011, Mohr Siebeck).md:1477-1479]

evidence.quote: this project is intentionally not that type of study
evidence.citation: [[Wissenschaftliche Untersuchungen Zum Neuen Testament  314] Ben C Blackwell - Christosis_ Pauline Soteriology in Light of Deification in Irenaeus and Cyril of Alexandria (2011, Mohr Siebeck).md:1468]

scholarly_argument_blackwell_methodology.finding: Section 3 'Route of Study: History of Interpretation', pp. 14-24 (lines 975-1490; headers '23' at 1410, '24' at 1458). Blackwell chooses history of interpretation over history of religions as 'two equally valid (and even compatible) paths' (pp. 14, 24) because patristic interpreters give 'fresh eyes to view Paul' (p. 24) and the focus is 'a comparison of Paul's thought within his context with theological constructions, albeit later' (p. 23). He does not claim that later developments 'illuminate rather than distort apostolic teaching'; he insists the project is 'intentionally not' theological interpretation and that patristic comments are not brought into play when reading the Pauline texts themselves (p. 24). The 'implications for free will and determinism' are the graph's extrapolation.

scholarly_argument_dettwiler_determinism.description: Dettwiler notes that 1 Th 5:18b is the one break in the rhythmic sequence of eight present imperatives (5:16-22) and then reads vv. 16-18 as a triad 'joy - prayer - thanksgiving'. What he says is not a 'human performance' but 'the act of God's Spirit' is the community's unity (p. 13) and, likewise, joy, understood as the expression of a human who discovers himself receptive to the God of grace (p. 14). He draws no conclusion about divine will versus self-determination from 18b.

evidence.quote: En fait, la séquence, à l'exception du v. 18b, contient une succession ininterrompue, à caractère rythmique - dans le texte grec, le verbe est toujours placé en dernière position -, de huit affirmations courtes, formulées toutes à l'impératif présent.
evidence.citation: [Une exhortation de Paul aux Thessaloniciens,Priez sans cesse.md:173-180] (Dettwiler 2007, p. 12)

evidence.quote: Ainsi, Paul rappelle indirectement que cette unité n'est pas à concevoir comme une performance humaine, mais comme l'agir de l'Esprit de Dieu.
evidence.citation: [Une exhortation de Paul aux Thessaloniciens,Priez sans cesse.md:231-235] (Dettwiler 2007, p. 13)

scholarly_argument_dettwiler_determinism.finding: Dettwiler mentions v. 18b only once, as the formal exception to the rhythmic run of eight imperatives (p. 12). He nowhere argues that 18b shows the triad 'corresponds to God's will', and the contrast with 'independent self-determination' is not his. His genuine claim that something is 'not a human performance but the act of God's Spirit' concerns the community's unity (p. 13) and joy (p. 14), not v. 18b.

scholarly_argument_dettwiler_moral_respo.description: Dettwiler reads 1 Th 5:12-22 as a conclusive exhortation to a very young community, exposed to outside pressure, spiritually inexperienced and deprived of its founder (p. 11). Ecclesial unity is experienced not only in prayer but 'perhaps above all' in concrete acts of mutual support and solidarity (v. 11, 13-14); the two perspectives do not exclude each other: 'religion and ethos are inseparable' (p. 13). Ethos is the grateful response to God's unconditional acceptance (p. 11).

evidence.quote: Le texte se présente pourtant bien comme une exhortation conclusive adressée à une toute jeune communauté, exposée à des répressions venant de l'extérieur, spirituellement encore inexpérimentée, orpheline de la présence physique de son maître à penser
evidence.citation: [Une exhortation de Paul aux Thessaloniciens,Priez sans cesse.md:113-121] (Dettwiler 2007, p. 11)

evidence.quote: Il est évident que ces deux perspectives ne s'excluent pas mutuellement, tout au contraire ! Religion et éthos sont indissociables.
evidence.citation: [Une exhortation de Paul aux Thessaloniciens,Priez sans cesse.md:220-223] (Dettwiler 2007, p. 13)

scholarly_argument_dettwiler_moral_respo.finding: First half is exact (conclusive exhortation to a very young, externally pressured community; concrete acts of support, p. 11 and p. 13). The tail 'rather than individual autonomous choice' is an imported contrast: Dettwiler's contrasts are 'performance humaine' vs 'agir de l'Esprit' and 'plan spirituel' vs 'actes de soutien concrets'; he adds 'Religion et éthos sont indissociables'. He never opposes communal ethics to individual choice.

scholarly_argument_dettwiler_freedom_in_.description: Dettwiler: the author of Colossians does not attack the adversaries directly nor dismantle their system; his aim is to 'immunise' the community against this alternative current by denouncing the judgmental spirit tied to its ascetic and ecstatic practices; his decisive weapon is christological (1,15-20): the community already shares fully in salvation, so adhering to another system would be anachronistic. The argumentative body (2,6-4,1) posits that the community already has access to the fullness of salvation (2,6-15) and needs no other doctrine of salvation (2,16-23).

evidence.quote: l'auteur de Col ne vise pas directement les adversaires et n'essaie pas de déconstruire leur système de pensée par une argumentation détaillée. Son but est plutôt d'immuniser la communauté colossienne contre ce courant alternatif
La partie la plus argumentative de l'écrit postule que la communauté destinataire a déjà accès à la plénitude du salut [2,6-15) et n'a donc pas besoin d'autres doctrines de salut [2,16-23).

scholarly_argument_dettwiler_freedom_in_.finding: Description is faithful but both sentences are on p. 893, not 892 (page_map: line 92 'immuniser' -> p. 893; line 109 'plénitude du salut' -> p. 893). The topic label 'ascetic determinism' is the KG's: Dettwiler speaks of 'une religiosité ascétique et extatique' and never of determinism.

scholarly_argument_dettwiler_human_agenc.description: On Col 1,1-8 Dettwiler notes that the author reworks the Pauline triad faith-love-hope by reading 'hope' no longer as a human disposition but as a transcendent good of salvation located 'in the heavens' (cf. Ph 3,20). The recipients are 'saints' not chiefly for their moral or religious qualities but because called by God and sanctified 'in' Christ; the author reminds them what their present religious identity is and how they reached it: by hearing the Gospel, received through Epaphras.

evidence.quote: « espérance » : l'auteur ne la conçoit plus comme une disposition humaine, mais comme un bien de salut transcendant qui se trouve « aux cieux » [voir Ph 3,20).
Les destinataires sont des « saints » non principalement à cause de leurs qualités morales ou religieuses, mais parce qu'ils ont été appelés par Dieu et sanctifiés « en » Christ.

scholarly_argument_dettwiler_human_agenc.finding: The reinterpretation of 'hope' is exact (p. 895; page_map line 172 -> 895) and identity reached 'dans l'écoute de l'Évangile' is there too. But 'rather than through ascetic self-determination' is not Dettwiler's contrast: on p. 895 the recipients are 'saints' not because of their moral or religious qualities but because called by God and sanctified in Christ. The asceticism theme belongs to the introduction (pp. 892-893), not to this comment on Col 1,1-8.

scholarly_argument_dodson_divine_causati.description: Orrey McFarland (ch. 6) argues that Paul, like Philo, can 'safely be placed' within the traditional use of 'prepositional metaphysics' (prepositions with technical meanings defining causation). Philo is the clear example: God is the first cause 'by which', the Logos the instrument 'through which'. Paul (Rom 11.36; 1 Cor 8.6) uses prepositions to distinguish God and Jesus in divine causation while identifying Jesus with God through reworked monotheistic formulas; Philo and Paul share the grammar but not identical views of causation. Human agency is not at issue.

evidence.quote: The argument is that while Philo and Paul both use prepositions differently, and have dissimilar views of causation, Philo’s use of prepositional metaphysics provides a way forward for placing Paul within the tradition of using prepositions with technical meanings for defining causation.
evidence.citation: [Dodson et Pitts - 2017 - Paul and the Greco-Roman philosophical tradition.md:826-830] (Pitts, Introduction, p. 7)

evidence.quote: for Paul, Jesus is the intermediary agent of divine causation – he would be the ‘instrument’ according to Philo – and yet he is also identified with God through Paul’s reworking of monotheistic formulas.
evidence.citation: [Dodson et Pitts - 2017 - Paul and the Greco-Roman philosophical tradition.md:7251-7253] (McFarland 2017, p. 132)

evidence.quote: Both Philo and Paul display forms of prepositional metaphysics that are influenced by multiple philosophical traditions, and yet each is able to use prepositions to define causation precisely as they intended to do.
evidence.citation: [Dodson et Pitts - 2017 - Paul and the Greco-Roman philosophical tradition.md:7199-7202] (McFarland 2017, p. 131)

scholarly_argument_dodson_divine_causati.finding: Hinted file (Paul and Seneca in Dialogue, Dodson/Briones, Brill) is a different volume; the right file is 'Dodson et Pitts - 2017 - Paul and the Greco-Roman philosophical tradition.md' (01_Philosophie_antique). McFarland's chapter (pp. 117-133) is about prepositions defining divine causation (Philo: God as first cause, Logos as instrument; Paul: Rom 11.36, 1 Cor 8.6, Christ as intermediary agent, God/Jesus distinction). The chapter contains no claim that divine causation 'does not eliminate human agency' or that 'human agency operates within divine causation'; every occurrence of 'agency' in it concerns the Logos/Christ as instrument. The KG invents the human-agency thesis.

scholarly_argument_dodson_stoic_fate_and.description: Several contributors treat Seneca's fate, fortune and providence as comparanda. Dodson (ch. 2) notes Seneca casts fate and fortune as 'terrorists in this age', whereas Paul never names them among his personified powers and draws on an apocalyptic tradition; yet 'Seneca and Paul both conclude that God's providence can be seen in creation' (pp. 50-51). Tabb (ch. 13) observes that Seneca views everything as determined by the divine will and urges embracing the decrees of Fate, while Acts 17 challenges and subverts the Stoic worldview (p. 275). Nygaard (ch. 12) touches on fate and freedom at p. 252.

evidence.quote: In addition to death, Seneca features fate and fortune as terrorists in this age.
evidence.citation: [Dodson et Pitts - 2017 - Paul and the Greco-Roman philosophical tradition.md:3004] (Dodson 2017, p. 50)

evidence.quote: Paul never names fate and fortune in his lists of personified powers. This shows that while the Stoic underlines the importance of pursuing philosophy whether life’s suffering is dictated by fate, sovereignty or chance (see Ep. 16.7–8), the apostle draws upon an apocalyptic tradition that encourages the saints to persevere despite the work of evil angels.
evidence.citation: [Dodson et Pitts - 2017 - Paul and the Greco-Roman philosophical tradition.md:3061-3066] (Dodson 2017, p. 51)

evidence.quote: As a Stoic, Seneca equates god with the material world’s efficient cause and thus views everything as determined by the divine will. Human beings should therefore willingly embrace the decrees of ‘Fate’ (Prov. 5.8)
evidence.citation: [Dodson et Pitts - 2017 - Paul and the Greco-Roman philosophical tradition.md:14388-14390] (Tabb 2017, p. 275)

scholarly_argument_dodson_stoic_fate_and.finding: Contributors do discuss Seneca's fate, fortune and providence (Dodson ch. 2, pp. 50-51; Nygaard ch. 12, p. 252; Tabb ch. 13, p. 275), but in Seneca's Latin terms, not the Greek 'heimarmene'/'pronoia' the node supplies, and none uses 'Stoic fatalism'. The contrasts are specific: Paul never names fate/fortune among his personified powers and draws on an apocalyptic tradition (Dodson); Seneca and Paul both see God's providence in creation (Dodson); Acts 17 subverts the Stoic worldview (Tabb). The flat 'distinguish Christian eschatological hope from Stoic fatalism' flattens these.

scholarly_argument_everson_ancient_vs_mo.description: Everson: twenty years earlier one could easily contrast ancient ethics (virtue and eudaimonia, the evaluation of a person's life as a whole, character) with modern moral philosophy (utilitarian vs deontological accounts of the right action). Because moral philosophy has since been deeply influenced by ancient writings, largely through a reaction against Humean assumptions about moral psychology, it has become harder to draw usefully broad distinctions between ancient and contemporary moral philosophy.

evidence.quote: No branch of philosophy has been more influenced by serious consideration of ancient writings in the past quarter of a century than has moral philosophy - or 'ethics', as it is often now called (a change in nomenclature which is itself a sign of that influence). This has made it more difficult to delineate helpful contrasts between ancient and modern moral philosophy.
evidence.citation: [[Companions to Ancient Thought] Stephen Everson (ed.) - Ethics (1998, Cambridge University Press).md:182-186] (Everson 1998, p. 1)

evidence.quote: whilst modern moral philosophers focused on the question of how to determine the right action in any given circumstance, the ancients were primarily concerned with issues of character and the evaluation of a person's life considered as a whole.
evidence.citation: [[Companions to Ancient Thought] Stephen Everson (ed.) - Ethics (1998, Cambridge University Press).md:199-202] (Everson 1998, p. 1)

scholarly_argument_everson_ancient_vs_mo.finding: The contrast (virtue/eudaimonia and the life as a whole vs determining the right action) is exact (p. 1). But Everson attributes the blurring to the influence of ancient writings on moral philosophy over the past quarter-century, itself driven by a reaction against Humean assumptions (p. 2); he does not speak of a 'revival of virtue ethics'.

scholarly_argument_fantino_determinism_v.description: Fantino: for Irenaeus the passage from the psychic to the spiritual condition (1 Cor 15,22 read through 15,44-46) is not the work of the human being but of the Creator (Haer 5,13,3), more precisely of the incarnate Word who gives the Holy Spirit. The gift of the Spirit, in turn, makes it possible to reject the desires of the flesh, or rather submission to them, a consequence of sin like death (Haer 5,12,3). Fantino does not describe a cooperative human agency.

evidence.quote: Ce passage n'est pas l'œuvre de l'être humain mais du Créateur (Haer 5,13,3), et plus précisément du Verbe incarné, le Christ Jésus, qui donne l'Esprit Saint aux hommes. Mais, le don de l'Esprit permet d'autre part de rejeter les convoitises, ou plus exactement la soumission aux convoitises, conséquence du péché, tout comme la mort.
evidence.citation: [Fantino - 1998 - The passage of the first Adam to the seconde Adam .md:191-195] (Fantino 1998, preprint p. 4; printed page unverified)

scholarly_argument_fantino_determinism_v.finding: First clause exact. But Fantino's second clause runs the other way: the gift of the Spirit is what makes it possible to reject the desires (or rather, submission to them); the 'yet humans must reject... and receive' plus 'cooperative but subordinate human agency' is the KG's gloss, not Fantino's. Printed pages unverifiable (preprint; passage at preprint p. 4).

scholarly_argument_fantino_free_will_and.description: Fantino reads Irenaeus's economy as a passage from the psychic condition of the first Adam to the spiritual condition of the second, accomplished by the incarnate Word who gives the Spirit; it is the Creator's work, not the human being's, and is determined by the incarnation, not by sin. Irenaeus's dissymmetry (Haer 5,12,2): turning to evil loses life, but doing good does not of itself give life; the Holy Spirit is needed in addition. Evil is 'second' and is used by God to bring the economy to completion.

evidence.quote: Le passage de la condition psychique à la condition spirituelle n'est pas déterminé par le péché, mais par l'incarnation du Fils de Dieu.
evidence.citation: [Fantino - 1998 - The passage of the first Adam to the seconde Adam .md:237-238] (Fantino 1998, preprint p. 6; printed page unverified)

evidence.quote: De même donc que celui qui avait été fait âme vivante, en inclinant vers le mal, a perdu la vie, ainsi ce même homme, en revenant au bien et en recevant l'Esprit vivifiant, retrouvera la vie (Haer 5,12,2).
evidence.citation: [Fantino - 1998 - The passage of the first Adam to the seconde Adam .md:140-143] (Fantino 1998, preprint p. 3; printed page unverified)

scholarly_argument_fantino_free_will_and.finding: 'Not achieved by human effort alone' softens Fantino's 'n'est pas l'œuvre de l'être humain mais du Créateur'; 'free will' and 'moral choices are real' are not his vocabulary. His frame is that the passage is determined by the incarnation, not by sin, and that evil is 'second' and used by God. The Haer 5,12,2 quotation does support the asymmetry (turning to evil loses life; returning to good and receiving the Spirit regains it). Printed pages unverifiable (preprint).

scholarly_argument_goodrich_identity_of_.description: Goodrich argues that echoes of LXX Isa 49-50 in Rom 7.14-25 evoke Israel's Babylonian captivity and the sin-exile-restoration paradigm, linking the allusions to Israel's early history (Sinai) in 7.7-13 to its later history in 7.14-25, so that the speaker's plight is analogous to Israel's deception, death and exile. He takes ἐγώ to stand 'first and foremost for Paul' (reconstructed autobiography) as 'a representative of Israel', and thereby for any person who encounters the law.

evidence.quote: ἐγώ, while standing first and foremost for Paul, represents any person who encounters the law and thus shares in Israel’s experience of deception, death, and exile begun at Sinai
recent studies have shown convincingly that Paul’s narrative functions as reconstructed autobiography
Largely assuming, based on other studies, that ἐγώ stands for unbelieving Paul as a representative of Israel

scholarly_argument_goodrich_identity_of_.finding: The 'analogous to Israel's experiences' and the Isaianic linkage are exact (abstract). But 'rather than individual moral autobiography' inverts Goodrich: he holds that the narrative 'functions as reconstructed autobiography', that ἐγώ stands 'first and foremost for Paul' / 'unbelieving Paul as a representative of Israel', and that it represents any person who encounters the law. Israel is the representative frame of Paul's own story, not an alternative to it.

scholarly_argument_haacker_relativizatio.description: Haacker: to support the thesis that God's word has not failed (Rom 9.6a), Paul first problematises the concept 'Israel' in 9.6b-13, relativising Israelite descent for participation in the history of election (only Isaac, only Jacob). This devaluation of physical descent recalls Philo's reflection 'on nobility' (Virt. 187-225), where descent from noble ancestors does not confer true nobility, only virtue does; Philo's passages have a different intention but a comparable structure of thought, with the closest contact in Virt. 207-210.

evidence.quote: unternimmt Paulus in einem ersten Argumentationsgang in Rom 9.6b-13 eine Problematisierung des Begriffs Israel
Diese Abwertung der physischen Abstammung erinnert an Ausfuhrungen bei Philo, die zwar eine andere Intention, aber doch eine vergleichbare Denkstruktur haben.

scholarly_argument_haacker_relativizatio.finding: The problematisation of 'Israel' in Rom 9.6b-13 is on p. 211; the Philonic parallel (De virtutibus 187-225) is on p. 212 and carries a qualification the node drops: Philo's passages have 'a different intention, but a comparable structure of thought'. Pages should be 211-212.

scholarly_argument_haacker_theodicy_and_.description: Haacker: whereas the rest of early Christianity explained the Jewish majority's rejection of the Jesus movement psychologically, judged it morally, or at most rationalised it as foretold in the OT, Paul in Rom 9-11 offers an interpretation of history that traces Israel's closure to the Christ message back to God's will and assigns it a positive meaning in God's plan. For Paul the Israel question is a question of theodicy: God himself is called into question by Israel's condition, because Israel is constituted by God's promises; hence the thesis of 9.6a that God's word has not failed.

evidence.quote: kommt Paulus in Rom 9-11 zu einer Geschichtsdeutung, die Israels Verschlossenheit fur die Christusbotschaft auf Gottes Willen zuriickfiihrt und ihr einen positiven Sinn und Zweck im Geschichtsplan Gottes beimiflt.
vor allem psychologisch erklarte und dabei moralisch bewertete oder allenfalls als im Alten Testament schon geweissagt zu rationalisieren suchte
Gott selbst ist durch das Erscheinungsbild Israels in Frage gestellt, weil Israel durch die ihm gegebenen VerheiBungen Gottes konstituiert wird.

scholarly_argument_haacker_theodicy_and_.finding: The core (Paul traces Israel's closure to God's will with a positive purpose; other early Christians explained it psychologically/morally) is exact, pp. 210-211, but Haacker names a third alternative (rationalised as foretold in the OT) and the theodicy question he identifies is whether God's word/promises have failed (Rom 9.6a; 3.1ff.), i.e. God's faithfulness, since Israel is constituted by God's promises. 'God's own responsibility' is the KG's reframing.

scholarly_argument_hayman_free_will_and_.description: Hayman: for the rabbis the source of evil in man is an impulse implanted at birth, the yetzer hara; by the second century man was pictured as a battlefield between the evil and the good inclination, the latter assisted by the Torah, created as the yetzer's 'antidote'. By keeping the commandments man can master his evil inclination, overcome his impulses to evil and so merit salvation; the Fall in no way affects man's ability to keep the Torah, which 'remains intact'.

evidence.quote: the source of evil in man derives from an impulse implanted in man at his birth and called the yetzer hara (the evil inclination).
By keeping the commandments of the Torah man can master his evil inclination, overcome his impulses to evil, and hence merit salvation.
the rabbis do not regard the Fall as in any way affecting man's ability to keep the Torah; that remains intact.

scholarly_argument_hayman_free_will_and_.finding: Substance is right (pp. 462-463) but the vocabulary is imported: Hayman never writes 'free will' or 'morally responsible' (rg finds neither); his terms are an impulse 'implanted in man at his birth', man 'can master his evil inclination', 'ability to keep the Torah; that remains intact', 'merit salvation'. Pages 462-463 rather than 461-464.

scholarly_argument_hyatt_divine_determin.description: Hyatt: the author of the Hodayot claims to have received a revelation of secrets from God (p. 277; 'These things I knew from thy understanding, for thou didst reveal to me wondrous secrets', 35.21). On the origin of man's frailty and sin the Hodayot are clear: God created man and predestined every man for good or evil; man is completely dependent on God ('nothing is known without thy will'), a 'strong sense of determinism' shared with the Serek's doctrine of the two spirits (pp. 280-283).

evidence.quote: The author of the Hodayot claims that he has received a revelation of secrets from God (35. 21; 38. 27-8; 41. 26-7; 45. 4; 48. 12-13; cf. 1 QpHab vii. 4-5).
God has created man, and has predestined every man for evil or for good, for destruction or for salvation; and man as a creature is completely dependent upon God.
The author has a strong sense of determinism, such as is found in Serek and other documents of Qumran, and in Josephus's description of the Essenes

scholarly_argument_hyatt_divine_determin.finding: Hyatt does report the revelation claim (p. 277) and the opening quotation (p. 278), and he does speak of a 'strong sense of determinism' and man's complete dependence on God, but he grounds these in the predestination and two-spirits passages (1QH 35.7-8, 37.22-3, 49.17-18; 1QS iii-iv) on pp. 280-283, not in the revelation motif. The node's inference from revelation to determinism is its own; the pages should extend to 280-283.

scholarly_argument_hyatt_suffering_and_d.description: Hyatt: the author of the Hodayot, probably the Teacher of Righteousness, experienced much suffering and sorrow, out of which God rescued him, 'though it was God Himself who sent the suffering upon him as discipline'. The suffering came through false teachers, friends and sect members who slandered him, and exile; he wrote the Hodayot to express gratitude for deliverance. Hyatt draws no inference here about divine ordination versus human choice.

evidence.quote: Yet, the author has experienced much suffering and sorrow, out of which God has rescued him, though it was God Himself who sent the suffering upon him as discipline. Among his enemies are false teachers
The author met opposition even from his friends and members of the sect, who slandered him to his enemies (39. 22-5), and he was taken into Egypt (39. 29; cf. 39. 5).

scholarly_argument_hyatt_suffering_and_d.finding: First sentence exact (p. 277). The second ('affliction divinely ordained rather than resulting from free human choices') is not drawn by Hyatt: in the same paragraph he lists the human agents of the suffering (false teachers, friends who slandered him, exile), and in n. 1 p. 283 he observes that the Covenanters did not see the contradiction between their determinism and their voluntarism.

scholarly_argument_laato_free_will_defen.description: In their introduction Laato and de Moor quote, without further comment, a closing note of J. L. Crenshaw's ABD article: modern calamities (Lisbon, the Holocaust) have raised theodicy 'to new heights', and 'traditional free-will defences have lost their power, partly because they are ahistorical, overly abstract, and rationalistic'. The judgment is Crenshaw's; the editors neither endorse nor reject it explicitly.

evidence.quote: At the end of his article there is a note that
evidence.citation: (Laato & de Moor 2003, p. vii) [Antti Laato, Johannes C. De Moor - Theodicy in the World of the Bible-Brill Academic Publishers (2003).md:130]

evidence.quote: Traditional free-will defences have lost their power, partly because they are ahistorical, overly abstract, and rationalistic.
evidence.citation: (Laato & de Moor 2003, p. vii) [Antti Laato, Johannes C. De Moor - Theodicy in the World of the Bible-Brill Academic Publishers (2003).md:134-136]

scholarly_argument_laato_free_will_defen.finding: The sentence is Crenshaw's (AncBD 6.447), quoted by the editors as 'a note' at the end of his article. The editors do not say they cite it 'approvingly'; they quote it without comment and move on to the existential crisis of unjust suffering. 'Approvingly' is an inference. Page vii confirmed (page map conf 0.90).

scholarly_argument_nystr_m_free_will_and.description: Nyström's book is a study of the literary and apologetic strategies of Justin's Apology, not of free will. It nonetheless addresses the theme directly in passing: Justin's 'focus on individuality and personal commitment' is the backdrop to his 'strong emphasis on free will over fatalism' (1 Apol. 43), the Stoic Fate governing choices being intolerable to him because it removes responsibility; 'free moral choices' are 'absolutely fundamental' to his gospel and to his construction of Christian identity (p. 51; cf. n. 90).

evidence.quote: The idea of free moral choices is absolutely fundamental to Justin’s presentation of the gospel and of salvation, and it is also intrinsic to his construction of Christian identity
In his polemic against Stoicism, Justin argues that free will and the capability to vice and virtue is fundamental to what it means to be human (cf. 2:6(7):4–7).

scholarly_argument_nystr_m_free_will_and.finding: Free will is not a central theme, true; but the node's 'does not directly address free will' is too strong. Nyström devotes a paragraph (p. 51, running header) to Justin's 'strong emphasis on free will over fatalism' (1 Apol. 43; 28:4; 43:6; 2 Apol. 7[6]:9), calling free moral choice 'absolutely fundamental' to Justin's gospel and identity construction, and n. 90 (ch. 3) repeats that free will is 'fundamental to what it means to be human'.

scholarly_argument_nystr_m_justin_martyr.description: Nyström analyses the function, not the content, of Justin's Logos doctrine. Its first and simplest use is to establish Christianity as 'a rational and sound faith' by identifying reason with Christ (p. 85). Its most important use answers the charge of newness: Christian doctrine equals what has been recognized as wise 'in all ages' through 'the partly innate Logos', so it is relevant to everyone and the wicked, who 'have chosen' to live without reason, are 'without excuse' (pp. 88-89).

evidence.quote: It is not part of our purpose to reconstruct Justin’s thought on the Logos, and nor shall we try to determine its primary philosophical sources.
Christianity is the true, universal wisdom, which every wise person in history has recognized and expressed, through the partly innate Logos. Therefore, foolish and wicked people are without excuse.

scholarly_argument_nystr_m_justin_martyr.finding: Nyström's frame is functional, not doctrinal: he declines to reconstruct Justin's Logos theology and studies four 'uses' of the doctrine in the argument; the first (p. 85) is to make Christianity 'a rational and sound faith'. Universality is treated under the argument from antiquity (pp. 88-89): every wise person recognized the truth 'through the partly innate Logos', so the wicked 'are without excuse' — they 'have chosen'. 'Sown in all humans' is not Nyström's phrasing. Pages from running headers (page_map AUDIT-FAIL, 4 low).

scholarly_argument_olive_translation_and.description: Olive reports Frede's suggestion that aition/aitia were perhaps wrongly translated 'cause', grants this 'option radicale' the merit of dissolving some pseudo-problems (e.g. final causes), but holds that a 'strictly lexicological' approach cannot suffice: translating aition as 'responsable' or 'ce pourquoi' yields meaningless statements. Cause must be studied as an 'opérateur intellectuel' in authors' reasoning. Frede's thesis then meets 'une difficulté de taille': the ancients did know the notion of productive cause.

scholarly_argument_olive_translation_and.finding: Correct in outline, but drops two qualifications: Olive first grants Frede's 'option radicale' a merit (it exposes ill-founded interpretive difficulties such as final causes), and his decisive objection is substantive, not only methodological — the ancients 'semblent n'avoir ignoré ni la notion de cause productrice'. Pages 2-3 confirmed from footers.

scholarly_argument_pironet_freedom_and_i.description: Reporting the post-Davidson debate, Pironet and Tappolet note that most now hold 'strict akrasia' (Mele) possible: the agent judges y better than x, is or believes himself free and able to do y, yet does x 'librement et intentionnellement'. Postulating that the akratic act is free distinguishes it from compulsive acts and admits that one can freely choose an action judged inferior. They add that some (Watson) reject this consensus precisely because they deny one can freely choose the worse option.

The node presents as the authors' thesis what they report as the general view ('on considère en général', 'la plupart acceptent') and drops their caveat that 'certains rejettent ce consensus' (Watson) on the ground that one cannot freely choose the action judged worse.

scholarly_argument_pouderon_determinism_.description: Pouderon's back-cover presentation says the apologists, besides defending Christians against pagan accusations and building 'un premier pont' between pagan philosophy and Christianity, fought closer adversaries: the gnostics, who 'au nom d'une interprétation supérieure des Écritures' distinguished the transcendent God from the creator Demiurge, denied the humanity of Christ and rejected the resurrection of the flesh; and the Jews, who refused to see in Jesus the promised Messiah. No claim about determinism, fate or human freedom is made.

scholarly_argument_pouderon_determinism_.finding: The source lines (35-38) are the back-cover blurb (line 47 = barcode '9 782204 07', price '35 €'), not an introduction at pp. 7-9. The blurb lists three gnostic theses (transcendent God vs Demiurge, denial of Christ's humanity, rejection of resurrection of the flesh) and says nothing about determinism, fatalism, predestination or human freedom. rg for déterminis|fatalis|prédestin|libre arbitre returns no such claim anywhere in the file (only incidental doctrinal summaries, ll. 3565, 3705). 'Gnostic determinism' and 'defended human freedom against pagan fatalism' are inventions.

scholarly_argument_pouderon_human_choice.description: Pouderon's back-cover text: under sporadic persecution tolerated by the Antonines, the apologists 'ont pris la plume', some addressing the emperors directly, others the pagan public, to defend their co-religionists against accusations (ritual cannibalism, incest, 'atheism') and to present and justify their way of life and doctrine 'd'une manière rationnelle, acceptable par les lettrés de l'époque'. Pouderon draws no conclusion about the addressees' capacity for free choice.

evidence.citation: [Bernard Pouderon - Les Apologistes grecs du IIe siècle.md:21-23] (back cover, unpaginated)

scholarly_argument_pouderon_human_choice.finding: Only the quoted clause exists, and it is from the back-cover blurb (not 'préface p. 9'). Everything after it — 'implying that rulers and individuals could make rational choices', 'presupposed that hearers had the capacity to evaluate and freely accept or reject' — is the KG's inference, nowhere stated by Pouderon. The blurb's own point is that the apologists wrote to defend Christians against accusations and to present their doctrine 'd'une manière rationnelle, acceptable par les lettrés'.

scholarly_argument_prigent_determinism_a.description: In the midrashic chapters Prigent finds signs that Barnabas depends closely on earlier Judaeo-Christian traditions which he adapts, 'parfois bien maladroitement', to his project; their theology differs in accent from the message of the Testimonia, the judgment on Israel's history being 'infiniment moins négatif'. Small traditional blocks remain visible, such as the apocalyptic fragment of ch. 4 whose explanation the author no longer seems to know, and a reference to an Enochic tradition. Prigent makes no claim about determinism or predestination.

scholarly_argument_prigent_determinism_a.finding: Prigent says nothing about determinism, Israel's fate being fixed, or an elect community. In the passage (ll. 178-190) he observes that the midrashic chapters rest on prior Judaeo-Christian traditions whose theology differs in accent from the Testimonia — notably the judgment on Israel's history is 'infiniment moins négatif' — and that small traditional blocks survive, e.g. the apocalyptic piece of ch. 4 whose explanation the author 'ne semble plus connaître', and a reference to an Enochic tradition. The node's quotation is a garbled mistranslation of that sentence. [OCR-degraded], no page.

scholarly_argument_prigent_free_will_and.description: Prigent: with 18,1 Barnabas consciously changes genre — no longer Testimonia or liturgical traditions but 'la morale concrète'; ch. 18 lays the theological foundation and chs. 19-20 list precise commandments and prohibitions as a double instruction prescribing the way of light and proscribing the way of darkness. Scholars now agree that Barnabas here 'a plus que littéralement copié' a Jewish moral manual circulating in early Christianity, the Duae Viae, appended as conclusion (parallels: Didache 1-6, Doctrina, 1QS 3,13-4,26).

But 'involves genuine human choice between morally opposed paths' is not stated by him — he describes 'une double instruction' prescribing actions of the way of light and proscribing those of darkness — and the node omits his central thesis: Barnabas 'a plus que littéralement copié un manuel de morale d'origine juive', the Duae Viae, added 'en guise de conclusion', paralleled in Didache, Doctrina, Qumran 1QS 3-4. [OCR-degraded], no page.

scholarly_argument_velardo_stoic_influen.description: Velardo states that Josephus's expression is characteristic of the literature of his time and reports ('se discurre que') that εἱμαρμένην belonged to Stoic phraseology as a terminus technicus evoking 'destino', citing Chrysippus's definition of fate as an eternal, immutable chain (pp. 129-130). In his survey he also records dissenting positions: Maier denies any relation to Stoic doctrine, Pines holds the term belonged to the general philosophical lexicon rather than to Stoicism (p. 132). Velardo's own conclusion is that the 'original' Stoic sense prevailed (p. 136).

evidence.quote: La expresión que emplea Josefo es propia de la literatura de la época.6 Se discurre que εἱμαρμένην formaba parte de la fraseología estoica como un ter-
εἱμαρμένην -junto a otros vocablos griegos-, no era un término propio del estoicismo; antes bien, pertenecía al léxico filosófico general.

scholarly_argument_velardo_stoic_influen.finding: The claim is hedged in the source ('Se discurre que …', with a footnote to Long 1971) and is a reported view, not Velardo's flat assertion; Chrysippus's definition runs over pp. 129-130 (quoted via Aulus Gellius). Velardo later reports Pines (p. 132) holding that εἱμαρμένην was not a properly Stoic term but general philosophical lexicon, and Maier denying any relation to Stoic doctrine — qualifications the node drops. Page 129 correct for the hedge; definition continues on 130.

scholarly_argument_wolter_faith_as_human.description: Wolter treats πίστις as the addressees' agreement with the proclaimed gospel — the response the message is designed to find (p. 71). On whether faith is a free 'decision' or a 'gift' given in a 'predestinarian' way, he holds that the problem lies with Paul's interpreters, not with Paul: Paul 'nowhere made the question about the origin of faith a topic of discussion', a gap exegetes fill with their own systems (pp. 78-79).

evidence.quote: Paul calls this response on the side of the address-
evidence.citation: (Wolter 2015, p. 71) [Michael Wolter - Paul_ An Outline of His Theology (2015, Baylor University Press) - libgen.lc.md:3445]

evidence.quote: it becomes clear that in this case the problem is not in Paul but in Paul’s interpreters. Paul himself nowhere made the question about the origin of faith a topic of discussion.
evidence.citation: (Wolter 2015, p. 78) [Michael Wolter - Paul_ An Outline of His Theology (2015, Baylor University Press) - libgen.lc.md:3806-3808]

scholarly_argument_wolter_faith_as_human.finding: §9 does define faith as the addressees' 'agreement with the gospel' (p. 71). But on the origin of faith Wolter's position is sharper than 'resists simple categorization': after listing the interpreters' alternatives (free decision of the will vs 'predestinarian' answer; Bultmann, Hofius, Friedrich, Eichholz), he rules that 'the problem is not in Paul but in Paul's interpreters', since 'Paul himself nowhere made the question about the origin of faith a topic of discussion' (pp. 78-79, running headers 77/79). The node turns Paul's silence into a Pauline 'complex interplay'.

scholarly_argument_wolter_free_will_and_.description: In §51 Wolter argues that Romans 9-11 ends in a 'theological aporia': Paul cannot reconcile 'gospel' and 'election'. He holds both that 'there is no distinction' between Israel and the nations, all being justified solely through Christ-faith, and (Rom 11:25-29) that Israel keeps its elected special place; in 11:25-27 he must resort to apocalyptic revelation. Paul has not resolved the problem of Israel; the tension separates 'the Jewish Paul from the Christian Paul' and is 'insurmountable' (pp. 413-422).

evidence.quote: Thus Paul has not resolved the problem of Israel in Romans. Rather, the consideration concerning Israel has led him to an aporia.
evidence.citation: (Wolter 2015, p. 421) [Michael Wolter - Paul_ An Outline of His Theology (2015, Baylor University Press) - libgen.lc.md:20063-20064]

evidence.quote: Paul wishes to take seriously two theological tenets that exclude each other. On the one hand stands the tenet formulated identically in two places in Romans: “There is no distinction” (3:22; 10:12).
evidence.citation: (Wolter 2015, p. 422) [Michael Wolter - Paul_ An Outline of His Theology (2015, Baylor University Press) - libgen.lc.md:20117-20119]

scholarly_argument_wolter_free_will_and_.finding: Wolter's 'aporia' (§51, pp. 413-422) is not about divine initiative vs human response or determinism vs freedom. It is the contradiction between two tenets Paul wants to hold: 'there is no distinction' between Israel and the nations (Rom 3:22; 10:12) and Israel's abiding election and special place (Rom 11:25-29). Paul 'has not resolved the problem of Israel'; the tension 'separates the Jewish Paul from the Christian Paul' and is 'insurmountable'. 'Deterministic or libertarian framework' is imported vocabulary Wolter never uses.

scholarly_argument_wolter_gospel_as_divi.description: Wolter: the gospel is 'God's gospel' and 'Christ's gospel' by its content, independent 'of the person of its preacher' (p. 59). Heard as God's word, it does what God's word always does — it has an effect. 'It is first of all faith that causes the gospel to become the "power of God for salvation"' (Rom 1:16); unbelief gains no part in its efficacy, and Paul speaks of the gospel as 'power' only on the side of faith and salvation, never as directly working perdition (pp. 67-68).

evidence.quote: Thus it is first of all faith that causes the gospel to become the “power of God for salvation” and unleashes its salv-
evidence.citation: (Wolter 2015, p. 67) [Michael Wolter - Paul_ An Outline of His Theology (2015, Baylor University Press) - libgen.lc.md:3377-3378]

evidence.quote: “Christ’s gospel” is in principle independent of the person of its preacher.
evidence.citation: (Wolter 2015, p. 59) [Michael Wolter - Paul_ An Outline of His Theology (2015, Baylor University Press) - libgen.lc.md:2932]

scholarly_argument_wolter_gospel_as_divi.finding: Wolter does not say the gospel's effectiveness is 'not dependent on human will or effort'. His claim in §8 is the reverse emphasis: 'it is first of all faith that causes the gospel to become the "power of God for salvation" and unleashes its salvific efficacy' (pp. 67-68); the gospel is 'power of God' on the basis of its content, and 'Christ's gospel' is 'in principle independent of the person of its preacher' (p. 59) — a different point from human will. rg for 'human will/effort' finds nothing in §7-8.

scholarly_argument_zetterholm_jewishness.description: Zetterholm, reviewing Ehrensperger (2004), reports her point that the traditional image of Paul 'has made him the chief model for the irreconcilable contradiction between Judaism and Christianity', so that the debate about Paul is 'basically a debate about Christian identity'; feminist interpretations, post-Shoah perspectives and studies of Paul's Jewishness have challenged this dominant discourse. Zetterholm's own reservation (p. 256) is that her Paul is 'perhaps too idealistic'.

evidence.quote: Ehrensperger points out that the image of Paul has far-reaching consequences since the traditional view of Paul has made him the chief model for the irreconcilable contradiction between Judaism and Christianity.
evidence.citation: (Zetterholm 2004, p. 254) [[Journal of Beliefs & Values 2004-aug vol. 25 iss. 2] Zetterholm, Magnus - A feminist Paul_ A hermeneutical experiment of combining recent Pauline studies with feminist perspectives (2004) [10.1080_1361767042000294035] - libgen.li.md:749-752]

scholarly_argument_zetterholm_jewishness.finding: The text is a review article of Kathy Ehrensperger's That We May Be Mutually Encouraged. The claim (traditional Paul as 'chief model for the irreconcilable contradiction between Judaism and Christianity', hence a debate about Christian identity) is introduced by 'Ehrensperger points out'; the challenge by feminist, post-Shoah and Jewishness-of-Paul studies is likewise Zetterholm's summary of her chapter 1. The node label presents it as Zetterholm's own observation. Page 254 correct (running header line 740).

scholarly_argument_gerson_plotinus_s_phi.description: The publisher's blurb (unsigned front matter) calls Plotinus 'the greatest philosopher in the 700-year period between Aristotle and Augustine' who produced 'a reinvigorated version of Platonism' later called 'Neoplatonism', and says the essays show 'how he was a founder of medieval philosophy'. Gerson's own Introduction is more guarded: Plotinus is 'probably the dominant philosopher' of that period. Neither text mentions voluntarism or free will as foundational.

He thought of himself as a disciple of Plato, but in his efforts to defend Platonism against Aristotelians, Stoics, and others, he actually pro- duced a reinvigorated version of Platonism that later came to be known as "Neoplatonism."

Gerson's own Introduction hedges: Plotinus 'is probably the dominant philosopher in the 700-year period'. 'Voluntarism' appears nowhere in the blurb or the Introduction; the blurb says the contributors show 'how he was a founder of medieval philosophy'.

scholarly_argument_tomberlin_divine_omni.description: Tomberlin and McGuinness set out an objection to the free will defence: if God is omniscient he knows, for any free possible person, whether that person would, if created, perform morally evil actions; with omnipotence and wholly-goodness this yields that no free person created by God performs moral evil. They defend the objection against Plantinga but concede at the end that its success turns on premise (19), i.e. on whether free will is compatible with causality; they themselves opt for (19)'s truth.

evidence.quote: It is equally true, so the objection continues, that if God is omniscient, then he knows, for every free person, whether or not this person would, if created, perform morally evil actions. Put in a nutshell, then, if God is omniscient, omnipotent, and wholly good, surely it follows that no free person created by God performs morally evil actions.
if (19) is true, the free will defence fails and (1) is not consistent with (3); but if (19) is false, the free will defence succeeds and (1) is consistent with (3).

scholarly_argument_tomberlin_divine_omni.finding: The omniscience premise and the entailment 'no free person created by God performs morally evil actions' are premises (5)-(6) of 'the objection' the authors set out on p. 456 and then defend against Plantinga. But their conclusion (pp. 474-475) makes the entailment hinge on premise (19), i.e. on 'whether or not free will is compatible with causality', which they treat as a 'basic opinion'; they 'would select the first' option. The node states as flat entailment what the authors present as conditional on (19).

scholarly_argument_bird_paul_s_view_of_s.description: Bird's Introduction summarises Schreiner's Reformed reading: Paul identifies salvation as deliverance from the consequences of sin, 'divine vengeance and eternal destruction'; sinners are saved by God's gracious mercy shown on the cross, not by merit, through Jesus' substitutionary death. In his own essay Schreiner adds that election secures but does not make unnecessary human repentance and faith, and that Paul teaches both divine sovereignty and human responsibility without a philosophical defence of their correlation.

evidence.quote: Concerning Paul’s view of salvation, in Schreiner’s estimation, Paul identifies salvation as deliverance from the consequences of sin, namely, divine vengeance and eternal destruction.
evidence.citation: [03_Paul/Four views on the Apostle Paul, Bird, Michael F._ the Apostle Saint. Paul_ apostel helgon Paulus_ Schreiner, Thomas R. (2012, Zondervan).md:154-155] (Bird, Introduction)

scholarly_argument_bird_paul_s_view_of_s.finding: The quoted phrase 'divine vengeance and eternal destruction' is Bird's editorial summary of Schreiner in the Introduction (l. 155), not Schreiner's essay as verified_reference claims. Schreiner's own essay adds a qualification the node drops: election 'does not make such a response unnecessary'; humans must repent and believe; Paul 'clearly teaches both' sovereignty and responsibility (Rom 9-11). No page markers in the .md and page_map confidence <0.90, so no printed page is given.

Its Introduction nonetheless registers 'affirmation du libre arbitre' as one of the recurrent, under-studied concerns of the Dialogue tied to divine judgement, inheritance and conversion (p. 39), and reads Dial. 88,5 on free will as a notation that may address gnostics indirectly, without requiring Prigent's hypothesis of insertions from the lost Syntagma (p. 154 n. 116).

scholarly_argument_coppins_pauline_freed.description: Coppins examines how freedom in Paul's letters has been interpreted in the 'German' tradition, with Luther's The Freedom of a Christian as a key reference point; he sets two aims — an English monograph on the Pauline freedom word group, and critical and constructive engagement with 'German' scholarship on freedom.

evidence.quote: Secondly, since the topic of freedom has been pursued with unrivaled vigor in the ‘German’ tradition, there is need for an English work on the topic that gives particular attention to this rich tradition of interpretation.
### 1.3 Martin Luther and The Freedom of a Christian

scholarly_argument_dettwiler_free_will_a.description: Dettwiler treats vv. 12c-13 as the evangelist's exegetical comments on 12ab. Theologically, 12c makes reception of the Logos explicit as believing in his name, showing the evangelist's early interest in faith; v. 13 adds that becoming children of God is possible only through God's own action, believers having their origin in God and not in a purely human sphere — a double explanation that anticipates the second-birth theme of ch. 3. He does not phrase this as divine generation versus human decision.

evidence.quote: Les vv. 12c 13 et 13. Beaucoup d'exégètes les considèrent comme des com- mentaires de 12ab (12c expliciterait 12a, 13 expliciterait 12b).

Le v. 13 est une deuxième explication exégétique, qui précise que « deve- nir enfants de Dieu» (12b) n'est possible que par l'action de Dieu lui-même. Les enfants de Dieu, c'est-à-dire les croyants, ont leur origine en Dieu et non en une sphère purement humaine

scholarly_argument_dettwiler_free_will_a.finding: Dettwiler does classify vv. 12c.13 as the evangelist's 'réflexions exégétiques' commenting 12ab (p. 187) and, in the theological section, says v. 13 states that becoming children of God 'n'est possible que par l'action de Dieu lui-même' — believers 'ont leur origine en Dieu et non en une sphère purement humaine' (p. 195). But he foregrounds v. 12c as the evangelist's interest in faith ('croire en son nom'), not an opposition between divine generation and human decision; the node's 'determined by divine generation, not human decision' is its own gloss. The Greek in the node is not in Dettwiler's file (its Greek is OCR-garbled); NA28 text should be cited from 03_Sources_critiques. page_map confidence for this file is 0.50; pages read from running folios.

scholarly_argument_dettwiler_free_will_a.description: Dettwiler reads Rom 6,1-14 as witnessing Paul's conviction of a profound religious transformation of the human being through baptism understood as an initiation rite (van Gennep/Turner), with a complex temporality he examines against Käsemann's 'eschatological reserve'. He cites Vollenweider's description of Rom 6 as the difference between two lordships marked by a death boundary, but warns that lordship-change language suggests a static anthropology: the new life under Christ is of another nature, essentially qualified by liberty.

evidence.quote: la conviction pauli- nienne d’une profonde transformation religieuse de l’être humain par l’acte du baptême, compris comme rite d’initiation.
4. VOLLENWEIDER, Freiheit als neue Schöpfung (n. 2), p. 324: «Thema [i.e. de Rm 6] ist die durch eine Todesgrenze markierte Differenz zweier Herrschaften».
Or, la vie sous la seigneurie du Christ est, selon Paul, d’une tout autre nature que celle sous la domination du péché, car la nouvelle vie du croyant est essentiellement qualifiée par la liberté.

scholarly_argument_dettwiler_free_will_a.finding: The 'profound religious transformation... initiation rite... complex temporality' claim is Dettwiler's (p. 273). But the 'death boundary' (Todesgrenze) is Vollenweider's formulation, quoted by Dettwiler in n. 4 (p. 275: 'Thema ist die durch eine Todesgrenze markierte Differenz zweier Herrschaften'), not Dettwiler's own. Dettwiler also flags the limits of 'changement de seigneurie' language: life under Christ's lordship is 'd'une tout autre nature', qualified by liberty (pp. 288-289). Running folios give 273 ff. (agentic_search: l. 190 -> p. 275).

scholarly_argument_oropeza_free_will_vs_.description: Oropeza notes that Rom 9-11 has been used to support 'everything from fatalism to the free will, divine foreknowledge to double predestination' (p. 57) and reads the chapters as a theodicy of God's faithfulness to Israel (p. 58). He then argues that the Jacob/Esau and Pharaoh sections concern corporate election, not individual predestination or eternal destinies (p. 63), that double predestination as a fixed state in ch. 9 would contradict the openness of ch. 11 (p. 75), and that it cannot explain Paul's anguish over Israel (p. 78 n. 66).

evidence.quote: This sec- tion does not address predestination; neither Paul nor his immediate sources speak to the eternal destinies of the historical persons he mentions. Paul focuses on election instead of predestination, and his emphasis rests on corporate rather than individual election.
evidence.citation: [02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/OROPEZA - 2007 - Paul and Theodicy Intertextual Thoughts on God's Justice and Faithfulness to Israel in Romans 9–11.md:331-335] (p. 63)

evidence.quote: If Paul were teaching double predestination as a permanent or fixed state in ch. 9, this could hardly be the case in ch. 11 without contradicting himself.
evidence.citation: [02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/OROPEZA - 2007 - Paul and Theodicy Intertextual Thoughts on God's Justice and Faithfulness to Israel in Romans 9–11.md:970-971] (p. 75)

evidence.quote: Romans 9–11 can be understood, then, as a theodicy focusing on the question of God’s faithfulness to the people of Israel.
evidence.citation: [02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/OROPEZA - 2007 - Paul and Theodicy Intertextual Thoughts on God's Justice and Faithfulness to Israel in Romans 9–11.md:66-67] (p. 58)

scholarly_argument_oropeza_free_will_vs_.finding: p. 57 does survey the range 'from fatalism to the free will' and p. 58 frames Rom 9-11 as a theodicy of God's faithfulness. But Oropeza does take positions the node denies: the Jacob/Esau section 'does not address predestination'; Paul 'focuses on election instead of predestination', corporate rather than individual (p. 63); teaching double predestination as 'a permanent or fixed state' in ch. 9 would contradict ch. 11 (p. 75); double predestination cannot account for Paul's anguish (p. 78 n. 66). 'Does not take a definitive stance' is false.

scholarly_argument_richardson_free_will_.description: Richardson's Early Christian Fathers (LCC 1) is a source collection with translations; his general Introduction (pp. 15-27) treats the history and classification of the 'Apostolic Fathers' corpus (Cotelier, Gallandi, the 1873 Didache discovery), not free will. The section introductions do contain theological judgements: Edward Rochie Hardy's introduction to Justin states that Justin 'formally' presents 'a simple doctrine of free will' while recognising that understanding God's truth comes only by God's gift (p. 236).

evidence.quote: Formally Justin presents a simple doctrine of free will which would suggest that the only salvation man would need is information, and the removal of the obstacles interposed by the demons. But as incidental references show, he is well enough aware that it is only by the gift of God that men are able to understand his truth.
evidence.citation: [06_Patristique/(The Library of Christian Classics) Cyril C. Richardson - Early Christian Fathers-Westminster Press (2006).md:9655-9660] (p. 236, section by E. R. Hardy)

evidence.quote: and Translated by Edward Rochie Hardy)
evidence.citation: [06_Patristique/(The Library of Christian Classics) Cyril C. Richardson - Early Christian Fathers-Westminster Press (2006).md:286]

scholarly_argument_richardson_free_will_.finding: Richardson's general Introduction (pp. 15-27: Cotelier, Gallandi, Byrennios 1873) is literary-historical, as stated. But the volume's section introductions do take positions on free will: the Justin section, edited and translated by Edward Rochie Hardy (not Richardson), says Justin 'presents a simple doctrine of free will' yet knows 'it is only by the gift of God that men are able to understand his truth' (p. 236); the index has 'Free will, 259, 327; and destiny, 269 f.' The node's blanket 'no philosophical or theological analysis' is too strong and would misattribute Hardy's judgement if extended to Richardson.

scholarly_argument_rousseau_editorial_me.description: SC 100 tome I is the introduction and apparatus volume for Irenaeus, Adversus haereses IV. Its Avant-propos recounts the edition's history (Sagnard's Book III, his death in 1957, the new team of Rousseau, Hemmerdinger, Mercier and Doutreleau); its Introduction studies the Latin translation, the Greek fragments and the Armenian and Syriac traditions as witnesses for establishing the text of Book IV as a whole. It does not present the edition as aimed at Irenaeus's teaching on human freedom.

scholarly_argument_rousseau_editorial_me.finding: The Avant-propos (OCR-degraded but legible) is the history of the edition: Sagnard's Book III (1952), his death in October 1957 while preparing Book IV, and the new team (Hemmerdinger, Mercier, Doutreleau). The Armenian and Syriac witnesses are handled in the Introduction ('Les traditions arménienne et syriaque', p. 95) as general text-critical work on the Latin translation. Nothing frames the edition as recovering Irenaeus's 'formulations on human freedom and divine justice'; rg -i 'libre arbitre|liberté' returns no hit in tome I. That purpose is the node's invention.

scholarly_argument_sagnard_free_will_and.description: Sagnard's Introduction to SC 34 (Book III) treats Irenaeus and martyrdom, the plan and sources of Book III, and Irenaeus's vocabulary of newness — a 'new economy of liberty' opened by the coming of the Son — and the Eve/Mary recapitulation. It contains no exposition of free will, of a created capacity for obedience and disobedience, or of freedom as the pivot of the anti-gnostic polemic; those themes belong to Book IV (SC 100).

scholarly_argument_sagnard_free_will_and.finding: Searched the SC 34 file (Avant-propos, Introduction, l. 66-2100) for 'libre arbitre', 'liberté', 'libre', 'obéiss', 'désobéiss', 'responsab', 'déterminis'. No passage presents Irenaeus as holding that humans were created with a capacity for obedience and disobedience, nor ties freedom to an anti-gnostic polemic against deterministic systems. 'Liberté' occurs only as Irenaeus's theme of the new economy of liberty (Introduction, p. 34-35 by folio), and obedience/disobedience only in the Eve/Mary recapitulation (p. 36). The node's own reference concedes the locus is AH IV.37-39 (SC 100), not Book III.
